THE DREAMS OF YOUTH. The dreams of youth may fade away. As flowers that early bloom. Like frosty winds deceit and wrong May bring, alas their doom. Yet other flowers will blooming grow. When winter's cold is o'er; And other men more blest will be For noble lives before. How many buds that cheer the earth In Bature's course must die Before the rove, in beauty's pride, Pertumes the sunny sky. Bo dreams of youth shall spring again; When vice shall not destroy The hopes of happiness ani love, Of friendship, truth, and joy. Methinks beyond this fleeting life, Uncertain, mixed with care. The dreams of youth may sh olow forth A world more bleat and fair. Warrington, January, 1881.
B. KENTON.

BEAUTY. What is beauty ? Full many a poet Has striven in burning words to show it; Many a soul hath in vain longed to know it. 'Tis a beautiful face, be it dark or fair, Though it be furrowed with grief and care, Yet bath whole-souled honesty printed there. Beautiful is the hair, though gray and worn, Which speaketh of sorrow cheerfully borne, Whose silvery locks 'tis a sin to scorn. Beautiful eyes are they that shine With the tender light of a love divine Upon those that weep and those that pine; Whose bright love-glow is the light of "home," Be it lowly cottage or palace-dome; In whose depths there is pity for those that roam. Beautiful lips are those whose words Spring forth from their cage like the song of birds, Yet whose every utterance charity girds. Beautiful hands are those that do Work that is honest and brave and true, Moment by moment, the long day through. Beautiful feet are those that go On kindly ministry to and fro— Down lowliest ways, if God wills so. Beautiful life is that whose span Is spent in duty to God and man, Forgetting " self " in all that it can. Beautiful calm when the course is run, Beautiful twilight at set of sun' Beautiful death with a life well done! Beautiful rest where the willows weep, Beautiful couch where ties moss lies deep, Beautiful life—then, .h! beautiful sleep! Beautiful heaven beyond the sky, Beautiful spirits in their home on high, Beautiful peace—the God of peace is nigh! Beautiful earth, beautiful sky and sea; But what is their beauty compared unto Thee, God, the all-beautiful, reigning eternally? —Leeds Weekly Mercury._

During the negotiations between Lord Devon and his Irish tenantry for the sale of their holdings over 300 tenants sent in offers representing from twelve to twenty years' purchase of their present rents. Those who offered the lower figure received an intimation that his lordship would not entertain their offers. The administration of the Agricultural Labourers (Ire- land) Act has been virtually blocked in the county of Limerick, owing to the great majority of the land- owners, including Lord Cloncurry, Lord Emly, the, Land Corporation, and others, refusing sites to the Board of Guardians for the erection of labourers' cottages in accord- ance with the provisions. ENSILAGE.—The Mayor of Bacup has just opened a silo, containing 22 tons of grass and two tons of corn, all of which was stored in July or August last. The corn was placed at the top, and when the silo was opened a little of it was found to be mildewed. The other portion, and the whole of the grass, was found to be good and sweet, and the cattle ate it with avidity. Simi> STFALtwa,—Thomas Harper, a labourer, was com- mitted at Stafford on a charge of sheep stealing. He was caught in a field between Handford and Trentham with a sheep belonging to Mr. John Bate, farmer. He had a large knife with him, and was struggling with the animal as if with the intention of killing it, when he was surprised by a policeman, who had been watching his movements. SHEEP WORRYING.—Qeorge Roberts was last week sum- moned at Chester for damages to the extent of £5 for pos- sessing a mastiff dog which worried a sheep belonging to Mr. Williams, butcher, so shockingly that it had to be killed. The dog was seen to run the sheep down and then worry it. The defence was simply a question of damages. The de- fendant was ordered to pay £3 155., the value of the sheep, minus the sum received for the carcase. According to the Newcastle Journal the tenants on the Malton estate of Earl Fitz william are being requested to sign a memorandum stating "That it is agreed between Earl Fitzvrilliam and his said tenant that Section 33 of the Agricaltural Holdings Act (extending notice to quit to a year) shall not apply to the contract of tenancy" existing between them, and" that half a year's notice shall continue to be sufficient to determine the tenancy as if the section had not been passed." Ac ALLEGED NEW POTATO —At a meeting of the Lin- mean Society, at Burlington House, last week, a paper was read by Mr. J. G. Baker on the species of solanum which bear the tuberous roots called potatoes. Out of the 700 species of solanum only one, the common potato, solanum tuberosum, has as yet been cultivated. There is, however, another species which grows in the moister portions of Chili, where the climate is even damper than in Great Britain. When growing in the wild state the roots are small and of a bitterish taste, some with red and others with yellowish skins. Under cultivation however, the plan were found to grow most luxuriously, sending out stems in all directions, so that two plants yielded in one year over 600 tubers, while the tubers showed a remarkable increase is size, and had lost entirely their bitter 'flavour. The best method, therefore, of preventing the potato disease is to grow that potato which is most suitable to the climate. CLAIM FOR COMPENSATION.—The following story I know to be, in every respect, true. You, Mr. Editor, I think will say you know I ant not likely to say thus much without having reason for doing so. An agricultural labourer last pay day got notice that there would no longer be work for him on the farm. Like Adam, in "As You Like it," the man is old (80), but age, as with him, is "frosty but kindly," and be is still able to do some work. He has worked on the farm, from which he is now dismissed, sixty years continuously. He has filled in turn every posi- tion of importance on that farm—head horse keeper, head ploughman, head stacker, lord in harvest, and been a good hand in every place—strong, regular, sober, and honest. Four tenants have held the farm in the sixty years, and now the old man must go. On no other employer has he any claim. Has he none on the occupier of that farm, of which he has helped to do the hardest of the work so long ? If the occupier of another man's land is now accepted as having a claim for compensation, has a workman to a tenant none.—Cor. in Agricultural Gazette.

ImPitovED num.—And the general interests of the farm are also being well served. Large numbers of heifer calves by good bulls from the dairy farms around are pur- chased, reared, and done well for two years, for sale as in- calf heifers of 24 and 30 months oil They are sure to be I an important item of the annual revenue. The cake bill is a security for fertility. Peat moss as litter, and also placed in the tank for sopping up the drainage from the stable and. the co whouse, is gaining a reputation. The use of bone dust on the permanent pastures; and feeding off, not with ewes and lambs in spring and early summer—the most ex- haustive treatment grass land an receive—but with cake- fed grazing beasts, are effecting a great improvement in the park. The plough land retains its old fertility. You can see in the 11th volume of the Journal of the Royal Agri- cultural Society—sOlOng ago as that—a paper on maintaining tlarr fertility of newly broken-upland. ,Tlie principle of that paper has guided practice here. These fields, when I first knew them, were poor, worn-out, weedy, water-logged old meadows. They were drained and ploughed, and some of them were pared and burned. Land not worth 108. an acre was at once made worth 305., and it is worth 303. and more to-day. Look at the young wheat, the young clover—a magnificent promise; the cabbages and the mangel heaps. The fertility has been more than preserved, and there is no reason why it should not last.—" Inspector" in Agricultural Gazette.

"It doan' look 'zactly right to see one man wnth ten millyon dollars an' anoder with tea cents (applause by Samuel Shin), bat yit if I wus de ten millyon dollar man I wouldn't keer wheder it looked right or not." (Sudden end to, the applause.) (The Judge subsides.) "It doan' look 'zactly right to see one man hold offis all de time, while anoder man has to shove a tack-plane far a libin' (great rustle in Pickle Smith's corner), hut he who shoves de jack-plane has de respeck of de community an' keeps outer jail." (Rustle dies away). "It don' look 'zactly right to see fo'ty lawyers rush to defend:a criminal who has stolen money in his pockets, while de offender who am mcueyless am left to dig his way frew a ten-foot wall vrid an ole knife- blade (grins on a dozen face); but if I was a lawyer I should aim my money any odder way except by sawin' wood. De public doan' loyk for any particklar dis- play of conscience on de part of lawyers, an' darefore suffer no disapintments." (Grins no longer observable.) "It dean' look 'zactly right fur one man to have a brick house an' anoder man a rough bo'd shanty, but 'long 'bout tax- time de man in de shanty kin sit on de fence an' chuckle over de fack dat he haint rich. It doan' look 'zactly right to see one man go pushin' an' swellin' an' crowdin' every- j body off de sidewalk to let de public know dat he am a king-bee, but such men have to carry de anxiety of bein' in ' debt to no tailor an' of dodgin' de grocer an' of subscribing 25 dol. to build a church widout de hope of bein' able to pay ten cents on de dollar. In fact, my friends, dar' am heaps an' heaps o' things dat doan' look zactly right to us at fast glance, but when ye come to figger it up an' divide an' subtract we've all got a heap to be thankful for an' to encourage us to git up airly in de mawnin'. A man can brace his legs an' lay back like a mule, an' kick away at de hull world an' hate everybody and be hated in return, or he kin pick up sartain crumbs o' consolashun, crowd inter a seat in de back cand of de wagin,an' take a heap o' comfort, knowin' dat somebody is truss of dan himself. Let us accu- mulate to bizness."—Detroit Free Press. ARMED WITH Tun BlBLE.—Sonae years ago an old man lived in North Carolina who was remarkable for his piety , and for his strong faith in the Bible. He made up his mind once to take a journey on horseback, through a part of the western country. At this time that part of the country was much infested with bands of robbers. The old man knew this well ; and when his friends urged him to take a pair of revolvers with him, he declined, and said he would take no other weapon than his pocket Bible. So he started. After travelling for some time, he reached the State of Mis- souri. One day he found himself in the neighbourhood of one of the worst bands of robbers in the country. It was headed by a desperate man, whose name was Jim Stevens. Towards the close of this day he met a gentleman travelling alone, and who had thus far escaped the robbers. The first question this gentleman put to him was: "Sir, are you armed ?" "Yes," said the aged Christian, drawing his Bible out of his pocket; "this is My weapon." The gentle- man, who was almost loaded down with pistols and bowie knives, laughed at what he considered the old man's folly. And then, in a sneering way, said: "My friend, if that is all the weapon you have you hadAsetter be saying your prayers pretty quick. The den of Jim Stevens is only about ten miles from here. You will get there before dark, and he cares no more for Bibles than he does for rattle-snakes." They talked together awhile, then each told the other his name and they separated. Presently night came on, and it grew 'dark. The traveller saw a light in a house far down a glen, a short distance from the road. He supposed it was the home of the robbers. But he must have shelter and rest, so he went up and knocked at the door. In a very rough way they asked him in. It was the robbers' home, and desperate- looking men they were. But he took the seat they offered him, and asked for something to eat. They gave it to him. Then he sat and talked with them about the country around. By and by, the captain, the famous Jim Stevens, came in. Seeing a stranger present, he walked up to him, and said, " Old man, aren't you afraid to travel in this part of the cauntry, among the robbers, alone and unarmed ?" "No, sir," was the old man's reply, as he drew out his Bible, say- ing. "This is my weapon of defence. I always read a chapter and pray, too, before going to bed. I know you are robbers ; but I'm going to read and pray here to-night, and shall be glad to have you join with me." The whole band burst into a loud laugh on hearing this. Not minding this at all, the old man began to read. Gradually they wyaal sl became silent; and, when he knelt to pray, every knee bowed. It was a strange sight to see that band of robbers and murderers kneeling and listening attentively to the old man's prayer. When he had finished, they showed him a bed on the floor, where he lay down and slept soundly. He arose early the neat morning, and read and prayed before breakfast. They refused to take any pay forhdissioioodnalLd lodging, but thanked him for the interest be had them. When he arrived at the next settlement he Lard of the death of the gentleman he had met the day before. who had such trust in his own weapons, and made mockery of the old man's trust in the Bible. "It is better to trust in the Lord than to put confidence in man. _London "Herald of Peace and International Arbitration." BAD FENCES.—There were a great many more hips than ' haws to be seen on my last journey through a cold clay part of the county of Essex—a great deal more, indeed, of anything than of the hawthorn to be seen in the fences which I passed. Why was this? Only thorn had origi- nally been planted ; and now the dog rose, covered with its scarlet hips, the blackberry, the sloe, the elder, and the maple had usurped its place, together with many root shoots, and lower branches of various stunted trees, elm and ash, &c., planted in the rows, not to speak of nettles, clema- tis, and grass. No fewer than eleven different kinds of wood had I counted in the course of half a mile. The list unfortunately has been mislaid, but all together had done their best, and yet there was no fence—it was broken, I gappy, good for nothing. All together had in fact done 1 their worst, and so the fence had been destroyed. And ' " LQok there, sir," said my driver; "do you see that bushy spray of growth with berries on it just inside the hedge?. That's asparagus—wild asparagus. I've known that same bush there for twenty years. The farmer ploughs over it, and ploughs it up 'most every year; but still it comes. I suppose he could get rid of it if he gave his mind to it, but he hasn't killed it yet, and it seems as strong as ever." "If he gave his mind to it " is a very good phrase indeed. No doubt weeds of all kinds could be made to disappear if the cultivator had It on the brain; in fact, weeds will prosper, and cultivated plants, whether in fields or fences, will 00111 e I to grief on any other terms. Here, for example, was one of the finest second crops of clover ever seen in full bloom, ready to cut nearly 30 cwt. of hay, which would be worth, when won, at least four rents of the land that was growing It. The barley had been grown on land clean and in good condition; the seeds had been sown among it under favour- able circumstances, and the weather and the seasons had suited ever since. The weather, of course, as you said the other day, dominates everything; but that crop had been on the mind of its cultivator long before he sowed it, as well as at its seed time, or it would not have been so good. And if these hedges had been equally on his mind, even before the thorn was grown, but still more after it was planted, there cannot be a doubt that his fences would have been like his clover field—without a gap and in full bearing—all , haws, and not a hip to be seen.

CATTLE DISEASE PREvEyrrow.—The meat supply of the country is not dependent upon the importation of live animals from abroad. These might be excluded altogether, so only that the cattle disease was excluded with them, with, it is contended, no loss to the consumer and no diminu- tion in our available supply of food. The trade in dead meat is already larger than that in live cattle, and it is in- creasing every year. If live cattle were shut out to the extent which Mr. Chaplin demands, there would be a loss of about four per cent, in the total meat supply of the country, and, it is estimated, a more than equal gain to set against it from the security of our herds and flocks against the destructive ravages of disease. The home growth of meat, it must be remembered, admits of almost indefinite expansion. It is discouraged by the foot and mouth disease. If this anxiety were removed, the result would be speedily seen in the greater amount of attention which would be given to cattle breeding in all its forms. It is of little use for Mr. Gladstone to advise his tenants to turn their thoughts to dairy farming as the best alternative for the less productive industries which foreign competition has gone near to forbid. The foot and mouth disease is in the way, and no cattle breeder can possibly feel safe against the ruinous results it maw entail upon him. The fortunate ones who have not sUffered from it know of friends and neighbours who have been less fortunate than themselves, and they cannot be sure but that it may be their own tarn next. When the disease shows itself, there is an end to all hope of profit from the year's work. It may not be fatal in its effects; as a rule, it is not; the animals affected by it recover for the most part, but they lose condition in every case. Fat stock ready for market droops and declines to a shadow of its former self. On the dairy farm it means this and a loss of milk besides. The milk from the diseased animals falls off in amount and in quality. There is little of it, and the little there is is absolutely unfit for use. It is not to be expected that farmers will face these risks and will go on extending their operations in spite of them. The consumer suffers with them from a curtailed supply of one of the most essential articles of food, and one which must be produced at home, if it is to serve for home use. Meat may be sent to us from abroad. In a frozen state it may come safely from any distance,and will be sweet and whole- some whenlit arrives. Forlmilk we must depend almost entirely on what our own animals can yield. Condensed milk is a poor substitute for fresh milk, and fresh milk is among the most perishable of goods, and once tainted be- comes of no further use. If it is in the interest of the dairy farmer to be protected against a disease which threatens his sale of milk, it is scarcely less the interest of his customer that he should obtain the security he has been asking for. f footmilk in this country is to become cheap and abundant, he and mouth disease must be shut out.—Times. theTßHEigAhNia"ndnAgis roiLMtuararrrral Society a recent meeting of by Dr. Aitken, chemist to the society. a repoistawriansg presented by year ten local analytical associations have sent in returns of their analyses for the purpose of obtaining the society's rant, and its aid in furtherance of the objects they have in view. THE WINSFORD LOCAL BOARD AND THE POSTMASTER-GENERAL.

The Local Board of Winsford having declined to allow a new line of telegraphs to be placed through their district, in continuation of the new line from London to the North, the Pestmaster-General has instituted an action against them. The CAS@ was heard by Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, county court judge, who sat as arbitrator. The sitting was prolonged till a late hour in the evening.—Mr. Casserley, barrister, of London, appeared for the Postmaster-General ; and Mr. Banks, of the North Wales circuit, was for the Local Board.—Mr. John Doherty, superintendent engineer if the North-Western District of the Post Office Telegraphs, said: that he had between SOO and 900 miles of overhead tele- graph lines under his control. The witness detailed the chief lines in Lancashire, and showed that in many places the telegraph poles were placed alongside commercial roads, over which there was a great amount of traffic. He had not received complaints of their being davgercius. He was constructing a line from Warrington to Carlisle, for the introduction of the 61 rate of telegrahping. With the exception of short sections, the whole of that line would be'carried on poles. There had been no objections with the exception of Winsford. He had obtained the con- sent of the necessary 'parties to a line from Warrington to Carlisle. There were no places along that line where they paid any acknowledgment for the poles on the highways.— , Mr. Edward Graves, chief engineer of the Post Office Tele- graphs, described the direction of the existing line from Loudon to Manchester. It was entirely a pole line, except throligh some of the large towns. It carried from fifteen to seventeen wires, though in some cases there were thirty. There were cases where they had had the permission of the road authorities to erect a second line of poles on the road. The Postmaster had reoeived unconditional power. In the case of the London and Liverpool line they had the consent in every case, with this exception. He did not see any practical objection or difficulty in carrying a line through Over. They had applied for consent to erect 900 miles of line, and had obtained it in every instance with the excep- tion of Over. The consent of over 100 local authorities bad been obtained. If they placed underground wires at Over, and other places took to the objection, the result would be they would have no cheap telegraph service. The importance of that case consisted in its forming a precedent. It would cost four times as much to carry the wireerunder- ground. The Government had authorised the spending of about 6400,000, and the Treasury had warned them that they would not allow a penny more. —For the defence, Mr. Joseph Waring, surveyor to the Winsford Local Board, said it would be dangerous to place telegraph poles along Swanlow-lane, the route proposed. The road was very narrow, and there. were houses along it. —Captain Turner, of Over Hall, a magis- trate, thought that if telegraph poles were erected in Swanlow-lane it would greatly impede traffic, as two vehicles could scarcely pass. He regarded the placing of poles there as dangerous.—Mr. Bankes asked if the witness objected to the wires passing through and by the side of his pleasure grounds, but the question was objected to. He thought all telegraph wires overhead were more or less dangerous on account of being blown down or struck with lightning. Coming down his carriage drive he objected to see the wires in front of hint.— Mr. R. Verdin, chairman of the Winsford Local Board and a county magistrate, said it was with the un- animous conient of the Board that these proceedings were taken. He considered that in one part of the Swanlow- lane it was se narrow that telegraph poles would be a source of danger. Property owners and ratepayers had written to the Board strongly protesting against the erection of these telegraph poles.—Rev. G. W. Nines, vicar of Over, objected to the wires because they were unsightly, and also made a noise.—Several other witnesses were called, and Mr. Bankes intimating that they had a number of others, the case was adjourned to the 9th February at Chester.
FEARFUL COLLISION IN THE ENG- LISH CHANNEL. SERIOUS LOSS OF LIFE.

Informaticn has been received of a disastrous collision in the English Channel on Friday night in last week, involv- ing, it was feared, the loss of some 20 seamen. It appears that the City of Lucknow, a large iron ship, 1,253 tons, be- longing to Messrs G. Smith and Sons, Glasgow, and bound from Adelaide to London with a valuable cargo, collided off Anvil Light, Isle of Wight, with a four-masted iron sailing ship named the Simla, 2,288 tons, belonging to Messrs. Devitt and Moore, of Glasgow, and outward bound for Sydney, with the result of the loss of the latter vessel, a portion of whose crew is missing. The Simla left London under the command of Captain Nicholson, with two passengers and a crew of about 45 hands, and a general cargo, bound for Sydney. On Friday night, about a quarter past eight, when the Simla was off the Anvil Light, a vessel was reported on her starboard beam. Blue lights were burned by the Simla; the side-lights of both vessels were also burning brightly at the time, and the other vessel, which proved to be the City of Lucknow, a full-rigged sailing ship, commanded by Captain Macdonald, showed first her port light, then her starboard light, and then her port light again. Captain Nicholson ordered all hands en deck, and a few minutes afterwards the.. City of Lucknow struck the Skala some distance abaft the beam. She re- bounded, but struck the Simla a second time, carrying away the two mtinmasts of the Sitnla, her mizzen and foretop masts, and her jibboom, the wreckage smashing her six boats. The captain and several of the officers and crew of the Simla jumped on board the City of Lucknow, which subsequently cleared the other ship, leaving about 22 persons on board the Simla, including, it was believed, one passenger. Some of the crew of the Simla took to the City of Lucknow's boats, from which they were picked up by the London and South-Western Railway Company's steamer Guernsey, which was proceeding from Southampton to St. Mato. The Guernsey, however, put back to Southampton with the rescued men, who consisted of Charles Arthur Payne, chief officer; Herbert C. Barnes, fourth officer ; Robert Dale, sailmaker ; James Henderson' steward ; Thos. Hogg, James Scott; Robert CuLquhoun, Charles Soul, B. Edgeberg, seamen; Harry Blackmore, boy; and James Cole stowaway, all of the Simla ; and six men belonging to the City of Lucknow. In addition to these, the captain and several of the crew and several of the crew of the Simla jumped on board the City of Lucknow before the 'vessels parted. Nothing was seen of the Simla after the collision, and it was supposed that she sank soon afterwards with the twenty-three people left on board. Luckily, however, this was not the case.

A Lloyd's telegram of Monday says :—"The Nicolas Vag- liano steamer arrived in Dunkirk Roads this morning, and has on board 23 men saved from the ship Simla of Glasgow, bound from London to Sidney, which vessel was fallen in with on the 26th of January at 6 a m near the Wight with 10 feet of water in her and masts beam through a collision. The sterner passed a hawser en board the Simla ant en- deavoured to tow her, but owing to the heavy weather the hawser parted." The City of Lucknow arrived off Grave- send about half-past nine on Monday morning, in tow of the tug Victor. The City of Lucknow appears to be bat little injured, the loss of the bowsprit and a fay small holes in her bows is the only injury apparent. After the collision the City of Lucknow put off two boats to render such assist- ance as the heavy sea would permit. The lifeboat of the City of Lucknow west towards the Simla, but could not get alongside, and the men on board her refused to jump over. Both the boats were afterwards swamped and lost. The sur- vivors on board the City of Lucknow were landed at Grave- send Pier. Many of them were shoeless.

Mr. WILL= having seconded the proposition, which was carried with acclamation, and Mr. ARMITAGE having replied, the business of the meeting concluded. BUTTERMARKET-STREET WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL.

The annual tea meeting in connection with this echo,' took place at the Public flall on Monday, and was presided over by the Rev. J. Eglinton. The annual report was read by Mr. Ilenshall, and it set forth the progress that had been made for the erection of new schools. The scheme was successfully launched at the last annual meeting, the hand- some sum of £502 being promised on that occasion. The result of that meeting greatly encouraged and cheered the committee. Though the progress made during the past year might have seemed slow, it had been sure, and no time had really been lost. Unexpected difficulties and delays had to be encountered in their negotiations for the purchase of the land for the site. These, however, had all been over- come, and on the 12th November, 1883, a deed of convey- ance was executed by Mr. Broadhurst and £396 paid as purchase money, the land thus coming into their possession free from any yearly charges for around rent. The trustees having appointed Mr. Owen as their architect, various plans for the new school were prepared and submitted by him, and after earnest and full considera- tion, certain plans had been agreed upon which would give them a school of which the following would be the prin- cipal features: A large hailer schoolroom 531 t. Pin. by 50ft. 6in., and having a height of 26ft , with a gallery round three sides about Oft. wide. Round three sides of this hall would be ranged class rooms, three large ones on the westerly side and two for adult classes, each 211 t. by 15ft. Pin., and an infants' room 17ft. by 20ft. Pin., with ten other class rooms, each about 10ft. square. The gallery in the large room would not be required so much for ordinary school purposes as to give extra accommodation at circuit meetings, lectures, thc. Mr. Owen had kindly prepared a perspective view of the proposed struc- ture, which they had all had an opportunity of examining that night. The cost of such a building they were not yet in a position to state, but it would, of course, be considerable. The trustees had given the architects in- structions to invite certain builders to tender for the work, and they hoped to be able to commence operations in the spring, and confidently expected that their next annual tea meeting would be held in the new school. Certain gentle- men had been deputed to solicit subscriptions, who had met ' upon the whole with a very favourable reception from the friends they had visited. The subscriptions promised last January amounted to £602. Since then subscriptions had been obtained making a further sum of £376. Then they had £5OO voted by the trustees of Bold-street Chapel from the bequest of the late Mr. James Dutton, and £43 3s lid balance of proceeds of the last bazaar, making a grand total of about £1,521. In addition to that there was the pro- perty in Buttermarket-street, consisting of the school and the two houses adjoining, all freehold property, upon which, however, there was a net liability of about £550. The committee and the Beld-street Chapel trustees were of opinion that when the new school was built this property should be disposed of, and the proceeds over and above the amount borrowed upon it should go to the new school fund. Of the total sum promised £564 had been paid in, and he would in the name of the committee respectfully urge upon those friends who had not yet paid their promised subscrip- tions to do so at their very earliest convenience, either to the treasurer, Mr. Carter' or to the District Bank to the new Wesleyan Sunday School account. Several of their friends had put it to them whether the amount was not too much to spend on the erection of Sunday schools. They would ask those who held such views to remember that the school they hoped to erect that year would not be put up merely for the benefit of the scholars now on their books, but that to generations vet unborn it would r remain a monument of what the Wesleyans of Warrington , had done in 1884 for the spiritual requirement of the young, both of their own day and of the generation to succeed them; and when they remembered that Warrington, from its special advantages of railway communication and clogs proximity to the coal fields was certain to go on extending and increasing, to say nothing of the great impetus which would be given to it should the Ship Canal ever become a "fact accomplished," he thought they had considerations sufficient to urge them to determine that the school should be erected worthy of the chapel to which it would belong, and which would provide ample accommodation for the in- creasing requirements of Methodism in this town for many years to come. They had been desirous from the first to complete the scheme without having recourse to a bazaar, and he hoped they would be able to do so, but r they would venture to throw out a suggestion to their lady friends that very valuable results might be obtained by their instituting sewing meetings during the ' present year, to prepare for a grand Christmas tree and sale of work to be held in the new school premises next Decem- ber or January. The report went on to state that the teachers and scholars continued to work harmoniously. The smsournldindgesairtstrabdaanee had awda sn oat difficultyb e ens o they not s alonethey in experiencing, as they believed it was felt in other schools both there anti elsewhere. Probably in their own case the t thatbest remedy would be found in the new premises to be erected. The number of teachers now engaged in the school was 42, of whom 22 were male and 20 female. They had 441 scholars on the books, with an average afternoon at- tendance of 264. The Band of Hope had been in vigorous operation, its members numbering over TO. The mission band in connection With the school had throughout the year regularly conducted their Sunday night services. In conclusion, the committee thanked the ladies who had kindly contributed trays, and also all those who had assisted in any way to promote the success of the meeting.— Mr. CART= read the financial statement, from which it ap- peared that the inoome of Buttermarket-street school tea meeting was £lB 12s sd; from the annual sermons, £47 9s gdi They commenced last year with £l2 treasurer After the total expenditure 34 s d ; 3.d total, dp e t 606 e there was a balance in hand of £9 Os Pd.-... THE CASE OF NEGLECTING A CHILD AT WARRINGTON.

- - - - THE INQUEST. On Tuesday afternoon an inquest was held at the Bowl- ing Green Inn, Warrington, before Mr. Brighouse, coroner, , on the body of Arthur Longton Irwin, six months old, the , infant child of Ada Irwin, a married woman, but separated from her husband, who died from convulsions on Saturday last. It will be remembered that last week Mrs. Irwin was 1 before the magistrates at the instance of the Board of Guar- dians for neglecting to provide proper treatment for the child, and she was then fined £5, the case at the time excit- ing a considerable amount of public interest. The mother took the youngster from the Workhouse on the following , day (Wednesday), and according to her own evidence she followed certain instructions given to her by Dr. Spinks as , regarded the food which should be given to the child, but ' death ensued as stated, on Saturday.—The Coroner, in open- ing the inquiry, said that the deceased child, who was six , months old, died at the house No. 7, Wellfield-street. off Liverpool-road, on Saturday last, where its mother, Ada Irwin, was living apart from her husband. On Friday , night mother and child, it appeared, went to bed, and in the morning the youngster was found dead. He proposed to call Dr. Spinks and Mrs. Irwin to give evidence, and if after hearing their evidence the jury were perfectly satis- fied in their own minds that the child died from natural , causes, say from constitutional disease or csnyulsions, and that there was no culpable neglect on the part of any per- son which would bastes or accellarate the death, then it was for them to bring in a verdict accordingly. If on the other hand they were not satisfied that there was no cul- pable negligence on the part of some person towards the child it would be their duty and his own duty to adjourn that inqueet to a future day so that the doctor might make a post mortem examination of the body, and that the police might bring any further evidence which they thought necessary. Mr. Percy Davies, who represented the mother, would also in that way be in a position to produce witnesses. With regard to the police court proceedings last week he asked the jury to banish from their thoughts anything they had heard, read or Been as to prior events, because it was the essence of that inquiry, that rumour, gossip, and any- thing that they had heard outside that room should have no , part in the decision they would come to that day. —He then called Ada Irwin, of 7, Wellfield-str et, who said she resided in lodgings there. The deceased was her child. She was the wife of George Irwin, of Manchester, goods manager at the Great Western Railway there, but she had not been living with him of late. Deceased was six months old. She found him dead its bed on Saturday morning. She saw him alive about five o'clock that mcrning when she re-filled his bottle, and it was about eight o'clock when she found him dead. By the Foreman: She had three children alive at present. His children. Her children had alerays been delicate until they had turned 12 months old, but the deceased had been more delicate than the others. She had never been able to nurse her children. She had two servants when she lived with her husband.—The Foreman: I take it you really did not know anything about the care of children ?—Witness: Before my first child was born I never even nursed a baby. She was not interested in the death of the child. If her right hand could have saved the child she would willingly have given it. In reply to Mr. Percy Davies, witness said that after the proceedings at the Police Court on the previous Tuesday arrangements were made for the removal of the child from the Workhouse, and it was taken away on that day. On the following day deceased was attended by Dr. Spinks, who gave her certain instructions' which she carried out up to the time of its death. The deceased was in an emaciated condition when it was born, and for the first three months had been attended by Drs. Edgar Brown, and Lupton, of Liverpool. She took the child to Dr. Richmond, at the Warrington Infirmary, about the Friday before Christmas Day. The child had been in an emaciated condition from its birth, and had been subject to sickness.—Dr. Spinks, surgeon to the Workhouse, stated that on Saturday, the 19th, he was called by the master of the Workhouse to see the deceased, whom he found in the hospital suffering from constitutional syphilis and debility. He prescribed accord- ingly. It had the appearance of a child of six months old, but, as usual with infants suffering from that complaint, it was very small. It would weigh, he supposed, 71bs. or Sibs. The child was nourished, but it was exceedingly thin and emaciated, and he did not think it could come to that condition without an omission on the part of some concerned. He was not in a position to say whether the infant had the necessary food or not. He formed an opinion at the time that the child had not had proper food, or had been fed by a person who did not understand feeding a child. One might feed a child and starve it at the same time. He did not think the disease it- self was capable of producing the result he saw on the Sat- urday night, the disease being so slight. He saw the child on Saturday, Monday, and Tuesday, and it seemed to im- prove under his treatment. On the Wednesday he gave the mother certain instructions as to the feeding of the youngster and the giving of medicine. A continual course of neg- lect would hasten and cause the death of .a child suffering from constitutional syphilis ; it would require special care. In reply to Mr. Davies witness said that on the Wednas- day the mother appeared to be very anxious as to the treat- ment she should provide for the child, but he could not say whether that anxiety was genuine. He sympathised with her. The immediate cause of death were convulsions, but he could not say whether the convulsions were brought about by neglect. He could not say whether the child died from natural causes-he should like to view the stomach first —By the Foreman: He had met with scores of other children suffering from the same disease. It was hereditary, as the child was born with the disease. A post morte»t ex- amination might or mieht not make him judge better as to the cause of death,—Dr. Richmond, house surgeon at the Warrington Infirmary, repeated the evidence which he adduced at the police court last week, and said that looking at the child superficially there was nothing in its appear- ance to lead him to say that it died by other than natural causes. He had met with children six months old quite as slim as the deceased.—The jury were satisfied that there was nothing in the nature of the evidence before them t ) lead them in saying that the mother was guilty of any cul- pable neglect in the treatment of the child, inasmuch as it had been in a delicate state of health since its birth, and a verdict of "Death from natural causes" was therefore re- turned.

A country laird, at hi a death, left his property in equal shares to his two sons, who continued to live amicably to- gether for many years. At length one said to the other, "Tam, we're getting auld now; you'll tak' a wife, and when I dee you'll get my share of the grund." "Na, John, you're the youngest and moot active; you'll tak' a wife, and when I dee you'll get my share." "Oh, Tam," said John, "that's just the way wi' you; when there's ony fash or trouble, not a thing you'll do at a'."

"Will you do me a favour ?" said young Brooks to his wealthy friend, Simon Hansom. "What is it, George ?" said Hansom. "I wish you to lend me £2O, sir." "Call at my counting-house," rejoined Hansom. George was not long in paying his respects. "What security can you give me, young gentleman ?" "My personal security, sir." "Very well, get in here," said Hansom, lifting up the lid of a large iron chest. "Get in here!" exclaimed George, in astonishment, "What for ?" "Why, this is where I always keep my personal securities."

A BACKSLIDER.—For some time the Aberdeen Railway Company have despatched a cheap train once a week from Aberdeen to Edinburgh. This privilege attracted, among others, a clergyman belonging to the north, who, the other day, having taken his seat for Auld Reekie, found himself placed beside some of those gents who make their living by shuffling cards in a dexterous manner. After the few games usual on these occasions amongst the gang, in which the one that risks is always sure to gain, the parson was induced to try his luck. The consequence was he lost £5 and his gold watch. On the train arriving at Perth, his reverence, getting ashamed of the company he had been travelling with, left the carriage and took his seat in another. but what was his astonishment when the guard, who had wit- nessed his proceedings on the previous part of the journey, looked into the carriage and said, "Gentlemen, take care of your money; there are sharpers in the carriage !" This was the finishing blow to the minister. The rest of the passengers, knowing one another, all eyes were turned upon him, and he shrank from observation in the corner of the seat, convinced, no doubt, of the truth of the text, that "the love of money is the root of all evil." SEEKING FOR THE WHITE MAN'S BOOK.—A NOBLE PIECE OF INDIAN ELOCATENCE.—I came to you over a trail of many moons from the Betting sun. You were the friend of my fathers, who have all gone the long way. I came, , with one eye partly opened, for more light for my people, ' who sit in darkness. I go back with both eyes closed. How can Igo back blind, to my blind people? I made my way to you, with strong arms, through many enemies and ' strange lands, that I might carry back much to them. I go back with both arms broken and empty. The two fathers , who came with us—the braves of many winters and wars— we leave asleep here by your great water and wigwam. They were tired in many moons, and their mocassins wore I Out. My people sent me to get the white man's Book of Heaven. You took me where you allow your women to dance, as we do not ours, and the Book was not there. You took me where they worship the Great Spirit with candles, and the Book was not there. You showed use the images of good spirits and pictures of the good 'land beyond, but the Book was not amongst them to tell us the way. lam going back the long, sad trail to my people of the dark land. You make my feet heavy with the burden of gifts, and my mocassins will grow old in carrying them', but the Book is not among them. When I tell my poor, blind people, after one more snow, in the big council, that I did not bring the Book, no word will be spoken by our old men or by our young braves. One by one they will rise up and go out in silence. My people will die in darkness, and they will go on the long path to the other hunting grounds. No white man will go with them, and no white man's Book to make the way plain. I have no more words.—Oregon, by William Barrows.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING,
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING,

The last three months of the year were probably the mildest we have had for 26 years, and the present month is likely to be the same; consequently fruit trees of all kinds are in an advanced state and ready to burst their buds, which reminds us that the planting of such should be drawn to a close. If our hopes should be realised in an early visitation of winterly weather, planting had better be de- ferred till there is a change. It is not wise to subject trees that are starting to grOw to the process of transplanting at this season of the year if there is any likelihood of frost and snow. The check is sudden and mischievous, and should such conthtions exist long, the trees are more liable to perish than when planted in November, and subject for two or three months to inclement weather. All apple or pear trees that may be infested with moss on their trunks should be attended to at this season of the year, and steps taken to remove the moss. Doubtless some of our readers may have seen the stems of fruit trees in different parts of the country licaewashed. That is one of the steps adopted to remove the moss as well as to destroy any vermin that may be lurking in the crevices of the bark, and the process is annually resorted to. The parasite is more troublesome in chalky and limestone districts than elsewhere, though it is prevalent enough on dry, gravelly soils, as well as in ex- cessively wet ones. If -the stems of the trees are scrubbed with strong brine every two years the moss will give little trouble.. The brine is also a better insecticide than the lime. Insects are sure to be present where the moss is, and it is well known how these attack the wood, flowers, leaves, and fruit. Those who use pea sticks will find it a con- venient time to secure them, so that they may be trimmed and pointed before more pressing work comes on. If the smaller pieces are placed by themselves, they are most con- venient to place to the peas when 4in. or fin, high. It is a mistake to place the large sticks in at first to early peas, because they shade the ground, and this is not beneficial. Tau FRONT GARDEN.—The yellow, flowering Jasmine Nudiflorum is now expanding its blossom, or so far ad- vanced that the shoots not likely to flower can be readily distinguished, and if they appear at all crowded they should be cat within one bud of the older growth, from which strong shoots may emanate and flower well next year. The plant is usually grown against the walls of the dwelling, and in some parts in the shrubberies, supported by stakes, and where, in the latter position, pruning is unnecessary. Clematis have made growth half an inch long, and their pruning can be proceeded with, leaving the shoots a couple of feet long for the present, as sometimes the frost injures the forward growth. Of late Years great improvements have been made in the quality and variety of the Clematis by the hybridist, so that we have close upon forty hardy kinds, an as many more reputed as such. Gem is a deep lavender blue, Flammula white and sweet scented, Rubella rich claret purple, Jackmanii intense violet purple, Lana. ginosa NiVee pure white, Lanuginosa pale lavender, Montana white, Lady Catherine Neville French white with mauve bars, Standishii light mauve. They are all very beautiful, free growers, and exceedingly floriferous, and stand in the first rank as climbers to cover our dwellings, bare walls, or bowers. Tam WINDOW.—Are plants in dwelling-rooms injurious to health? The question has been frequently asked, and is based on the allegations that plants absorb oxygen from the atmosphere, and give out carbonic acid, a destructive gas to animal life. Mr. Haseldine Pepys, in his careful experi- ments on "Vegetable Respiration," arrived at the conclu- sion that no carbonic acid whatever is parted with, either by day or night. And the late Professor Lindley has re- marked—" Whether plants do or do not give off some small quantity of carbonic acid, this is at least certain, that they do not in this way deteriorate the atmosphere in any appre- ciable degree. If there is one absurdity among popular prejudices greater than another, or leading more to pri- vation of comfort when most wanted, it is that of fancying that growing plants vitiate the air of an apartment by the carbonic acid they emit. It may be true that plants destroy oxygen gas and form carbonic acid, but a human being consumes more oxygen,.and gives off more carbonic acid, in five minutes, than all the plants in a sitting-room in 24 hours. It is wonderful that this notorious fact should not have removed the prejudice about plants deteriorating the air of sitting-rooms. •Lt is one of the most beautiful provisions we know in nature, that the deleterious air breathed forth by animals is purified and rendered salubrious by plants; if it were otherwise the globe would become un- inhabitable." A few spoonfulls of water, if permitted to remain for any length of time in the saucers, will soon be- come offensive and create more mischief than a room full of plants; and we would urge cottagers, for the sake of the inmates as well as the plants, to empty the water out after every watering. Decayed leaves and flowers should be speedily removeJ.

"How many comets do you say there were ?"inquired the Judge of the prisoner, who had been locked up over night for deranging the symmetry of a neighbour's features during an astronomical controversy. "Three, if it plase yer honour." The court smiled incredulously, upon observ- ing which Patrick added, "J'm after tellin' ye the truth. Mickey Farrell, he saw wan; Mrs. Dinnis, she saw another; and 'twas myself that saw the third." . _ _ _ _

In the school of C—, Aberdeenshire, one day a dull boy was making his way to the master for the third time with an arithmetical question. The teacher, a little annoyed, exclaimed, "Come, come, John, what's the matter now ?" "I canna get ma questin richt," replied the boy. "What's wrong with it this time ?" " I've gotten auchteenpence ower muckle." "Never min'," said a smart boy in a loud whisper (with a sly glance at the master), "keep it tee yersel', Jock." Self-ease is pain; the only rest Is labour for a worthy end, ' A toil that gains with what it yields, And scatters to its own inerease, And hears, while sowing outward fields, The harvest song of inward peace. A day or two ago, as the passengers were leaving a ferry boat, a gentleman who stood behind a Customs officer re- marked, " When I see a poor fellow like that, I am consoled for not being rich." "Who 2" "Why, that man with the hump on his back. I hat rather be poor all my days than be deformed and have millions of money." "I can cure him in about five minutes—come and see," replied the officer, as he walked towards the unfortunate and invited him to pass upstairs. There was a kick, but he had to go, and three or four minutes' time sufficed to remove his deformity, which consisted of twenty-two yards of flannels and six pairs of socks. "Party smart !" growled the smuggler, as he was allowed to go. "Not so very," was the reply; "a man who carries a hump on his back should carry a stiff neck. You didn't." Noßmsr, WEIGHT. —lt is desirable for all persons, whether suffering in health or otherwise, to know as near as possible what the normal weight should be. We are in- debted to the late Dr. Hutchinson for weighing alone 2,600 men of various ages. There is, indeed, an obvious relation between the height and weight so particularly weighed and measured. Starting with the lowest men in the tables, it will be found that the increased weight was as nearly as possible 51b. for every inch in height beyond 61in. div.p: FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE:

M. Ferdinand de Lesseps is a candidate for the vacant seat in the French Academy. A telegram from St. John's states that the twenty persons who have been committed for trial for murder during the recent riots were all Catholics. A detective officer has been shot dead in Vienna by an Anarchist. The assassin had upon his person a dynamite bomb, a revolver and a poisoned dagger. GREAT FIRE IN NORWAY.—A fire broke out at Lauric on Monday morning in the most closely built part of She town. Many houses have been burned down. A Renter's telegram from Washington states that Mr. Mor- rison, chairman of the Ways and Means Committee of the HousP, has drafted a Tara Reform Bill, in which he pro- poses a general reduction of 20 per cent. GENERAL GORDON AND THU NEWSPAYER CORRESPON- numrs.—General Gordon left Cairo on Saturday night, and took with him several proclamations for the Sheikhs. Be' fore he departed an attempt was made to interview him, but his reply was that he was "worried to death, and time WAS too short." BLOODSHED IN Z7LDLAND.—TherO are indications in a Durban telegram that more bloodshed is probable in North Zulnlaud, as the Transvaal Usutu party is co-operating with the Usutu party in Zululand to harry the territory of Oham, whose forces are, it is said, fully prepared to meet the attack.

Tne French Budget Extraordinary was finally passed by the Legislative bodies on Tuesday. The Chamber per' sisted in its refusal to allow any more money to be spent on railways in Senegal, and struck out of the Budget an item of £120,000, which the Government had demanded for the work in question. CETEWAYO Rumeiten AWAY.—DeteWaro "escaped" frora Ekhowe a few days ago, but was promptly followed and re- captured by his military guard. A telegram from Pieter- maritzburg says that the natives in the Reserve are in an ea- cited state, consequently the women and children are flocking towards the Natal boundary. A Madrid journal of some authority states that the Spanish ambassador in London has been instructed ho endeavour to obtain "better terms" for Spain than those which Sir B. Morier is prepared to grant. In any case, however, El Liberal says that the Spanish Government will accept the result of the negotiations. 'fas JEANETTE tXPEDITION.—TeIegrams received at St. Petersburg from Samara and Pensa announce that the re- mains of Commander de Long, of the Jeanette expedition, and his nine companions, passed through those places ot! Saturday, and were received by the principal officials Oa the public with much ceremony. DEATH OF THE FATHER OF THE FRENCH Smera•-- The death is announced of M. Gaulthier De Romilly, the senior member of the Senate. The house, on being informed of the event, suspended the sitting as a mark of respect for the deceased. There is no fonndation for the report cur" rent here that au unsuccessful attack was recently made upon Bacnich. TEE FRENCH IN TONQUIN: RUMOURED REPULSE.—It was stated in the Paris lobbies on Thursday that Admiral Courbet, at the head of a considerable force, lately at' tempted to take Bacninh by asaault, or at least carry some of the advanced works and invest the place, but found the approaches too strong, and retired. Many deputies expreel great astonishment that his despatch should have been kep secret.

FIGHTING IN Monocco.—Further intelligence received from Count Chavagnac's party states that fighting, in whicu there were several killed and wounded, has broken ont among the hostile rstives on the Riff Coast, in the vicinity' of Penon Gomera. It is added that Count Chavagnae has consequently decided-to return hero, but before starting will await instructions from the French Minister ill Morocco.

KING KOFFEE KIDNAPPED —A servant of Koffee Kai' calli arrived at Cape Coast Castle about a week ago with $ message from the ex-King of Ashantee imploring the Ge" vernor to have him brought to the coast, as he was being very ill-treated, and was kept without food. Two dais afterwards another servant arrived with the news that Xal' calli had been removed from his place of csnfinement du- ring the night and had been carried no one knew whither. SUPPRESSION OF FRENCH BETTING AGENCIES.--It is re' ported that the French authorities, aroused by the car plaints of persons who have been swindled by betting agent! in Paris, have decided to suppress the agencies which hal° again commenced business in this capital, principally in the Rue du Quatro Septembre, and which are daily becomiaft more numerous. A raid upon them is anticipated, an several bookmakers have decamped during the present week.

Accounts received at Berlin from the interior of Russie state that the agrarian agitation continues. At Vitebsk, en important town in the south-west, the Governor asked the Czar to order the withdrawal of the troops which he had sent to maintain order, or otherwise a collision with the peasant° would be inevitable. In White Russia—that is, the western provinces generally—appeals are being made by the leadere of the peasants to the educated classes to aid them in the struggle against absolutism. ANOTHER SUICIDE AT MONTE CARLO.—Madame Ferrnt' wife of a stationmaster at Monte Carlo, has committed suicide. Her husband went up to her room during the afternoon, and, finding the door locked, imagined she bac! gone out for a walk. On the return of his son from school the latter also tried the door, which was still fastened. gr' Perrot then obtained access to the room through the windoset and was horrified to find his wife lying on the floor deed, with a brazier of charcJal still alight by her side. MURDER OF A RUSSIAN DETECTIVE,—A 6i central News" telegram from Kharkoff (via Gumbinnen) date.,4 January 26, says :—" An officer of gendarmes, M. Sobielout who was sent by the late Colonel Soudaikin to make int' _ie. tigations into tbe Nikilist organisation, was assassinat.et this evening. He was found dead, having been stabbed w!l'' a poinard. Stimulated to increased energy by this shoclpil crims, the police redoubled their efforts, and the same nigh they discovered a clandestine printing office, in which We: found a mass of secret correspondence between the terrori chiefs. The documents revealed the fact that a plan.tlen been formed for a general rising of the peasants in Little Russia. They also disclosed a plot to ; lace one of Pe, persons employed in the Imperial bakery to pet strychnaL°' in the bread, so that the Czar and his family might a° poisoned. Numerous arrests have been made. The naive. of Sobieloff's assassins are known to the police, and the/ will probably be soon arrested. • TEE SOUDAN REVOLT.—Telegraphic communication bee been established between Suez and Suakim. Baker FOP arrived at Trinkaba, near Suakim, on the 28th ult., and nrld Tuesday night 3,006 of his troops bad landed and entrench(' themselves. The Arabs were only a short distance Wl° the camp, and as they occasionally fired at Baker's rrooPe the English war steamer Sphinx fired at them with shell; which had the effect of driving them off. It is hoped the' Baker—who has already severely punished the reber skit' mishers—will be able to advance immediately with falls 5,000 good troons, and if the garrison of Sinkat can hol. out a few days longer their deliverance may be achieyeun: From Khartoum it is reported that the Sheikhs in the nelk, bourhood have received a letter from General Gordon ee't leg thorn to meet him in that city. It is not stated by w" means of communication a letter has been sent in advaoen,6 of the General himself. Sir S. Baker fears that the General mission to Khartoum will be unsuccessful, because he" neo not expect the tribes to rally round a leader who has order only to forsake them."

MTQPELLANDJUS. The death is reported of Sir Richard Williams Bnlkeley, Baronet, of Baron Hill, Beaumaris, after a long illness. The bill for legalising marriage with a deceased's wife's sister will in the coming session be in the bands of Mr.

Bio-a—dh-urst. Five men have been seriously injured by an explosion of fire-damp in the Yew Tree Colliery, Rowley, where they were working with naked lights. It was stated at the Central Criminal Court, on. Menday, that the Trcasury did not intend to proceed with the prose- cution in the explosives case, and the Court ordered the dis- charge of the prisoners Wolff and Bondurand. AN ABSCONDING CLEAR --,-Aclerk named Darks, engaged in the Nottingham Bank at Mansfield, is missing, together With a sum of between £5OO and £6OO in notes. The magis- trates have granted a warrant for his apprehension. Abe, from St. Chad's College, Denstone, Uttoxeter, 'has obtained an open theological scholarship of the value '3l £6O a year at Durham. This is the third £6O scholar- -41111) during the last four years gained at Durham by a Denstone boy. MUNIFICENT ENUEST TO vas BLIND.—Vice-Chancellor Bacon, on Sa,urday, approved of a scheme for the distribu- tion of £2%000, left by the late Mr. John Harrison, of Grosvenor House, Bath, on behalf ,cf the blind, subject to certain other bequests. Seven of the boys lately undertraining on board the ship Clarence, moored in the Mersey,'Were on Monday committed for trial on a charge of setting fire to the vessel and causing her destruction. The prisoners had confessed that their ob- ject was to escape from the ship. TEE FOSTMAN AND THE SALVATION ARMY.—A postman vfho pleaded guilty at the •Cld Bailey on Monday to steal- ing letters, said the Salvetion Army were always telling him that he could not go to heaven unless he had a uniform, and he stole in order to be able to buy one. This ridiculous excuse did not serve the silly fellow, who was sentenced to`lB month' imprisonment. Before the conclusion of the first National Radical Con- ference in L9ndon, on Monday evening, a resolution was carried unanimously expressing sympathy with the High- ‘and crofters, and indignation at the conduct of the land- -lords who have evicted tenants for giving evidence 'before the Royal Commissioners, and calling on the Orovernment to take steps for the protection of the wit-

messes. BARNUM'S ELEPRANT.—AcCording to a contemporary the "white elephant" comedy is being played with consunaa 'mate skill. The London public is flocking to see the sue- lessor to Jumbo, although some openly denounce the whole affair as an imposture ; and we now learn that a couple of Burmese priests have arrived in this country to take charge Of the " sacred " brute. These reverend strangers " ex- Pressed great anxiety" as to the condition and treatment of the elephant. They had had "a brief interview" with Mr. Barnum :n New York. HOAXING WRITCHURCII TRADESMEN.—During the past three weeks large numbers of Whitchurchmen have received orders by letter to attend the residences of gentlemen, noblemen, lawyers, bankers, ministers., farmers, and others miles away from the town, but to their great chagrin they lost valuable time and incurred expenses for no return what- ever. Ten pounds reward has beau offered for information as to the writers of the letters, and a local solicitor hasiust returned from London. having placed the whole of the let- ters and other documents in the hands of an expert. ALARstiNG FIRES.—A fire broke out about midnight on Saturday on the premises of Mr. Boetock, draper, King. Street, Yarmouth, and the building and stock were de- stroyed. A large public-house adjoining was partially burnt. The damage amounted to several thousands of Pounds.—The Salvation Army Hall at Wisotch was de- stroyed by fire on Saturday morning. The roof fell in Within half an hour of the discovery of the fire, and the borough firemen had difficulty in preventing the spreading of the flames to the adjoining houses. A horse in a stable next to the Hall was burnt to death. LORD WOLSELEY AND THE Alum-Croakers often say that the Army is "going to the dogs," but Lord Wolseley, speak- ing at the annual dinner of the Artists' Rifles on Saturday evening, gave quite another account of it. According to the Adjutant-General of the Forces, the Army is, man for man and officer for officer, in a more effective condition than prior to the Crimean War, and the successful manner in which the Commissariat Department has done its duty in South Africa and an Egypt is in itself a strong confirmation of this opinion. That recruiting has lately been attended with remarkable Success recently-published statistics have abundantly shown, but in this, as in many ether matters, figures prove little or nothing. Phys'que is equally, if not more, important than numbers—at all events, numbers are worth little without physique. It is, therefore especially satisfactory to have Lord Wolesley's assurance that the men enlisted within the last few years are as fine, if not finer men than those who enlisted when his lordship first entered the Army, thirty-two years ago. In fact, " England has at no period of its existence had an army more worthy of the nation. Desesanocs COLLIERY EXPLOSION: ELEVEN PERSONS KILLED.—A disastrous explosion occurred on Sunday Morning, at a fiery colliery in the Rhondda Valley at Peny- graig, near Pontypridd, in the naval steam coal colliery at which a terrible explosion occurred some years ago. The day repairing shift had only been down the pit a short time when the whole district with an explosion that shook the earth Ike an earthquake. Soon people congregated at the top of the shaft, bat it was not until eleven o'clock that a descent could be made. Then anxiety arose through no- thing being beard of the explorers fora long time, and the excitement heightened when news was received that some of the explorers had in all probability been suffocated. According to latest accounts this report appears to be too true. These gallant men had penetrated a distance of about 800 yards, and then one of the party being unable to go further returned, but Mr. Daniel Thames, proprietor and manager of Dinas Colliery, Mr. Thomas Lewis, the under manager at Penygraig, and Mr. Edward Watkins en- deavoured to go further, and perished. Fortunately, though the pit employs a large number of men, only eleven were down when the explosion occurred. All these are dead. A LIVERPOOL DTVORCE CASE: SAD DISCLOSURES.—In the Probate and Divorce Division of the High Court of Justice on Saturday, the Right Hon. the President (Sir James Hannen) had before him the case of Roose v. Roose, which was a suit by the wife, Jane Roose, for a dissolution of her marriage on the ground of the cruelty and incesmous , adultery of her husband, Stephen Rouse. Mr. Bayford ap- peared for the petitioner, and stated that at the time of thml marriage, which took place on the 7th of May, 1874, at Liverpool, respondent was a grocer's assistant, he being now a photographer. The respondent seemed to think the main use to which he could put his wife was that she should go Out and earn money for his support by prostitution, and en- deavoured to compel her to do so. Because she refused to do so, he thrashed her, turned her out of the house, and said that he would not permit her to return until she brought him £5. Finding that he could not induce her to adopt ---such a life, he left her in May, 1876. He then started busi- ' • ness as a photographer at Haltown, near Manchester, • where he was visited by hie wife's sister, whom he took oc- casion to seduce, aria who h.d had a child by him.—These facts having been proved in evidence, his lordship pro- nounced a decree nisi, with casts. A FARMER CONVICTED OF ARSON: EXTRAORDINARY Saturd ler Edgar John Rowley, aged 28, farmer, apd Margaret Rowley, aged 42, his wife, surrendered at ' Chelmsford Assizes to talk their trial—the woman for mali- ciously setting fire to certain farm property, and the male ••'- prisoner for aiding and abetting his wife in the commission ~ of the offence. The mile prisoner occupied Badger Hall Farm, near Southend, and at the beginning of November was' in pecuniary difficulties. He had accepted as a partner a Young man named Ileagee who advanced £2OO, and the male prisoner subsequently proposed to Hedges that he Should take in another punier and ply him out, so that there should be a big fire. The coatention of the prosecu- tion was to the effect that an arrangement was made between the prisoners that while the hush Ind was in London the wife should set fire to the farm buildings. Ac- cordingly, on the night of the 11th of November, a fire broke out, and the premises were destroyed, with the exception of the dwelling-house. The property was insured for £1.,000, but the furniture was stated to be worih £lO.
