The health a s:iir Moses Monteflore is giving considerable
anxiety to his 'friends. A Mossle,y publican named Nield was on Wednesday fined Lig and costs for hay.ng sold rum adulterated with

, 15 per cent of methylated spirit. Thomas Wood, late manager of a Stafford bank, was, on Wednesday, sentenced to 20 months' imprisonment for on= bezzling about £1,500 from a local building society of which

he was the treasurer. • The Monmouthshire farmer, named Donne, who was ar- rested for threatening to shoot the Prince of Wales on the occasion of His Royal Highness's visit to Bristol, is declared to be insane, and will be placed in an asylum. A large meeting of Oldham spinners on Tuesday night agreed to the issuing of a circular asking the trade to run their mills for only four days a week, so as to meet the lessened demand of the manufacturing districts. At C I erkenwell Police Court on Wednesday, Sidney Clay, a tobacconist, was committed for trial at the Central Crim- inal Court on a charge of endeavouring to persuade a medi- cal man to murder a child aged two months by slowly poisoning it. Lord Derby, it is said, has under consideration some further correspondence from the Transvaal, received on Monday evening, and relating to a, subject communicated to his lordship at an interview with Mr. Du Toit, one of the

delegates, last week. Dr. Price was charged at Pontypridd on Wednesday with attempting to burn the body cif his infant child. The Bench committed him for trial at the assizes upon charges of burning before the inquest, and indecorous exposure of the body by cremation. Bail was accepted. Damage to the extent of nearly £15,000 was caused by fire on Wednesday at the dyeworks of Messrs. Alexander Reid and Sons, Milngavie near Glasgow. Three different buildings were destroyed, a large quantity of dyed cotton yarn. In consequence of the fire part of the works will be stopped for several weeks. ELscrinc LIGHTING rt,r Tneaws.—A very interesting and successful experiment took place with the electric light on the South Eastern Railway on Tuesday night, when a sa- loon was lighted by means of three incandescent lamps, the light being produced from a primary battery, only on the Cheesewright system, no motive-power whatever being ap-

plied. - A FEMALE FEALM.—At the Birmingham Police Court, on Wednesday, a young woman of prepossessing appearance, who gave her name as Marquessa Sturgetzdaman, but whose real name was Mary Jones, was committed for three months for stealing a watch. In several instances she had gone to well-known philanthropical gentlemen in the town and taken advantage of their compassion and credulity by steal- ing any valuables she could from the rooms she was allowed

to occupy. MR. 0813ORNE MORGAN AND THE HOMES OF THE POOR. —Mr. Osborne Morgan, M.P., presiding at a conference in London on the subject of the homes of the poor, gave it as his opinion as a lawyer that they could tell a landlord that the law would not allow him to claim rack-rent value for property which was unfit for habitation. The law was strog,and with very little alteration it could be made to deal with such cases. What they wanted was to have men who would administer the law. THAMES v. Tvent.—A boat race between the accredited representatives of the Thames and Tyne took place on Monday afternoon over the Thames course, for £4OO. Bur- bear beat Elliott by four or five lengths. Elliott got off well at the start, and was soon in front, but at the soap works Burbear closed up, and having once passed his op- ponent, the race was practically over, Burbear winning as be chose. The day was very fine, but the water was lumpy, as a strong wind was blowing. A. COSTLY Kiss.—At the Greenock Police Court, a pipe- fitter named James Dakin, belonging to Bolton, but now re- siding at Johnstone, was charged with assault and breach of the peace. It appears that on Saturday night the accused entered a third-class railway carriage in which two women were seated, and after the train had left Paisley he insisted on kissing one of them, a married woman. She resisted, and in the struggle he smashed a basket containing ten eggs and other goods. He was convicted, and fined two guineas or thirty days' imprisonment. Be went to gaol. A BURGLAR'S LEAP FOR LIBERTY.—On Wednesday morning, the police entered the room of a notorious bur- glar named Copeland, in Great Chapel-street, Westminster, London, and, finding property they suspected to be stolen, arrested him. Copeland, who was only partially dressed, with one extraordinary leap jurfmed through the window, which was opened at the top, and thence to the adjoining leads. He subsequently jumped into the park, and then either fell or leapt on to the underground railway at St. James's Park Station, where he was re-captured, having sustained severe injuries. CHARGE OF DRUNKENNESS AGAINST A CLERGYMAN.— Upon the resumption on Wednesday of the inquiry under the Church Discipline Act with regard to charges of drunkenness against the Rev. H. F. Limpus, vicar cf Twickenham, the defendant stated that he could not pro- ceed further with his defence, and he therefore threw him- self on the mercy of the Bishop. The Commissioners decided that there was sufficient prima facie ground for far- ther proceedings, and the accused signed a declaration con- senting to submit to the Bishop's sentence without further proceedings. CURIOUS BREACH OF PROMISE CASE.—A curious action for breach of promise of marriage, which had occupied the Anglesey Assize Court for the greater part of two days, was concluded on Tuesday. The fair plaintiff obtains a ver- dict for one shilling by way of damages, and Mr. Justice Stephen directed that each side should pay its own costs. There was no question of sentiment or "broken hearts " in the case. The parties had been brought together by an amiable lady who had received a sort of commission from the defendant to supply him with a wife. The plaintiff was willing to accept the position, but the negotiations only landed the parties in the Nisi Prius Court. ENGLISH PATENTS. The following patents amongst others, published In the Patent Office Official Journal, were sealed during the week ending January 26th, 1884:—James Macqueen, of Bury, for improvements in machinery for pre- paring, spinning, and doubling cotton and other fibrous substances; Thomas Taylor, Bolton, improvements in mills with vertical runners,for grinding paint, or other oleaginous pigments, and for other substances; John Walter Reedley, Bradford, improvements in fellers and in the preparation of flax, silk, wool, or ether fibrous substances; Samuel Wright, Egremont, improvements in machinery for making corks for barrels; John Henry Topham, Manchester, improvements in means for supporting trousers; Roughsedge Wallwork, Manchester, improvements in arrangements and mechanism for grinding, glazing, and polishing articles of metal ; Briggs and Ralph Taylor, Darwin, improvements in or re- lating to the boiling pans and feed ef sizing machines.— List supplied by Mr. George Davies, CE., Fel. Inst., P.A., Patent Solicitor, 4, St. Ann's-square, Manchester. MR. GLADSTONE ON FRUIT FARMING.—(To the editor of the Examiner.)—Sir, Referring to the Premier's speech at the atnual rent audit at Hawarden, Mr. Gladstone is incor- rect in stating that preserves are charged from 7d to 9d a lb, and that this is owing mainly to the energy of the French, Belgian, Dutch, German and American fruit growers. All the gooseberries, raspberries, strawberries, black currants, damsons, and blackberries used by Me are entirely English—no foreign whatever being used—and to prove that the quantity is not particularly small, my usual season's make is :—Gooseberry, 300 tons. Raspberry, 300 tons. Strawberry, 200 tons. Black currant, 400 tons. Damson, 600 tons. Blackberry, 100 tons. And they can be bought retail from ready-money grocers in two and three- pound stoneware jars at the following prices :—Gooseberry, , 5d to 53/4cl per lb. Raspberry, 6d to 60. Strawberry, 63 to eid. Black currant, 51d. Blackberry, 51d. Raspberry and Gooseberry, al. Plum, 4d. Greengage, 6d. Damson, 7d. Orange Marmalade, 4d. Jars extra, one penny each. , Yours, dm., WM. P. HARTLEY.—BootIe, Liverpool. RIOTOUS DISTURBANCE AT PRESTON.—A disturbance, which would probably have terminated in a serious riot had not a body of police appeared on the scene, took place in New Hall-lane, Preston, on Tuesday night. It seams that just after the mills had closed, at six o'clock, some hun- dreds of factory operatives, consisting mainly of those lately employed at Messrs. Brindle's Alliance Mill, assembled in I the street named, and, headed by the effigy of the manager of the mill (Mr. Ainsworth), marched to his residence in Bright-terrace. Three attempts were made by the police to grasp the figure, but they were knocked down, kicked, and pelted with stones. The effigy was set in flames on Mr. Ainsworth's doorsteps, and blunt amid hooting and yelling. By this time mud and stones were thrown about so freely that two or three shop windows were completely smashed, ''and many shopkeepers put up their shutters. Whilst police-sergeant Hornby was making his way to quell the disturbance he was struck in the face by a woman, and be- fore he could capture his assailant was knocked down and kicked violently in the face and otherwise roughly handled. A man named Nelson was taken into custody, and within an ,bour afterwards the street was cleared. At a meeting of the Weavers' Association on Tuesday night, a resolution con- rilemning the action taken by the roughs, in New Hall- ane, with reference to the strike at the above mill, was passed. 1, oEcXETTRA._2ID.Ivvicei Tam PCRc4artezr,EDcronSer Iftfor EAast CO R Surrey 0 flr o' flu Wednesday re-opened an inquiry respecting the death of a woman whose body had been found in the Thames, off Rotherhithe Wall. On Monday a man named Murray iden- tified the body as that of his wife, from whom he had been separated for some time, and his evidence was confirmed by that of his IWO, who was equally sure that the body was that of his mother. Murray added that his wife's life was insured in the Prudential Office, and he produced the neces- sary form, which the Coroner filled up. The Jury returned an open verdict, and the Coroner made out the certificate of death in the name of Phcebe Murray, and the inquiry ter- minated. The same afternoon, in consequence of the result , of inquiries made, the Coroner was communicated with. He I ordered the ce-tiflcates of dsath and for the burial to be .withdrawn, and the body was subsequently identified in the most conclusive manner as that of a woman named Eliza- beth Catherine Musk, the wife of a cellarman. The Coroner remarked on the extraordinary evidence given by Murray and his son, the latter of whom lee said he believed had been "coached." The Coroner also understood that Murray had been seen with his wife the previous night at Battersea.— The Coroner's officer said that Murray's wife was now living at 63, lauffie:ictstreet, Clapham Junction. The jury returned a verdict that the deceased committed suicide by drowning while in a state of mental derangement. POLITICAL. . The A.aress in the Hones Of Lords will be moved by the Marais of Tweeddale and seconded by Lord Vernon. Lord Randolph Churchill has accepted an invitation from the Birmingham Conservatives to contest the constituency at the next general election. elThe Address in the House of Commons in answer to the Speech from the throne will be moved by the Hon. Arthur Mott, M.P. for Roxburghshire, and seconded by Mr. Sand. Smith, M.P. for Liverpool. Speaking at Oldham on Saturday night, the Hon. E. L. Stanley, M.P., said that although he was in favour of a re- distribution of seats, he would not imperil the extension of the franchise by seeking to pass too much. WHAT Ma. BRADLAUGH WILL Do.—Mr. Bractlaugh, M.P., has consented to an arrangement by which any interruption of the business of Parliament on Tuesday will be avoided. He will not present himself at the table to take the oath until February 11, and in the meantime Sir S.Northcote will not bring forward any resolution on the subject of the hon. member's claim. MR. HENRY GEORGE AND MR. BRIGHT.—Mr. Henry George, lecturing on "Progress and Poverty," on Thursday night, at Newcastle, referred to Mr. Bright's speech, and said that in his strictures upon advocates of the nationalisa- tion of land Mr. Bright had no more idea of what he was talking about than the babe unborn. Mr. Bright used to be denounced as be (Mr. George) was now, and ought to know better than take opinions from his opponents. The disease was too deep to be cured by superficial remedies. LORD R. CHURCHILL'S RECENT SPEECH: LETTER FROM MW GLADSTONE.—A Liverpool gentleman has received the! following letter from the Prime Minister :—" 10, Downing- street, Whitehall, January 28, 1884.—Sir,---I am directed by Mr. Gladstone to thank you for your letter e the 24th instant respecting Lord R. Churchill's recent speech. Mr. Gladstone prefers to leave such unfounded assertions and indiscriminate abuse to the impartial judgment of all fair-, minded persons.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, G. LEVESON-GOWER.—Mr. T. Robinson." LORD RANDOLPH CHURCHILL'S SPEECH AT BLACKPOOL. —Mr. Robert Leake, M.P., and Mr. William Agnew, M.P., the members for South-East Lancashire, who have been very busily occupied meeting their constituents during the recess, were on Saturday present at Norden, near Rochdale, assisting at the inauguration of the new Liberal Association. In the speeches that were delivered some hard words were applied to Lord Randolph Churchill and the " party " of which he is the leader, Mr. Agnew characterising his Lord- ship's Blackpool oration as "an amalgam of lies, spite, and buffoonery; humour, humbug, and insolence." LORD "RANDOM'S "ORATORY.—Lord Randolph Churchill met another portion of his constituents on Thursday night, and indulged in one of his characteristic speeches. After reiterating his conviction that the principles and policy of the Radical party were "all humbug," the noble Lord turned upon Mr. Bright. He accused Mr. Bright and Mr. Cobden of being a pair of "political cuckoos," who waited until Mr. Villiers had borne the great burden of the Corn Law agitation and then stepped in to secure the glory. The remainder of the speech was mainly a criticism in the freest language of Mr. Bright's actions whilst in and out of the Administration. THE MARQUIS OF SALISBURY AT HERTFORD. The Marquis of Salisbury was present at a Conservative ilinner at Hertford on Wednesday evening. He referred to the ex- tension of the franchise. He said he had given no pledge in reference to measures he had not seen, but it was a question whether so large a revolution ought to take place without people having a voice in the matter. Any attempt to represent the House of Lords as inclined to set itself against the people was a gross falsification. Respecting the visit of the Transvaal delegates to England he said it meant that the Boers were resolved to get rid of that suzerainty of which so much had been mad. Turning to India, he said the Ilbert Bill would leave the coloured men in a worse position than before. He looked forward to the future of Egypt under the present policy with considerable apprehension. SIR S. NORTHCOTE AND EDINBURGH UNIVERSITY.—III his rectorial address at Edinburgh, on Wednesday, Sir Stafford Northcote was neither philosophical or critical, but he was eminently practical, and fully redeemed his promise not to introduce any jarring notes into the celebration of the tercentenary of the University. Speaking on the training of youths for political life, lie displayed to advantage the Liberal side of his character, declaring that he would rather see in students a little misdirection of their partisanship than a dull indifference upon important questions or a sel- fish insensibility to the interests of their country. Referring to the advantages of a classical training, he announced his intention of giving a prize for a historical subject, and spoke of the advantage of an adequate study of modern languages and of the national interest in the progress of seience and the provision of means for its study. Mr. Herbert Gladstone, M.P., speaking at Leeds last week, and after remarking that the wearisome duty of the recess had been the searching after an idea in the speeches of the Tory leaders, proceeded to discuss the proposals of Mr. Henry George, who, he said, had wrecked himself in refus- ing to concede any right of compensation to those whose property he was ready to take away. Mr. George's projects, if carried out, would infallibly land the country in civil war. On the question of reform Mr. Gladstone said that in the coming session the Franchise Bill would be carried, and that for the first time in 40 years without a window or a head being broken. Speaking on Egyptian affairs, he said the Government were not responsible for the insurrection in the Soudan, but they would endeavour to assist the threatened garrisons in retreating safely, or in relieving the menaced posts. The Government had responsibilities in Egypt which they would bear, and which they would not resign to others. LORD " RANDOM " AT IT AGAIN. Lord Randolph Churchill, M.P., in a speech at a Conservative gathering at Woodstock on Tuesday evening, mentioned that he had received an invitation to stand at the general election as one of the Conservative candidates for Birmingham. He said his feeling was that in the coming struggle, on which the entire English Constitution would depend, the place where a loyal Tory ought to be was where the battle might be hottest, the odds the greatest, and the hopes the slightest; and, therefore, if he should receive from the Tory party in Birmingham a formal summons to become one of their can- didates, to Birmingham he should go. He knew that the ancient borough of Woodstock would never be dishonoured by having a representative of the Radical school. Refer- ring to the threatened disfranchisement of the borough, he said that Parliamentary reform was no child's play, and had wrecked before now governments more powerful than the present one. Behind Mr. Gladstone there was the tribunal of the English people, and on this tribunal they might hopefully rely. MR. GOSCHEN, M.P., ON THE SUFFRAGE.—Mr. Goschen addressed his constituents at Ripon on Wednesday night, and spoke for an hour, chiefly on the franchise and redistri- bution. He said he was not sanguMe of the time and temper of Parliament permitting the Government to pass a satisfactory Local Government Bill next session. After expressing deep interest in the London Government Bill, he said that, while not converted to the expediency of the franchise extension, he admitted that the question wee practically settled. It would he impossible not to satisfy expectations raised among a million and a half of people by promises publicly made. He claimed liberty of action' but cordially hoped to be able to support the Government both as regarded the time and plan for redistribution. He trusted they would take the House into their confidence early in the session ; and if their programme was satisfactory in that respect, they need fear 'no worrying opposition on his part on the extension of the county franchise. He was against that recasting of the electoral system which would be necessary to introduce either the principle of every vote being equal in value, or that of one man one vote. He desired to preserve variety of _representation, so as to re- flect English provincial life. Tan MEMBERS FOR BIRMINGHAM —Mr. John Bright, Mr. Muntz, and Mr. Chamberlain, the members for Bir- mingham, addressed a meeting of their constituents on Tues- day evening in the Birmingham Town Hall. The senior member (Hr. Bright), replying to a resolution which ex- pressed confidence in the representatives of the borough and in the Government, referred to the virulent language and extravagant charges brought against Her Majesty's Government by Tory orators during the recess. He bad I been struck with one fact which ought to cause some sorrow ' —namely, that the higher the simial rank of the speaker the more extravagant and the more virulent was the lan- guage used. His conclusion was that the Tory party, in its essential qualities, was unchanged for what it had been in times past. The party was, four years ago, brought before the final court of appeal, namely, public opinion, which pronounced an emphatic verdict against it. That verdict was not new likely to be altered. With regard to Ireland, it might be, as the result of some admirable and necessary legislation that there would be a return to a more tranquil condition of mind, and that the Irish people might come to the conclusion that the Government and people of England were as anxious to do full justice to the five millions in Ire- land as they Were to do justice to any five millious of people in Great Britain. At this moment there was no pro- mise from the Tories of anything they Would do for the great mass of the people of this country if by any accident they should be returned to power. They gave no promise of penitence or of amendment; and so long as they were in that frame of mind he would entreat the working men of England, especially if they had any regard for their own order, to make up their minds in every constituency that the party which had so injured and in- sulted them in the past should, while they remained im- pAefntietre ar d m uunnct zh abnagde d s, pbo ke efno,r me ye! r Cehxacn übdeerdl a fromi n said otwh in the coming measure of reform, he had no doubt that largeords ; majority.bn t th eH was e w t Conservatives would endeavour to impede its passing by all manner of obstruction ; but he was certain that it would wasn s theo t ll o certainuse one subject upon which he had no doubt, and that was, that if the Bill was frustrated by the peers, then the Government might appeal with a clear conscience to the people against oafbo Cuotnlthmeon lisou with of L the peers- and there was no question in English politics on which he would more cheerfully consult the opini qt of the constituencies. at sea. The law at present gave a premium te negligence on the part of the shipowners. They frequently made a profit out of a shipwreck and the deaths of those brave men who follow a disagreeable, la- borious, and perilous calling while carrying the English I flag honourably into every quarter of the world. Often they went to sea as on a forlorn hope. This great scandal and evil he would, with the help of God and the help of every honest man, do something to stop.—Mr. Bright, ad- dressing the same club, said that after the franchise was extended, the most pressing question for the Reformed Barliament was the reform of the Land Laws. He utterly condemned Mr. Henry George's proposals as a wild and impractical scheme of confiscation, and an insult to the common sense and honesty of the English people; but while saying this he considered our system of land tenure should be freed from its present trammels, 80 that natural forces of accumulation and dis- persion might have full effect. The result of such a reform .would be that the laud would gradually and naturally come into hands most requiring and desiring it, most able to pay for It, and meat capable of, working it for the public advan- tage. The abolition of the law of primogeniture and entail, and the facilitating of the transfer of land would be easy. The people of England should try these reforms before hav- ing recourse to wild extravagances. .

ILLEGAL REMOVAL OF CATTLE. A BATCH OF OFFENDERS AT DARESBURY. At Daresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Daniel Isher- wood, farmer, of Appleton, was summoned for removing two pigs from Warrington to Appleton, on the 19th Decem- ber, without a license.—Sergeant Booth said that on the 19th December he saw the defendant driving the pigs from Warrington to his house, and he asked him to produce his license. The defendant replied that he had not got one, and that he was not aware he ought to have one.—A fine of Is and 8s 6d costs was imposed.—William PalM, farmer, Walton Inferior, Richard Ho'croft, butcher, Appleton, and James Knowles, farmer, Appleton, were each summoned for removing certain animals into the County of Chester, with- out having made the necessary declaration in accordance with the Contagious Diseases Act —Mr. Jenkins appeared for the defendants. Sergeant Booth having proved the case, each defendant was fiaed Is and costs, with the exception of Knowles, who was fined 2s. and costs, he having removed two animals.—Thomas Miller, butcher, Whitley Superior; John Priestner, butcher, Frodsham ; George Shepherd, butcher, Frodsham ; John G. Hamilton, farmer, Walton Inferior ; Patrick Lyons, labourer, Walton Inferior; John Rippon, farmer, Walton Inferior; and Alfred Jones, a boy. Appleton, were each sum- moned for having, on the 24th December, brought into the couty of Chester, for the purpose of slaugter, certain knimalq which were not branded with the letter "5" in accordance with the require- ments of the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act.—Mr. Jenkins, who appeared for the defendants, contended that none of the animals were brought into the county of Chester; that they were bred and put up for sale within the limits of the county, and that the place of slaughter was also within those limits.—The Magistrates' Clerk (Mr. Nicholson) advised the Bench that if the animals were taken across the boundary line for five minutes only, and then brought back, the defendants had committed a technical offence, and were liable.—Supt. Williamson deposed that the authority of Chester joined the authority of the borough of Warrington near to the foundry, a little way past Wilderspool Brewery, and that it did not include the place where these animals were sold, namely the Norton Arms. Animals from various counties were sold at this place, and came in contact with those which might be taken there from the county of Chester, and therefore it was necessary that the police should take this precaution.—The Bench Mid that they felt bound to inflict a tine, but it would be a very small one. Each defendant would have to pay costs and Is. per head of cattle. Miller had removed three animals, Priestner aod Shepherd one each, and the remainder two each. INTERESTING LETTER FROM A WINSFORD MAN IN FLORIDA.' The following letter, which may interest:our readers, has been sent to us • for publication : " Okahumka, Sumpter Co., Florida, U.S.A., Dec. 23,1883. —Dear Sir,—According to promise I write a few lines to give you some idea of this part of the United States. I cannot speak of the farming districts, net having seen them, but I understand there ere some parts of the State where farming is extensively and profitably carried on. The chief industry about here is orange, lemon, lime, citron, grape fruit, and all of that family. Pine apples, grapes, bananas, plums, pears, and many other choice fruits are grown here, and when well cultivated give very large returns for the cost and labour. There are a good many groves around here coming into bearing, and many of the trees are well stocked with fruit -, the income from a bearing orange grove is considerable. A halfpenny each is the lowest price given for oranges on the tree, the purchaser gathering, packing, and shipping at his own expense. I have seen several trees with over two thousand oranges on, as many as from six to ten on quite a slender branch. A friend from England (Mr. Bolton) has been staying a few days with us, he has visited many groves in different parts of this county. He was over a grove about seven or eight miles from here on Friday last, six acres in extent, the trees were eight years old; last year the yield was over 1,700 boxes, this year over 3,000 boxes, which, after paying all expenses, will give to owner about £l,OOO clear for this year. The cost of working this grove does not amount to more than £lOO per annum. The income will go on increasing for some years to come. Pine apples can also be grown with large profit; they cost about 2d or 21d each, and take 18 months to come to perfection. They will find a ready market at from is to 4s each, the worst samples would sell for 6d to 9d each. Anything that will grow here, if well cultivated, will pay a good profit to the cultivator. The natives are too idle to give much attention to cultivation. Nature does so much, they are content to let it do all for them, consequently they do not succeed like people who come here from the North of Europe. Vegetables of all kinds can be raised and sold at very high prices in almost any section of the State. The climate is mild, somewhat relaxing; but very healthy when people become , acclimatised. Any person willing to work may come out here and do well; but hard work for four or five years is indispensable. Here the diligent hand maketh rich (not always the case in England). In 10 years an indus- trious hard-woreing man can secure an income for life, which many a hard-working tradesman would be glad to secure at the end of a life's toil of 30 or 40 years in England. The spade, the hoe, rake, axe, and any other implements for cultivating the soil, cutting down trees, loading honses, Sze., are necessary, and must be used. Joiners and carpen- ters could find employment at 103 5d per day. Tailors and shoemakers are much needed, and would do welt—l am, dear sir, yours truly, ABEL PENNY.

Mr. John Henry Parker, the eminent publisher, of Oxford I and London, and a well-known antiquary and explorer of ancient Rome, died early on Thursday morning. He was 78 years of age. THE WIGAN TRAMCAR ACCIDENT. Thomas Hale, manager of the Wigan Tramways Company, and J. Thoum• son, engine driver, were charged before the county magis- trates at Wigan, on Thursday, with the manslaughter of Mr. Barker. The Bench decided that there was not suf- ficient evidence to juetify them in sending the accused for trial. TKO' GLOBE" LIBEL: A Timm Bum Form:l.—At the Central Criminal Court, en Tuesday, the Grand Jury found a true bill against Captain Armstrong, proprietor of the Globe newspaper, for libel on a Consul: and on Mr. Montagu Williams stating that a rule had been obtained for the re- moval of the trial to the Queen's Bench the case was ad- journed until next sessions. An inquiry has been conducted by the Leicester Guar- dians into the death of a woman named Ward, who, it is alleged, died from fright through the enforcement of the Vaccination Act. The police visited her house when near her confinement, to seize the furniture for vaccination fines, which she had no money to pay. The fright brought on syncope, which, according to the doctor's certificate, caused death. MR. BRIGHT AND DISERTABLISHMENT.—Mr. Bright, in in- timating his inability to be present at a disestabliehrnent meeting in Liverpool, writes :—" The discussion of the ques- tion will be useful, and may serve to help forward discs- tablishment not in Wales only, but also in England ana Scotland. But the churches hug their chains, and hence the main difficulty of those who would offer them free-

dom." THE CoLuEnz EXPLOSION : Tim INQUEST:A coroner's inquest as to the disastrous pit accident in Carmarthen- shire, by which 10 men were killed, has resulted in a ver- dict of accidental death. The jury thought that one of the workmen had contributed to the accident by his mismanage- ment of the levers, but in face of the evidence of the Go- vernment Inspector that the breakage of the rope was due to its being wok through being exposed to steam from the upcast shaft the man could hardly have been convicted of criminal culpability. SENTENCES OE DRAM—Taro men have been sentenced to death at York Assizes. John Lowther, a collier, was con- victed of the murder of a gamekeeper in Cleveland, on evidence almost entirely circum- stantial. Charles Nowland was found guilty of the murder of his wife at Hull. The convict pro- tested that he was the "victim of two perjured women." In the same Court, Martin Kevill, indicted for the horrible murder of his young son, was found guilty, but declared in- sane, and he will be detained as a criminal lunatic. Ltvunpoor. Rummetsm.—A very unpleasant specimen of the Liverpool rough was on Tuesday committed to the Assizes. The prisoner already stood committed for trial for participation in the murder of a Spanish seaman in the streets of that city. In resisting arrest on another charge he stabbed 'a police officer so severely that the man was still, after the lapse of five weeks, an inmate in the hospital. Prior to this outrage the prisoner waylaid a lady who was collecting rents, and, temporarily blinding her by throwing cayenne pepper in her face, he managed, with the aid of an accomplice, to get possession of her satchel, which contained about £9. The prisoner, whose name is Michael McLean, is only 17 years of age. Kty's COMPOUND, a demulcent anodyne expectorant, for Coughs and Colds. Bold by all Chemists, 90., la. lid , 2s. 9d. —Advt.

APPLETON. AN UNFOUNDED CHARGE OF ASSAULT.—At atresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Henry Arnold, Samuel Parsons, and Thomas Welsby, of Appleton, were summoned for assaulting William Bostock on the 21st December, and Bos- took was charged with assaulting Welsby and Arnold.—Mr. J. Moore appeared for Bostock, and Mr. Percy Davies for Arnold, Parsons, and Welsby.—Bostock stated that on Fri- day night, the 21st December, after attending several raffles at different places—one being at the Black Bear Inn, Latchford—he was prozeeding home along the side of the canal with Arnold, Parsons, Welsby, and a man named Starkey, when he was assaulted by the three first-named. When the assault was commenced he was near Barber's Bridge—a swing bridge that crosses the canal. Parsons came up to him. and "tore his tongue from under his arm." The tongue was a trophy of one of the raffles. Arnold struck him a number of times and knocked him down the embank- ment, nearly breaking his arm. While he was down Welsby attacked him, holding him down by the head, and punching him as hard as ever he could punch him." He asked Welsby to spare his life, but the latter replied "You —; I've a good mind to finish you." After getting to the railway bridge Welsby knocked him into the hedge, and Arnold knocked him out again. Arnold after- wards got him down and kicked him in the ribs. When he had proceeded a little further along the road Arnold felled him a third time, and before he could recover an upright position someone came to him and kicked him in the face, cutting a gash just above the left eye. The men then ran off, and he got home as best he could. He could not say that Parsons struck him.— The case against Parsons was here dismissed, the Bench re- marking that there was no evidence against him.—Dr. Willett, of Appleton, said that Bostock came to him after the night of the assault, and he had a number of bruises on the face. On the left eyebrow was a gash which penetrated nearly to the bone.—Joseph Starkey was called for the de- fence. He stated that on the night of the 21st December, when Bostock left the Black Bear Inn to go home he was drunk. Welsby and Arnold accompanied him on the canal side, one being on each side of him to keep him from falling into the canal. Bostock began boasting about his prowess, and said that at Northwich he once made six men run, add- ing that if he were not drunk he could fight all the men there. Bostock afterwards struck Welsby, and a fight ensued , between them, Arnold trying to separate them. The fight ' was continued all along the canal aide until they got to Wilderspool, where Bostock and the other men separated.— The case against Arnold and Welsby was dismissed, and Bostock was bound over to keep the peace for six months. ASHTON. ASSAULT ON AN ASHTON CONSTABLE. -- At the Wigan County Police Court, on Monday, before Messrs. Horace Mayhew and J. C. Eckersley, James Clark, labourer, Rose Hill, Park-lane, was charged with being drunk and disor- derly and assaulting Police Constable Moyers, at Ashton, while in the execution of his duty. On Saturday night prisoner was creating a disjurbance in Gerard-street, Ashton, and was requested to go away by the officer whom he struck in the breast, tupped him, and kicked him severely.—Pri- soner was ordered to pay the costs, and 103 and costs for the assault. ASHTON RECREATION SOCIETY: ANNUAL MEETING.— The annual meeting of the members of the Ashton Recrea- tion Society was held at the Local Board offices on Monday evening last, when there was a large attendance. The chair was occupied by Mr. Valiant, and there were also present Messrs. J. Gasket', J.P., Boardman, Mitchell, Livesley, France, Holbrook, Melling ,Astle, and Marsh. It was stated' during the evening that the society - was in a very encouraging position, and during the winter season the cricket ground bad been con- siderably enlarged, while the large pavilion had been con- verted into a reading room, which was being exceedingly well patronised. The balance sheet for the r ost year was presented, and it showed receipts amounting to £lOO los nia, including a balance of £2B 17s 10,1 brought forward from last year, and the expen- diture £7B 145 7d, leaving a balance of £2l 16s 34el in favour of the society. The accounts for the past year had been audited, and were passed. The election of officers afterwards took place, Mr. A. B. Moubert being re-appointed president; Mr. Valiant, treasurer; Mr. J. Livesley, bowling captain; Mr. Pierpoint, cricket captain; and Mr. Jenkinson, football captain. The secretary (Mr. W. J. Painter) ex- pressed his intention of retiring, and it was resolved that Mr. James Hill be appointed in his place. The committee were elected as follows :—Messrs. J. Gaskell, W. Latimer, W. Boardman' W. Painter, W. Lowe, P. Ball, W. Leach, T. Holbrook, W. France, G. J. Byrom, D. B. Marsh, P. Roberts, J. Melling, W. Rowe, J. McGeever, J. Mitchell, J. Tanen, R. Vernon, J. H. Middlehurst, C. H. Astle, and J. Ferguson. Several rules were discussed and altered, after which the meeting closed with a vote of thanks to the chairman. UNLAWFULLY WITHHOLDING MONEY FROM AN ASHTox FRIENDLY SOCIETY.—John Smith, late secretary of the Ashton Amalgamated Association of boo, steel, tin, brass, and other workmen, was summoned at the Wigan County Police Court, on Friday last, for unlawfully withholding the sum of £9 7s. Bd., the moneys of the society, after the same had been demanded from him.—Mr. bilis, who ap- peared to prosecute, said that the summons was taken out mnder the provisions of the Trades Union Act, 34 and 35 Vic., chap. 31, and the rules registered under the provisions of that Act for the regulation of these societies. The Act authorised that in case a secretary or other officer of the society retained money belonging to the society after it had been demanded from him, the society could summon the offender before the magistrates to recover the same. The penalty in such a ease was not exceeding MO.—Mr. Trow, general secretary of the association, produced the certificate of registration of the Ashton society under the provisions of the Act. Defendant's duty was to receive the subscriptions from the members and hand them over to the stewards. Defendant had been asked for the money which be held in his hands, and his only excuse I was that his wife had been ill.—George Ganderton, auditor of the society, said that in December last the sum of £9 75 eLd was due from prisoner to the society. He asked Smith for the money, ani be said he would go home and fetch it. Smith returned and said that the box that the money was in at his house had been broken open and the money taken out.—Samuel Bladen, a steward of the society, proved that defendant had £9 7s 63 in his hands at the time the last witness made his audit —William Shaw, general president at the society, said that on the 2nd January be applied to defendant for the amount he held. He replied that his house had been in oken open and the money stblen. Wit- ness asked him why he had not given information to the police, and he said he bad not thought it worth while to bother about it. On the 6th January defendant said he ex- pected to get a situation shortly, and he would pay the money as soon as he could.—DAendant urged that he had not wilfully kept the money; it had been stolen from his house.—Tne Bench made an order for payment of the amount due within a month, and imposed a penalty of lOs and costs, in default one calendar month's imprisonment. CADISHEAD. Two weeks special religious services were held in the large vestry of the Cadishead Wesleyan Chapel, commencing every night at 7-30. They were well attended upon the whole, considering the stormy weather. Practical addresses were delivered by Messrs. Jackson, Hopewell, J. Owen, Bescoby, and the minister of the circuit. These services have been a great blessing to the people generally. On Monday evening, January 28th, a tea meeting and entertainment were given in aid of the funds of the Cadis- head Cottage Gardeners' Society, in the Wesleyan Day School. There was a large attendance. The chair of the meeting was occupied by Mr. J. A. Holmes, of Cadishead. The entertainment commenced with a selection of mnsiC from "Norma," by the band. Then followed a reading by Mr. B. Brierley, 'Adventures of a stuffed monkey ;" part song, "The sea is England's glory," Tonic Sul-Fa Class; reading, Mr. B. Brierley, "Clogging new clogs ;" band, "Con a moil," fantasia; part song, "Might with the right," Tonic Sol-Fa Class ; reading, Mr. B. Brierley, "Catching a weasel asleep" (eacere); response, "Sailing for b icon." These readings were rendered in the Lancashire dialect. Finale band, " Ged save the Queen." The meet- ing was thoroughly in accord throughout. CUERDLEY.

----- FATAL ACCIDENT TO A FARMER —Oa Saturday, Mr. Wm. Leather, faunal., of Barrow's Green, sJuerdley, received in- juries from which he died on Monday morning. The deceased was engaged cutting some hay on the top of a small 'stick, when he observed some rooks upon afield which had been newly sown with wheat. He got up for the pur- pose of frightening the birds away, when the hay, which had just been cut, gave may with Mr. Leather. He fell upon some bards and injured his spine. Dr. tlooth SAW the in- jured man, but the case was hopeless, and death ensued about three o'clock on Monday mommy. The deceased was well known and much resPected. div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

ENTERTAINIIENT.—The Farnworth amateur negro troupe gave an entertainment in the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Tuesday evening, and elicited loud applause by their eccen- tricities. A sketch by A. G. Davies and F. W. Wareing, in which the topical duet, "By and bye," was introduced, caused much amusement. The proceeds were in aid of the Frodsham Parish Church Bible-class Brass Band, and the above company kindly gave their services. GOLBORNE.

---- -- WELSH Wxmarmax TEA PARTY —The Welsh Wesleyans of Golborne held a tea meeting and entertainment on Tues- day evening. A goodly nnmber of persons Fartook of a very enjoyable tea, which was served in the meeting-mom, Heath-street, after which the company adjourned to the Wesleyan school-room (which had been kindly lent for the occasion). Here a miscellaneous entertainment was held, under the presidency of Mr. Roger Yates. Selections were given in both Welsh and English, the proceedings through- out being of an enjoyable character. A WOMEN'S QUARREL AT GOLBORNE.—At the Petty Sessions at Newton Town Hall on Saturday last, Hannah Holden was summoned for assaulting Susannah Taylor, at Golborne, on the 18th inst. Mr. Stuart, of Wigan, ap- peared for the complainant, and Mr. Buckley, of Leigh, represented the defendant.—From the evidence given on behalf of the complainant it seemed that on the date named the women, who are neighbours, and reside in Bank-street, Gol borne, had a quarrel, and after strong words had been indulged in, the defendant struck Mrs. Taylor on the head with a brush.—For the defence, it was alleged that the complainant went to the defendant's door with a knife in her hand and called out to Mrs. Holden, "Come out, you Irish —, and I'll rip your heart out." As the defendant stopped inside the complainant attempted to enter the house, and Mrs. Holden, in defending herself, hit ,Mrs. Taylor on the head.—The defendant was bound over in the sum of £lO to keep the peace for six months. THE CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.-1/1 connection:with the Golborne branch of the Church of England Temperance Society a public meeting was held in the Parish Church Schoolroom, on Monday evening, when there was a good attendance. The chair was occupied by the esteemed rector, the Rev. C. T. Quirk, who, after his recent illness, was warmly welcomed. The meeting was disappointed in the non-appearance of the Rev. S. Wilkin- son, of St. Paul's, Warrington, who had been announced to deliver an address, but in his place the Rev. Mr. Pratt, curate of the same church, attended to give an address. He spoke of his experience in the temperance cause at Liver- pool and the Potteries (Staffordshire), and clearly showed the benefits that were to be derived from temperance in con- trast with the misery and degradation than caused by drunkenness. At the close a hearty vote of thanks to the Rev. Mr. Pratt was moved by the Rev. W. Thorpe (curate of Golborne), seconded by Mr. A. Caunce, and supported by Mr. Roger Yates, and was accorded with acclamation, after which the meeting closed with singing and prayer.—A miscellaneous entertainment was held on Wednesday even- ing, when there was a fair attendance. The proceedings were greatly enjoyed by those present. HALTON.

MUTUAL latercovnarnmr SOCIETY.—The weekly meeting of this society was held on Monday evening, when the fol- lowing gentlemen made impromptu speeches, namely:— Messrs. J. Looker, J. Hancock, W. Moors, J. Kay, J. H. Gamon, W. Cooke, and J. Speed. The president (Rev. S. Mees) occupied the chair. HAYDOCIC. TRANSFER or LICF.NSE.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, the license of the Hire and Hounds pub- lic-house, Haydock, was transferred to John Tunstall, the former holder having being the late Joseph Ratcliffe. A TIMELY WARNING—Thomas Hornsby, a collier, was summoned at Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday last for being drunk and disorderly at Haydock on the 12th Janu- ary.—The defendant pleaded guilty.—The Bench observed that the defendant had been previously before them, but they would on this occasion impose the same fine of 5s and costs. They would give him warning, however, that if be was brought up again his fine would lse increased. ALLEGED THEFT OF A FowL : LUCKY ESCAPE.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, before Colonel McCorquodale, T. J. Gillespie, and C. Pilkington, Esqs , Thomas Bailey, of Haydock, was charged with stealing a cock, value ss, the property of Thomas Dearden, of Clips- ley Cottages, Haydock.—The prisoner was represented by Mr. Browne, solicitor, of Warrington.—On the case being called Superintendent Weir said: I have looked carefully through all the evidence that can be given in this case, and I think I should not occupy the time of the Bench in going Into it. There is really not sufficient evidence to convict the prisoner.—Mr. Browne : I ask for the prisoner's dis- charge.—The Bench : Then the case is dismissed. OLD FOLKS' TREAT AT LIAYDOCK.—A meeting of the committee appointed last year to arrange inutile annual old folks' treat was held in St. James's School; Haydock, on Monday evening, when there were present the Rev. 11. Sherlock, the Rev. H. Mason, Messrs. Thomas Turnbull (hon. secretary), James Worsley, William Hardman, Edward Leyland, James Livesley, John Turton, William Cawley, Thomas Jackson, and Samuel Aspinall. The committee decided to give another treat to the old folks on the 12th February, collectors were appointed for the different dis- tricts as last year, and the hon. secretary (Mr. Turnbull) was instructed to secure tenders for the provisions. &c. It was stated that there was a balance in hand from last year's treat amounting to a little over D. STEALING CHUBS AT BILLINGE.—OR Monday, at the Wigan County Police Court, James Barker, collier' Bil- lings Chapel-end, was charged with stealing a box of cigars, the property of Peter Dewar, tobacconist, Bridge- street, St. Helens.—lt appeared that on Friday evening lag, about half-past five the prosecutor's cart was standing on the highway at Billings Chapel-end in front of a shop whilst he WO doing some business, and during that time the cigars were abstracted from the cart. Prisoner was met about that time with a box of cigars by a. person named Peter Green, and the two went together to a public-house and had some beer. There the prisoner was very liberal with the cigars, and admitted he had got them out of a shandry. He was turned out of the house, and was subse- quently apprehended by Police-constable Adamson, to wkom he said he had not bought the cigars.—lle was committed to gaol for 14 days. BILLININE AND WINSTANLEY FRIENDLY SOCIETY. On Monday evening the members and friends of the Billings and Winstanley Friendly Society gave a very enjoyable entertainment in the Parish Church Schools, before a large audience, the Rev. IL St. George, M.A., being in the chair. The rev, chairman, in his address, said that although the club had during the past year grown both as regards funds and the number of members, it had not met with the suc- cess it deserved, though it was without doubt on a sound foundation, and a good investment for all young men in the district. All the songs rendered were very favourably re- ceived, encores being the rule, not the exception. The comicalities of Messrs. Hugh Mather and J. Williams (Ash- ton) created roars of laughter, and each of them was voci- ferously applauded. Mr. G. Makin read and recited in a very creditable manner, and Miss St. George's playing of a pianoforte solo (Gavotte by Rameau) was very much ad- mired. Two juvenile artistes, Messrs. Richard Mather and , Elias Anderton, played a violin duet so well that they were recalled and went through it a second time. Two dialogues, "Handy Andy" and " Shaving done here on the shortest notice," were given by members of the society' and the ex- cellent manner in which they were performed reflects the highest credit on all concerned, showing plainly that no . pains had been spared on their part to make the entertain- ment successful. Mr. John Smith accompanied through- out in a very able manner. HORNS SMITHY. We'are given to understand that the Social Club in con- nection with the Horns Smithy Mission is this week to be discontinued for the present. HUYTON. HUYTON AND ROBY Scnoors.—A distribution of prizes took place in the above schools on Wednesday evening last week by the vicar, the Rev. Canon Penrhyn, to 20 girls and 15 boys belonging to the Sunday school, for good conduct and early attendance. Prizes for proficiency in letsons and Biblical knowledge had been given previously by the teachers 0 the several classes. The Rev. W. T. Southward was also present during the proceedings. HUYrON QUARRY. CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY: RUYTON QUARRY BRANCII.—The usual fortnightly meeting was held on Monday evening, the Rev. Canon Penrhyn presided; there were also present the Revs. W. T. Southwaid and H. D. A. Hubbard. Pianoforte duetts were played by Mrs. T. Evans and Miss Harrison, songs were contributed by Messrs. Moysey and Lunt, and a reading by Mr. James Middle- burst. Mr. 11. B. Parr (of Liverpool) gave an address on total abstinence.

ARIATEIIR MINSTREL ENTERTIINMENT.-011 Saturday night, an entertainment, under the management of Mr. George Hall, was given to a crowded house, and the pro- ceedings were much enjoyed. BAND OF HOPE—The second meeting of the series was held in the Mission Hall, on Monday night, when Mr. T. Miller, secretary of the Church Diocesan Temperance Society, delivered an address. The chair was taken by the Rev. G. W. Guest, M.A., rector, and a musical programme was excellently performed. There was a good 'attendance.

_ _ PADGATE. PADGATE WESLEYAN MIITI7AL heitorrisENT SOCIETY. —Oa Thursday, Mr. W. ff. J. Jenkins read an interesting paper on "The Wesleyan hymn book," and, whilst depre- cating portions of the preface and showing that many of the hymns were quite open to criticism, expressed a high opinion of the work and its authors and contended that it contained specimens of sacred poetry of the very first order, illustrating his views by several appropriate quota- tions. Messrs. A. Bennett, F. Wright, and J. Dakin after- wards spoke on the subject, and the meeting terminated wit!s an able reply from Mr. Jenkins. RAINFORD.

AN IMPUDENT THEM—James Chisnall, a middle-aged man, was, on Wednesday, charged before Mr. J. C. Gamble, St. Helens, with having stolen 8d from the Eagle and Child public-house, Rainford, on Saturday last.—The- prisoner, it seemed, had gone into the public-house and been served with some liquor. He wanted another glass, but the young woman in charge thinking that he had sufficient refused to let him have any more. She left him by himself in the bar, but had only been out a short time when she heard the puking ef money, and on returning the defendant was standing near the open till with some money in his hand. On being asked, he, however, gave up 8d in copper, and was then allowed to go. The facts of the case, however. came to the ears of the police and prisoner was apprehended.— He was remanded till iriday. A BEFR&C`TORY COLLIER—At the St. Helens County Petty Sessions, on Monday, a collier named Walter Ashton was charged with having infringed the roles in force at Rainford colliery made under the provisions of the Coal Mines Regulation Act, 1872. Mr. J. 0. Swift prosecuted, and Mr. Buckley, of Leigh, defended. Special rule 42, which is in force at the colliery, provides that no man shall go down or up or into the pit contrary to the direction of the banksman or the looker-on. On the 7th mat, about nine o'clock in the morning, the defendant went to the pit hot.. torn and asked the looker-on, named Bowen, if he might go up. Bowen told him he could not go up till dinner•time, which was the time prescribed. The defendant, however, after Bowen went away from the place, get into a cage and went up.—A fine of lOs and 15s costs was ineposed. RAINHILL.

The effects of the gale were very severely felt at Rainhill on Saturday evening. About half-past five o'clock a terrific squall struck the house of the Rev. T. Kiernan' and carried away nearly the whole of the roof, happily without any-in- jury to anyone. A number of slates and some lead were also forced from the belfry of the Catholic Church, built by the father of the late Mrs. Stapleton, and close to the hall.

THE LARGE BEQUEST TO THE POPE: THREATEXEH lArloanow.—The London correspondent of the Freeman s Journal says :—I learn on good authority that the will of Mrs. Stapleton Bretherton, who recently bequeathed £200,000 to the Pope, is likely to ly:coma the subject of liti- gation. Some of the relatives most nearly interested have already taken the initial steps towards contesting the valid- ity of the instrument on the ground of want of testamentary capacity. The legality ot the bequest will be further dis- puted as being made to an alien, but this does not appear to afford a very strong ground of objection, if, indeed, it is admissable at all. The plaintiffs, whose beneficial interest in the will is of the most trifling kind, are n 3 doubt actuated by the hope that his Holiness may offer to recog- nise the claims they put forward without proceeding to litigation.

SHOCKING CATTLE OUTRAGE AT SPESE.—A beautiful little heifer, the property of a Spekc farmer, was found last Sunday morning in a field most shockingly and brutally injured. The poor beast bad to be slaughtered. A reward is offered for the discovery of the perpetrators of the crime.

WESTON. A WOMEN'S ROW AT WEsToN.—At Runcorn Petty Ses- sions, on Monday, Sarah Whitby, an elderly woman, was charged that she being quarrelsome in the Dock Hotel, Weston, did refuse to leave the premises when requested.— Mr. W. H. Linaker appeared for the complainant, and the defendant was represented by Mr. Burton.—lt was alleged that about hall-past eight on the evening of the 12th January Mrs. Whitby entered the Dock Hotel, where her daughter-in-law was. She commenced a d:sturbance with the latter. Mrs. Rouglasedge requested her to discontinue her noisy conduct, but she refused, and had to be forcibly ejected by the landlady. In the street defendant contintred the disturbance for ten minutes. Evidence in support of . . . . . . . . _

this statement was given by Mrs. Roughsedge, Mrs. Mary Ann Bailey, and Lily Myers.—The defendant was sworn, and stated that she was 66 years of age, and had never been in the police court before. On the evening in question her daughter-in-law's children had male a bonfire with sticks and paper under the staircase in the kitchen,
and the youngest boy had set his curls on fire. She put the fire out with two buckets of water, and thew went for _ .
her daughter:in-law .in the Dock .Hotei;
She asked Mre.
Roughse'dge if." Toe's wife" was in Mrs. Roughsedge said
she w-ould-not have her "rowing" with her customers, and
she shook her until blood came out of her mouth and nose.

She was then pushed down the steps, and roughly kicked on the legs. Her daughter took her home "as bloody as a pig."—Cross-examined by Mr. Linaker, defendant said she had often had hot whiskey and wa'er in the Dock Hotel, bat she had had none on the day in question.—Mr. Burton hav- ing addressed the Bench, the defendant was fined lOs and costs, 13s el, Mr. Reynolds (the chairman) observing that there was some excuse for her being excited, as the pantry was en fire. WESTON POINT.

ACTION FOR DAMAGES BY THE WESTON POINT TOWING CoatrAmr.—At the Liverpool County Court, on Friday, before Mr. J. F. Collier, judge, assisted by Captains Hamill and Sinott, sitting as nautical assessors, an action was tried in which the Weston Point Steam Towing Company, Limi- ted, owners of the steam tug Gladiator, sued Messrs. Henry Cruce and Co., trading as the Hercules Steaintug Co.. owners of the tug Conqueror, for £25 damages sustained by collision in the river on the 25th of October last. After hearing the evidence OR both sides, the learned judge, after consulting with the asseqsors, held that the defendants' vessel was alone to blame, and he pronounced for the plain- tiffs with costs, the amount of damages to be referred to the registrars of the court. Mr. W. J. Stewart (instructed by Messrs. Masters and Rogers) appeared for the plaintiffs; and Mr. T. G. Carver (instructed by Mr. John Woodburn) for the defendants.

CONSERVATISM IN C"R—ES.II7RE.LA large Conservative meeting was held at Winsford on Wednesday in connection with a new club. Mr. Verdin presided. Mr. Ifurleston Leche proposed a resolution declaring that the affairs of the country had been grievously mismanaged by the pre- sent Government. Captain Turner seconded, and the motion was carried. In reply to a vote of confidence, Mr. H. J. Jollemache, M.P., condemned the policy of the Govern- ment, and said their mismanagement of both home and foreign affairs had alienated the confidence of the country. Mr. John Brooks, Conservative candidate for Mid-Cheshire in place of Mr. Egerton Warburton, who is resigning, =I; with a most cordial reception.

ANOTHER LIVERPOOL SHIP AND 26 LIVES LOST.—The Liverpool iron ship West Ridge, 1.400 tons register, which is posted as missing, had a crew of at least 20 bands. Twenty-eight signed articles in Liverpool to proceed in the vessel, and two neglected to join. It is believed that two substitutes were provided, and in that case 28 lives would be lost with the vessel. OPPOSITION TO THE ESCAPED NErN.—On Thursday evening a mob of several hundred persons assembled in front of the Co-operative Hall, 91dh m. and made a hostile demonstration against Edith 0 Gorman, the escaped nun. it happened, however, that she was not lecturing. The , i feeling of many of the Irish is intense against her, and treats were made of a violent character.
