THE disestablishment of the Church. in Wales is one of the questions now pressing to the front, and when it has been accom- plished, as it -certainly will be soon, the establishments in Scotland, and England must be swept away also. This fact is, it is quite apparent, recognised not only by Non- conformists but by Churchmen as well, and they are very wisely preparing for the inevit- able. Some Churchmen are probably more alive than others to the rapid strides which the Liberation Society has recently made to- wards its goal ; all are more or less agreed that the incessant war which that society is waging against the alliance of Church and State must in the end be successful. Alluding to the question of disestablishment, the late Dean ALFORD, one of the most sagacious of the clergy, wrote—" Whether years or de- cades of years be taken for the accomplish- ment of this, however it may be deprecated, and however opposed, accomplished it will certainly be." And he added, "History has for ages been preparing its way. In past changes it has been conceded over and over again. God's arm is thrusting it on, and ' man's power cannot keep it back." These words were written fifteen years ago, yet they are as true to-day as they were then. The Church has failed to fulfil its mission, it is out of sympathy with the people, to a section of whom only it ministers, and that being the case, it ought not to receive State recognition to the prejudice of other existing religious bodies, A conference, which was fol-

lowed by a public meeting, of persons favour- able to the disestablishment of the Welsh Church, was held in Liverpool this week, and a perusal of the papers then read and speeches made must carry conviction to the minds of all that in Wales at any rate the Church occupies a most anomalous position, and one which to every intelligent individual is utterly untenable. A few facts from these papers will serve to show not only the vitality of Nonconformity in the Principality, lint on the other hand how lifeless is the National Charch. Of the r,000,000 Welsh speaking and worshipping population, the National Churoh I includes within its fold only 200,000, whilst the adherents of the Nonconformist churches number Soo,ooo. But what is more notice- able is, that even if the majority of the wor- shipping population in Wales desired to attend the church, there is not accommoda- tion provided for them. Were all the churches in the Principality filled to their utmost capa- city they could not accommodate more than .4.00,000 ; whereas the Nonconformists have built 4,36! places of worship, and provided • accommodation for 59 per cent. of the whole worshipping population, or almost a million people. In one district alone, Festiniog, 27 Nonconformists chapels have been built, giving accommodation to x 1,800 worshippers, and connected with these places of worship there are 4,200 communicants and 6,700 Sun- day school scholars; on the other hand, in this same district there have been built only four churches belonging to the establishment, giving accommodation to 1,200 people, and connected with them are but soo communi- cants, and a like number of scholars. Here the church is shown to be very far behind. It • is sometimes said that the Nonconformists exist only on paper, but as the Dean of Ban- gor once sagely observed, "paper adherents do not give money." What, then, are the facts as to the giving of money for chapel purposes by these Welsh Nonconformists. Accurate returns are not obtainable, but it is confidently asserted by those who have given this matter every attention that the Noncon- formists of Wales have spent upon their places of worship something like £3,000,000. That surely is a princely sum to have been contributed voluntarily by the people, and speaks volumes for their attachment to their principles. It has been stated by the Dean of Bangor, with evident satisfac- tion and as zomething to be proud of, that during the last 4.0 years the Churchmen of Wales have spent on rebuilding churches £1,089,247; but the Calvinistic Methodists of Wales alone have spent in 30 years £1,096,608. The Churchmen, then, have nothing to boast of on this point. Though the great portion of the wealth of Wales is, we believe, confined to the church people, yet so little of it is expended upon their places of worship that we find not all thq Nonconformist denominations together, but only one of them surpass Churchmen in pro- viding accommodation. It is also the fact that in providing for missionary or other reli- gious purposes the Welsh Nonconformists contribute very much more than their brethren of the church. In Liverpool there is a larger Welsh population than there is probably in any other city or borough in England, and it is found that in Liverpool the Welsh church has no hold upon the Welsh people. It is 60 years since a Welsh church was first built there, and there is only one such church still; but the two or three small and insignificant Welsh chapels that existed in Liver- pool then have ;increased to more than 5o now. The number of communicants at the Welsh church in Liverpool is only 273, whereas the Welsh Nonconformist bodies have ro,ooo communicants, and they col- lected last year for religious purposes no less than £20,000. The advance which Welsh Nonconformity has made in recent years has been most marked, and it is all the more re- markable that it has been accomplished in spite of the persecution to which it has been subjected at the bidding of Welsh church- men. The facts we have quoted point to but one conclusion, that the Church in Wales has ceased to be the church uf the people, that it ministers to a minority, and that a very small one, of the population, and it is therefore an injustice that it should be pro- tected by the State We believe it would be found to be to the interest of the Church it- self that it should be unfettered by State control. If it were free to do its work in its own way, if its adherents were compelled al they ought to be to pay for the ministrations of the clergy, and if the clergy were imbued with a deeper sense of the responsibility of their office, we have no doubt much more satisfactory results would be achieved. It was said that the Irish Church when disestab- lished would die, but so far from that being the case it has shown more vitality since dis- establishment than it had done for many years previously; and we have every con- fidence that this would be the case in Wales as Well. The reasons urged so successfully for disestablishment in Ireland may be urged with even greater force for disestablishment in Wales, and we hope the day is not far dis- tant when, like Ireland, Wales will be rid of an institution so inmical to its best interests. Meetings such as those held at Liverpool this week serve, as Mr. BRIGHT says, to " help forward disestablishment not in Wales only, but also in England and Scotland," and we are sure that one immediate result from them will be to strengthen Mr. DILLWYN when he submits to Parliament his resolution in favour of the disestablishment of the Welsh Church, a resolution which, we submit, deserves the support of every Liberal mem- ber of Parliament, and the sympathy of all lovers of complete religious equality.

BUFFALO BALL AT WARRINGTON.—The annual ball of. the Royal Antediluvian Order of Buffaloes was held in the Drill Hall, Legh-street, on Monday night. About 200 per- sons assembled, and, to the charming strains of Mr. Brims-, low's band, found pleasure in thG evolutions of the "light fantastic toe" until the "wee sma' hours" of Tuesday- morning. Several grand lodge officers from Liverpool were in attendance, as were also a number of military, brothers from Orford Barracks. Mr. J. MaClew (secretary) and Mr. G. Reynolds officiated as masters of ceremonies. For the occasion tho hall was beautifully decorated with Rags,- banners, bannerettes, de., kindly lent by Mr. .Tesper and. Mrs. Brarley, of Sankey-street, and Messrs. Johnson or . Bridge-street. The refreshments were provided by Mr. lobri Allen, of the Pelican Inn, Buttermarket-street, The pro• rends of the ball are to be devoted to the widows and orpita.ris' tsnd, and after payiag the expenses. there will be a harad- some balance for that purpose loft in the hands, et the treasurer, Mr. J. Lingley.—To tho fund Captain Ridgway had kindly subscribed ss. REFERENCE TO TRH LATE MR, MOORN, AT DARES/AMY

—At Daresbury Petty Semions, on Tri sday, Mr. Edward Greenell (chairman) referred 1) ths death of the late Mr. G. T. Moore, and said that a,tboogh he had known the de- ceased a great number of yea 3 he did ma remomber one single occasion when there had b!en ashtdo of conflict be- tween Mr. Moore and the Bench. Respect aad consideration ' he had invariably shown to the Bench, and he could not let that opportunity to pass without expr,.ssiag his sympathy on behalf of the Bench for Mrs. Moore and family.—Mr. Nicholson (magistrates' clerk) also nude a few appropriate remarks.—Mr. Percy Davies said that as a solicitor who bad met Mr. Moore perhaps oftener than any otner practitioner in Warrington and district, he might say that it had been It great grief to him to miss Mr. 211-n.re's kind and genial face from that court and other courts wh;ch ha had attended. In all his experience he never saw Mr. Moore vexed or lose his temper in the slightest degree. Ile endorsed what had been said as to the sympathy which they all felt for Mrs. Moore and family.

Sr. Joare's CHURCH, RUNCORN.—The annual Congrega- tional meeting in connection with St, John's Presbyterian -Church was held in the school-room on Monday evening. The accounts of the past year were read by the treasurer (Mr:James Pritchard), and they showed s very satisfac- tory state of affairs. Addresses were delivered by the Rev. E. Jerman, Wrexham, and Mr. Bailie, Chester, who attended as a deputation from the Presbytery. ALLEGED DESERTION OF PAIHILY.—At Widnes Police Court, yesterday, Michael Flynn, a labourer, was charged With deserting his wife and family. About a fortnight ago the prisoner left the tows, leaving no trace of his where- abouts, and his wife and family were compelled to seek Parish relief. On Thursday he was found working on the new railway line that is being made at Ditton, and was apprehended.—The ptisoner WAS remanded to Prescot Petty Ileadens. SINGULAR DEATH AT IiALTON.—A young man named Robert Hinde died under singular circumstances on Friday last week. The deceased had been ailing for a few days, and had remained at home from his work. On Friday he went for a walk into the garden adjacent to his father's house, and half an hour afterwards his sister found him lYing lifeless on the ground. Dr. Carruthers certified that death resulted from heart disease, and the Coroner deemed an inquest unnecessary. The following appeared in a Canadian paper—the London Advertiser' January 9th :—" A gentleman in this ellY has received aletter from Mr. William Littler, Runcorn, Cheshire, England, in which he states that from a visit here last autumn he took a great fancy to the city, and Purposes making it his home and place of business in the hi+ ure. He was favourably impressed with Canada in many respects. Mr. Littler is negotiating for the purchase of Churcher's soap works." Mr. Littler was formerly con- nected with the Press in Runcorn. TANNAKER'S JAPANESE TROUPE.—It Will be seen from our advertising columns that this celebrated troupe of male and female artistes are to give three of their wonderful per- formances in the Public Hall, Runcorn, this week. The "company have acquired a deservedly popular name by the Clever and daring character of their exhibitions, and we have no doubt that those who patronise them will be well repaid for their visit. A feature in connection with the entertainment is the fact that each of the audience receives a present of some article of Japanese manufacture. LODOINO-HOUSE ROBBERY AT WOOLTON.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Albert Lloyd, a middle-aged Than, was charged with stealing a waistcoat, value 10a, the property of Martin Cule.—Cule keeps a lodging-house in Grave-street, Woolton, and on the night of the 27th January the prisoner stayed there. Next morning, imme- diately after his departure, the waistcoat was missed, and P.C. Blackthorne ascertained that the prisoner had pledged it for 2s 81 with James Brooks, pawnbroker, Woolton.—The Prisoner, who pleaded guilty, was sentenced to a month's bard labour. A DANGEROUS PRACTICE AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions on Monday, before Mr. H. Gaskell, senior, and Mr. G. Pdkington, Thomas Daley, a tramp, and Win. Kinchley, a pedlar, were each sentenced to seven days' im- Prisonment for sleeping in a chemical works on Saturday flight; and for committing a similar offence, Thomas Lewis, a labourer, and James Molyneux, a young man, were sen- tenced to a month's hard labour as incorrigible offenders. The Bench expressed their determination to stop the dan- gerous practice of sleeping in chemical works, which In- Vector Wood observed, was caused by the men spending their money in drink, and thus being unable to obtain SCALDED TO DEATH BY A CuP OF TRA AT RUNCORN.— At the Anchor Inn, Runcorn, on Monday afternoon, Mr. Coroner Ridgway held an inquiry touching the death of a Child, three years of age, named Robert William Dillon, of Brunswick-street. The evidence showed that on Friday the boy was standing on a stool at the table for the purpose of eating a meal. The stool slipped, and the child in order to save itself from falling clutched the table cloth, pulling a Cap of tea upon its chest. It was severely scalded, and the usual remedies were applied. Next day worse symptoms appeared, and Dr. Bagnall was called in, but the child lied on Monday morning.—The jury returned a verdict of Ac- eidental death." CRUELTY TO A HORSE AT WlDNES.—Before Mr. Hol- brcok Gaskell, sen., and Mr. W. D. Holt, at Widnes ?etty Sessions, on Wednesday, Joseph Preston, a greengroct was charged with having on the 17th January worked a horse Whilst in an unfit state. P.S. Clarkson gave eviden e that the horse was in fair condition and had no sores u on its body, but it was very lame and not in a fit state to ork.— The defendant said he did not wish to do anything wrong. The animal was lame on the fetlock joint, and as would have cost a considerable sum to cure it, he destrr .ed the horse.—Mr. Gaskell said it appeared the defenelant e stroyed the animal to save his pocket—A fine of is and c sts, 15s cid, was imposed.

• OAKLAND-STREET METHODIST FREE CHURCH, WIDNES.— The members of the Band of Hope in connection with this church gave on entertainment to a good audience on Monday -evening. The Rev. W. Vause presided. Ark excellent pro- gramme of songs, recitations, kc., was gone through in capital style, the following members taking part :—Mrs. Joseph Betney, Misses Jessie Hughes, A. Betney, Mary Wilcock, Ellen Ferber, Ethel Atherton, E. Betney, A. Atherton, E. Robinson, M. Smith, E. Gough, Harrison, Johnson, and Rimmtr ; Messrs. H. Wilcock, E. 0. Evans, T. Whitehead, John Ferber, and W. Price. Under the leadership of Mr. Joseph Betney the children sang several melodies in good style. Mr. Alfreil Ogden ably officiated at the harmonium. THE DANGERS OF THE STREET.—OR Wednesday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, John Douglas, 15 years of age, was summoned OD a charge of throwing stones.—P.S. Strick- land said about half-past ten o'clock on Saturday morning, the 19th January, he saw the defendant throwing stones from a catapult in New-street, Widnes. He gave a wrong :tame and address to the sergeant, who had considerable trouble with him.—Superintendent Barker said this was a most dangerous game, as not only did the boys throw stones, but small bullets. He had had several complaints about windows being smashed with bullets —Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, Sen., said a person's eye might be knocked out, and a great deal of damage done by such an instrument.— The defendant, whose mother appeared, was fined Is and costs, Ts flcl.

• EXTRAORDINARY FATALITY AT WIDNES.—A boy named Joseph William Greyson was killed at Widnes on Tuesday Right, under peculiar circumstances. His parents were on the tramp, and were walking from St. Helens to Widnes. When they had reached Bold they were overtaken bv a lorry. The driver, Charles Smithson, who lives at the Volunteer Arms, Lugsdale, offered to give the boy a ride, and his mother gratefully consented. The boy, who was four years of age, was placed on the front of the lorry. In Moorfield-lane the waggon was passed by a trap, and imme- diately afterwards Smithson missed the boy from his seat. 'The mother went back, and about fifteen yards behind the hlff.Y she found her child lying on the ground fut his back. He was bleeding from the nostrils. and apparently in a cly'ng state. George Plumpton a labourer who lived in the lane,took the child to the Castle Inn and attempted to administer brandy, but it was then dead. The body was conveyed to Widnes Police Station in the trap of Mark Johnson. and was afterwards placed in the Grosvenor Hotel, where Mr. Brighouse held the inquest on Thursday. Evidence bearing out the above narrative Wae given, and the jury came to the conclusion that death occurred accidentally, and that no blame was attributable to any person. WinNee LIBERAL ASSOCIATION: DITTON AND CHONTOR DIVISION—The annual meeting of this division took place ...00 Friday night, at Chestnut Lodge, Ditton. Mr T R Warne was in the chair, there being also present Messrs W Berry, W Turton, T Dennett, D Stone, T Booth, E Warne, and 11 B Shores (general secretary). The committee ap- Pointed was constituted as follows :—Messre P Glover, T Booth, M Taylor, J Peover, J Gardner, W Turton, C Robin. Son, E Thompson, W E Oakden, A G Kyle, W Bowerman, • t,Russell, J Brown, Job Glover, W Ireland, I Hunt, J Swift, R Gardner, J Barkley, J Taylor, T R Warne, P Higgins, J Kelsall, E Warne, P -Dannett, C H Watson, J Williamson, G Cole, W Clarke, J Gordon, R Leadbeater, H Leadbeater, T Stone, W Donaldson, A E Smith, J Hough, D Warr, J Penny, and G Glover, The Ex cutive Committee was formed as follows :—Messrs P Glover, T Booth, M Taylor, T B Warne, J Peover, J Williamson, W Clark, A G Kyle, C H Watson, I Runt, J Gardner, W Turton, C Robinson, W $ Oakden, and James Brown.—..lte was ,announced by Mr Shores that Mr P lover :1 the chairmanship of the division, Parner Ile a desire to resign secretary testified to the services rendered by Mr Glover during vote of tebasiLsyears he bad held the otfice.—A unanimous as accorded to Mr Glover; and on the motion of Mr Below: seconded by Mr Stone, Mr J Warne was appointed chairman of the division for the ensuing year.—Mr J Booth was re- appointed bon. sec., on the motion of Mr Turton, seconded 09 Mr Dennett, and he was heartily thanked for his past services. TEE STORM AT WIDNES AND RUNCORN. The gale which swept over the neighbourhood on Saturday last Caused a considerable destruction of property. The works of Messrs. William Dainteth and Company, at Halebank, were almost entirely detnoliehed, and the cost to the owners will be heavy. The works consisted of two large sheds about 50 feet in length, one being two stories high and the Other a single storey. Aeout half-past four on Saturday afternoon the roof of the large building was carried com- pletely off by a large gust of wind, and the remaining part of the building then fell with a heavy crash. Some of the timber was carried 100 yards. About 20 minutes previous to the occurrence Mr. Rogers, who is a partner in the firm, With his wife, were seated in the shop. Had they delayed a little longer there is no doubt they would have been buried In the ruins. Only one of the machines in the shop was damaged, and the wire and other valuable material was soon carried to a place of safety. By the same gust of wind a large hen cote was carried away from a home near into Ditton brook, a distance of several yards. The shop of Mr. Leather, butcher, suffered considerable damage, and the slaughter- house adjoining was partly unroofed. A large piece of galvanised iron was carried from the shop of Mr. Roxburgh at the same place, and whirled with great violence at the "aP Gate Hotel, where it narrowly escaped a window. At a cottage, the wind blew open the back door, and a violent gust took the panels clear out of the front door, which stood uPposite. At Appleton, numerous slates were dislodged and windows broken. The vestry at St. Bede's Catholic Chapel Was unroofed. The demage done at Runcorn was compara- tively small, but the traffic at the port was stopped on Saturday and Sunday in consequ.mce of the storm. The Pitt Diamond, laden with slack, was overturned when enter- ing Weston Point dock behind a steamer. The crew were rescued by the next fiat in tow.

FORTHCOMING LIBERAL DEMONSTRATION AT RUNCORN. —On Thursday next the annual demonstration in connec- tion with the Runcorn Liberal Association will be held in the Public Hall. Mr. R. Shaw, the president, will occupy the chair, and Mr. Joseph Arch,. Mr. W. R. Kennedy, Mr. G. W. Latham, and Mr. J. Brunner are expected to take part in the proceedings, which will no doubt be marked by the usual enthusiasm. A VIOLENT ASSAULT AT RUNCORN. —At Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, before Mr. A. Thomas and Captain C. W. liazlehurst,.Wm. New, a pilot on the river Mersey, was brought up under a warrant charged with having, on the 26th January assaulted John (Santley. The two men had been engaged in raising a sunken flat, belonging to Mr. Bate, at the Old Quay Dock. When the work was com- pleted Santley was paid, and he handed the prisoner his share. The prisoner was dissatisfied with the amount he received, and on the day in question went info Santley's house. Santley was lying on the sofa unwell, and the pri- soner dragged him off on to the floor, and severely abused him about the head and ribs, kicking him savagely about the bead and body. His condition was considered so dan- gerous that Dr. MacDougall was called in and his wounds dressed. When the prosecutor's wife appeared before the magistrates for a summons she said the prisoner made her husband's ribs" grater together,'' but the prosecutor :now wanted to entirely withdraw the charge, and it was with difficulty the above facts were elic'ted from the witnessea.— The Bench fined the prisoner 405 and costs 13s, or in default a month's hard labour. ENTERTAINMENT AT ST. MARY'S SCHOOL, WIDNES.— An entertainment of a miscellaneous character was given on Monday, at the St. Mary's Catholic Schools, Widnes. The entertainment was under the charge of " Dr. Branni- gan," of Liverpool, who was assisted by several well known local performers. The St. Mary's Total Abstinence League brace band, under the conductorship of Mr. Farrall, of War- rington, gave several pieces during the evening in very good style. The St. Mary's Glee Class gave the two choruses " Awake," /Milian lyre" and "The stars that above us are shining," with much harmony. Mr. Cierraghty was again very successful in his humorous song " More drink and less talk," and was encored. Mr. Lawton gave the song "Every bullet has its billet " with admirable power ; while the duet of the Misses Hewitt, " List to the convent bells," was marked by an artistic style and sweet- ness of delivery that won much applause. Mr. John Carroll (Dr. Brannigan) in his Egyptian tragedy, entitled " The pest of the Pyramids; or, the domineering donkey driver of Damanoor," was highly amusing, and the audience bestowed well merited applause upon the per- formers. The Rev. J Oldham gave the favourite song "The Village Blacksmith," with much feeling and expres- sion. Mr. John Quinn's recitation of "Molly Muldoon" was clearly given, and was warmly encored. The duet 'Larboard Watch" was given by the Rev. J. Oldham and Mr. Oakden in capital style. Mr. Samuel Quinn gave the comic song "The Complaints of Life" with much humour, and the piece was encored. Miss Hewitt was also encored for the tasteful manner in which she sang " When swallows homeward fly." Mr. J. Carroll again caused infinite amuse- ment by his inimitable performance of "The Miserable Man," and he was vigorously applauded. Miss Cullen very efficiently acted as accompanist. The I M. Ryan was in the chair, and at the close delivered a W comments on the performance. He remarked that the, vere very grate- ful to all who had assisted, and tnanks we due to the Rev. J. Oldham for the assistance he had rend ed in getting up the entertainment. There were about 60 persons present. A concert in behalf of the widow al children of the &au-Ilan Pendlebury, who perished during eof the recent storms, was given in Halton Parochial S 00l on Monday evening, and a good sum was realised.
PRESENTATION TO AIR. AZ‘ MRS. S. K. MUSE'RATT, OF WI NES.

An exceedingly pleasant ceremony took place on Satur- day, at Flint, when the local employes of the well-known firm of Messrs. Muspratt and Sons, of Liverpool, Widnes, and Flint, presented Mr. Sydney Knowles Muspratt, a mem- ber of the firm, with a beautiful and valuable testimonial in commemoration of his recent marriage. The presentation consisted of four pieces of silver plate, which bore the in- scription, "Presented to Mr. and Mrs. S. K. Muapratt, on the occasion of their marriage, by the employes of Flint works, November 27th, 1883." Opportunity was also taken on the occasion to offer for the acceptance of Mrs. Muspratt a magnificent gold bracelet set with five brilliants which also had a suitable inscription. The marriage of gr. Muspratt occurred in November last, but a lengthy honeymoon- tour in the South of France and Algeria frustrated, for the time being, the amiable plans of the many hundreds of workmen with whom he is brought into continual business rela- tions' to mark their sense of the regard and esteem in which they hold him, as well as to signalise their gratification at the auspicious event. The wedded couple only recently re- turned home from their trip, and a week ago became the re- cipients of a costly and admirable testimonial, made by the Widnes workmen of the firm, the proceedings being of a very interesting nature. The men engaged at the Flint works chose Saturday for the purpose of testifying their ap- preciation of one who is always considered in the most popular light amongst them; and, notwithstanding that the weather was of a very tempestuous character, some hun- dreds of the employia assembled at the works shortly be- fore four o'clock in the afternoon, and accorded Mr. and Mrs. S. K. Muspratt and other members of the family a hearty reception. There were on the platform Mr. and Mrs. S. K. Muspratt, Mr. and Mrs. It' chard Muspratt, Miss F. Muspratt, Miss Moon (aunt), Mr. and Mrs. James Muspratt, Mr. Alfred Dyson (mana- ger of the works), Mr. C. E. Dyson and others. Mr. Alfred Dyson made the presentation to Mr. Muspratt amid the acclamations of the assembled workmen, and Mr. Maspratt, who seemed deeply moved, acknowledged the gift in a few appropriate sentences. He observed that the esteem and regard of the workmen would encourage him to further strive to promote their welfare individually and collectively, both as regarded the board schools in the borough and in sanitary and other matters connected with the Corporation. (Applauss.)—Mr. Dyson then presented the bracelet to Mrs. Muspratt, and Mr. Muspratt responded on behalf of his wife, who desired him to say that whenever she wore it it would always bring to her recollectidn the men of Flint. (Ap- plause.)—Other short speeches were made, and the proceed- ings concluded. On Friday afternoon at the Liverpool office of Messrs. James Muspratt and Sons, Mr. Sydney K. Muspratt was presented with an illuminated address on vellum (designed and executed by Mr. James Orr Marples in his usual skil- ful style), as a memento of his marriage, which was cele- brated in London on the 27th November last; also as a token of the high' esteem in which he is held by the em- ployes of the above firm at the Liverpool office. The presentation was made by Mr. H. C. Banister, manager to James Muspratt and Sons, in the Presence of Mr. Richard Muspratt (Mayor of Flint), Mr. James L. Muspratt; J.P ' and others. Mr. Sydney K. Muspratt, in reply, expressed his heart- felt thanks to Mr. Banister and the staff for their kindness and good wishes, which he would never forget, and hoped that the present good feeling existing between employers and employes would long continue.

div.head: WIDNES ITUBLICAN IN COURT. A DOUBTFUL CASE.
div.p: A WIDNES ITUBLICAN IN COURT. A DOUBTFUL CASE.

At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Mr. W. D. Holt (in the chair) and Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, Robert Herriman, landlord of the Mersey Hotel, Mersey-road, was summoned to answer a charge of having, on the 13th Jan., kepthis house open during prohibited hours. Joseph Heap and William Morley were charged with being upon the premises during prohibited hours. Mr. J. 0. Swift, of St. Helens, defended.—P.S. Clarkson said he visited the defen- dant's house on Sunday, the 13th January, at a quarter to four o'clock. The door was open in the same manner as it was on week days. He went into No. 2 room, where he saw four men, and on a table in the room were four glasses, which centained beer He knew Morley and Heap, Who were there. He called the landlord's attention to the men. The landlord replied, "I saw Morley at the door. He looked starved, and knowing that he had been ill, I asked him if he would come in and have a glass of beer." When he MS taking the names of the men Morley said "1 have only just come in, Mr. Clarkson." Two of the men stated that they belonged to a ste imer at Weston Point, and he had since ascertained that this statement was correct. The landlord subsequently said he was sorry, but he had only had two of the men to die- ner.—Cross-examined by Mr. Swift, the witness said he knew that Morley was in bad circumstances and living on his club money, and that the landlord and he were on friendly terms.—P.C. Cheers, who was with the last wit- ness, corroborated his evidence.—For the defence Mr. Swift said Heap and Morley were in the house for the purpose of having dinner with the landlord, who was the friend of Morley. A short time before the 13th Heap's mother came from Greenfield on the line from Huddersfield to Man- chester, and she stayed at the defendant's house, as they could not find rooms for her at her son's lodgings. On the Wednesday pwevlous to the Sunday in question' the land- lord told Heap that as his mothsr was there he had better come in for dinner on Sunday, and he also asked Morley. As soon as dinner was over, about half-past three, the two men each took a glass of beer into the room overlooking the river, and they had not been there long when the officers made their appearance. Neither of them had ordered or paid for any drink. The defendant, who was formerly butler to a gentleman of position at Wootton, had been landlord of the house two years, and he had always conducted it in a respec- table manner. Morley had been out of work five or six weeks, awl the defendant had behaved very kindly to him, sometimes givinv him a glass of beer and sometimes a meal. Mr. Swift pointed out to their Worships that a landlord could enter- , tain his friends, and if he could prove that he had only I been doing so on this occasion, he should ask for his dis- charge.—Herriman was then called, and corroborated his advocates' statement. In cross-examination by Saperinten- dent Barker, be said his house never was closed on a Sun- day, because it was a regular house for travellers.—Mr. Swift was not aware that a landlord was compelled to keep his door shut.—By Superintendent Barker: He did not hear Morley say he had just invited him in.—Joseph Heap, time- keeper at Messrs Mathieson's works, living with George Williams, at Buck-terrace, off Parsonage-road, and William Morley, labourer, Cholmondeley-street, also gave corrobora- tive evidence.—Richard Jones, the barman, proved that the men dined with the landlord.—Mr. Holt said there was a doubt in the magistrates' minds whether the men did dine at the hotel, but they should give the landlord the benefit of the doubt, and dismiss the case —Mr. Gaskall : Don't put yourself in a doubtful position again.—The case against ' Morley and Heap was withdrawn.

. again. So he liked to watch the driver and see how the great machine burst through the air at a mile a minute. But the responsible driver was always at his post, and that responsible driver drove. One of the most interesting social gatheriogs of the week was Mr. Mackenzie's lecture to actors and actresses on the subject of how they were to manage their voices. Nearly all the profession were there, and all the audience came by invitation. What the aurist said was of course said with authority, but I think the advice he gave with most authority was that stays were an enormity. He did not go in for their abolition. I suppose no Hartley-street doctor has the courage to do that; but he showed that tight lacing, which is chargeable with all sorts of calamities in the dis- trict, that is tight laced actually extends its baleful in- fluence so high up as your throat. In one or two other points he gave very practical and unexpected advice. We all know that when a boy's veice or a girl's voice is "cracking" the singing master should get his conge. The lecturer did not think so at all. Here was a piece of news that every- one heard with astonishment; but there was another , announcement more remarkable still. It is "interesting to public speakers, members of Parliament, clergymen, and I others." The glass of water on a platform table is a mistake. If your tonoe is parched—go on. If your lips are dry—go ; on. You'd have to do it if you were on the floor of the House, or in the pulpit. If you can't go on, stop. But whatever you do—no water. And as the lecturer gave this excellent advice, he emptied his glass into which he had previously emptied the water bottle.

Even the South-Eastern is going to take electricity. Of course, it has a system of its own. They all have. But its system is singular. I suppose it is storage. At all events, there is no engine. There is a primary battery, such as there might be in any electric contrivance. But that great engine, panting and thudding, and bursting, is not to be scheduled in the list of South-Eastern nuisances. And then there is another remarkable thing about this new South-Eastern illuminant. The company have not only tried the experiment, but they are going to adopt the electricity. That really is very singular. All over Eng- land Companies are trying experiments, which prove emi- nently satisfactory. But no sooner has this been settled to the absolute content of shareholders, directors, and the public, than the company reverts to gas. Why, even at Buckingham Palace, where there are no shareholders, and for the most part of the year no inhabitants, electricity, which was so successful in the State apartments last season, will not be used this year. There seems to be always some but, after everything has gone smooth, which shuts off the current and lays the gas.

The decision of the Court of Appeal in the Bournemouth Breach of Promise case seems really to have been very hard on the unfortunate defendant. The litigation at every stage has given surprise. The defendant's counsel expected the verdict would go against him, but thought the damages at most would be a couple of hundred. When the jury came out with their sensational £3,000, no one thought it would be upheld. It was only to go to the Divisional Court and get it upset. But the Divisional Court stood to the lady, and so now has the Court of Appeal. Juries are often very inscrutable in their verdicts, and especially so in this kind of action. Judges generally have common sense,and seldom have much sentiment. But even with judges breach of promise makes an exception. There's the chWalric judge and there's the commercial judge, and when sentiment comes in they take such opposite views. And it is so easy to take a big handful of damages out of another man's pocket and give it over to the woman. The Master of the Rolls is a sort of knight ertant, his lance always in rest to succour the damsel whose lover cries off. Sir Ballot Brett delights in "cases of public interest," and when he tries them he gener- ally makes the interest greater. Sooner or later this form of action will disappear, and the verdict in Miller v Joy is the kind of occurrence which is wanted to bring the action into additional. disrepute.

OUR LONDON LETTER.

HER MAJESTY'S MOVEMENTS-THE SPEAKER'S DINNER-THE DEATH OF THE MARQUESS OF HERTFORD - GILBERT'S NEW PLAY AT THE LYCEUM-MARY ANDERSON-THE HAYMARKET -MISS KATE TERRY'S FIRST APPEARANCE- THE LATE LORD GROSVENOR-AN AUDIENCE OF ACTORS-TIGHT SPAYS AND LOUD VOICES -RAILWAYS AND ELECTRICITY, THE SOUTH.- EASTERN-"MILLER V. JOY."
LONDON, THURSDAY.

This year Her Majesty's foreign movements have been very fully and freely predicted. If she goes to the Riviera when all the shopkeepers of all the little towns along the Mediteranean are having a very bad time, and are looking forward to a very good one, it is to Mentone she will go, and it is Mr. Hemfrey's villa that Her Majesty will occupy. But before the London season begins there will be a Forrestry Exhibition in Edinburgh, in which Her Majesty takes great interest. So we are to see the Queen at Holyrood. And lastly, there is the German marriage at Darmstadt, at which it is expected Her Majesty will "assist." The Queen's engagement book is pretty-well filled up.

I hear that in the festivities which usher in a new session there will next week be a notable gap. That wonted full dress Parliamentary dinner, with which the Speaker lightly begins laboure which become grave as they progress, will not be held. Sir Henry Brand is indeed still the Speaker of the House of Commons, but everyone knows he will hold that title only a few days after Parliament has mat, pos- sibly for a very short time. Mr. Peel could net very well give the Speaker's dimmer till he is the Speaker, and so the custo- mary official banquets will be reduced by the loss of one of the most important and the most pleasant. One hears nothing but praise of Mr. Arthur Peel. " The most conscientious mars in the house "—said an old Tory— "with but one fault, that he is on the wrong side." With the impartial hand of which Horace speaks, Death has knocked at the doors of two of the greatest of eur old English families this week; I suppose no man ever was so popular amonst the comparatively few who knew him as the late Lord Hertford. He was a Conservative, and took office ten years ago as Lord Chamberlain, but the animosity which politics will engender bad no part in his composition. He was a personal friend of the Prince Consort and the Queen, and lived a good part of his life at Windsor. Not succeeding in the direct line to his title, it was perhaps less annoying to him to find that his cousin, the Marquess of Hertford, had left everything away from him th4t he could. That was the old Marquees, whom Thackeray has endowed with a terrible immortality as Marquess of Stevne, the wicked nobleman, in the pages of "Vanity Fair." Thackeray was a young man living in Paris, where the old Marquess had taken his abode. Hertford House, the family mansion, was in Picca- dilly, fronting the Green Park, I suppose one of the hand- somest of all mansions in Piccadilly. That roadway used to be macadamised, but a good many years ago, there arose a kind of mania for paving the London streets with blocks of granite. It began in the City, but it soon spread to Piccadilly. The Marquess remonstrated with the Nestry. The Vestry acted as though they did not cars twopence for the Marquess. Then—said Lord Hertford—l'll make you care. The moment the objectionable pavement was put down he closed the shutters of Hertford House, would not live in it himself, and would not let it to anyone else. For years upon years one of the handsomest mansions is Lon- don remained without an occupant. But during those years the offending Vestry lost the rates which would have been paid it the house had been inhabited. This, indeed, was amputation of the nostrils, with a view to irritate the physiogomy.

The one dramatic event of the week has been the produc- tion of a one-act play at the Lyceum, written by Mr. Gilbert for Miss Anderson. The plot gives every opportunity for a great actress to show all her powers. Clarke, a French actress, secretly married to an actor, is insulted by the profligate Due d'Orleans. Her lover tries to protect and to challengo the Prince, but the DilC pleads his rank, and won't fight with an actor. So Clarice tries stratagem. She affects to have quarrelled with her lover, and invites the Prince and all his profligate companions to supper. There is a very, gay scene beautifully put on the stage at the Lyceum, and then the guests disappear and the lovers are together. At this moment the husband rushes in, tears off his actor's trappings, and forces the prince to a duel. The combatants retire to a garden behind the house. The gay friends and boon companions of the prince come trooping in. Clarice, anxious and terrified at the drama that is going on, has to be light-hearted and frivolous with her guests, and the sus- pense is kept up till her husband rushes in, having avenged his case and her honour. The play has some defects, but it certainly gives every opportunity to the actress. Miss Anderson quite failed. All the subtlety and delicacy, all the subdued feeling, the ground swell of emotion, and what artists would call the modelling of the character, she passed over. Her attitudes were very graceful, and evidently very well studied and there did come at the end an intensity of feeling and a a burst of tenderness and passion which were very fine. But that we should expect from any actress of capability for tragedy. It is curious how society has gone mad about this pretty Amerioan. There seems to have arisen a necessity to have one reigning beauty whom people can talk about at dinner parties. It used to be Mrs. Langtry. Ills now Miss Anderson. Every one is a judge of beauty. When the three goddesses came to Paris we did not hesitate at all, but gave the apple to Venus. The Yankee Venus has gone on the stage, and the people who are sure she's a first rate beaty are equally sure she's a first rate actress. The critic may shake his head, but the public evidently think there is nothing in it. Miss Mary Anderson is very pretty and very lady-like. Her face is too short and too broad to belong to the highest order of beauty. She is well proportioned, and is able' to place herself in attitudes which are graceful and seem natural. Her voice is dis- agreeable. She is naturally a good average second-class actress, who by conscientious study has made the very most of her powers. So far as one can see from her per- formances in London, she seems quite destitute of genius.

Mr. Pinero's play is not much of a success. Pieces put on at the Haymarket are sure of a certain run. The manage- ment has been too long at its work to risk Si complete failure. But a questionable success can be played on till the dresses and mounting are paid for. Now they are rehearsing "Peril," which will appear in the bills in a fort- night. "Peril" is aversion of "Nos Intimes," one of the first of Barden's great successes. It is interesting, amongst other reasons, because like "Norma and Grisi," it was the occasion of bringisg Kate Terry first prominently before the public. That was two-and-twenty years ago, when Kate Terry was hand very like what Marion is now. Time hasit e d dealtn with Kate Terry. Marrying the chief slight,uin Iv d tner of Lewis and Allenby she has become very rich, la par and being gado humoured and rich she is—well, not so slight as she was 20 years ago. _

I have seen an absurd report that Wilson Barrett is going to play Hamlet so soon as the run of Claudian is at an end. This is mere conjecture. Every actor who comes to the front is credited with the intention of playing Hamlet. Claudian shows no signs of defective vitality, and, unless I greatly mistake, the next play at the Princesses will be by its authors. Very much has been said about Lord Grosvenor's death, and more about the life of this amiable and rather retiring young nobleman. Like the Duke of Devonshire, who would have been a great mathematician if he bad net been a Duke, Lord Grosvenor might have been a great mechani- cian if he had not been the son of a Doke. There is an absurd story told that he used to drive the Wild Irishman occasionally from Chestef up to Easton. He no more drove the mail engine than Handel's organ blower played the pastoral symphony. Lord Grosvenor was never so happy as when he was surrounded with pipes and valves and mechanical contrivances. He understood all the mechanism of an engine; could take one to pieces and pat it together
