div.head: RUNCORN YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION.
div.p: RUNCORN YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION.
ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual meetinee of the Runcern Young Men's Chris- tian 4lesociation was hal in the asSociaaari's rooms, High• street, on Mondry evening. Before the commencement of the business the members sat down to an exc a lent tea pro- vided by Mr. NV. Moore, of the Duke of Westminaer Cocoa Rooms. Subsequently Dr. Steele presided, and amongst those present were the Revs. W. Prestou, M A., F. al. Arms. son, and George Hack; Messrs. J. Simpson, a. C. Beckett, F. A. Lake, J. E. Meredith, T. Handley, W. estaw, J. Craig, S. Coventry, C. Pownall, J. W. Woodland, J. D. Jones, H. A. Hankinson, F. J. Norman, S. H. Dawson, G. Howard, Johnson, and W. Pownall, jun. (hon. sec.) The HON. SECRETARY read the ninth annual report, which stated that the association still occupied a prosperous and useful position among the institutions of the town. The balance sheet as produced by the treasurer would show a satisfactory state of affairs, but apart from the pecuniary success of the association, the renewed vigout which had ckaracterised several branches of the work undertaken had been a source of much encouragement to the committee, and they trusted the present vitality would be permanent and conduce still further to the development of the Young Men's ,Christian Association. Greater interest was being taken in the work of the historical society. Unfortunately, al- though several important and instrnctive lectures were , delivered, the attendance was never se large as might have , been expected, but this could be accounted for by the fact of the late commencement, several of the lectures running , into the summer months, when it is difficult to offer sue- , cessful indoor attractions to the public. To Mr. J. A. Smith thanks were due for the efficient manner in which • the secretarial duties were performed, while to Mr. William , Handley the committee were also indebted for his services , as president. Taught by experience, the committee cone- i menced the second season at the beginning of the winter , months, and they were happy to say they had , been largely attended. The Bible class had continued its career, and its meetings bad exercised beneficial influence amongst the members of the association. It would be remembered that a debt of £9 was incurred in providing a treat for the aged people of the town and a free breakfast for poor children. The committee made several attempts to liquidate the amount owing (which it may be observed was advanced ont of the association funds), which proved un- successful. Arrangements were eventually made with Mr. A. Alexander, the director of the Liverpool Young Men's I Christian Association Gymnasium, to give an assault-at- arms on behalf of the object. The committee of the Run- corn Football Club also consented to play a match with the Gymnasium Club, and with this kind co-operation a profit of £5 lie. Gil. was realind. The annual pic-nic took place to Weaverham Wood on July 14th, the proceedings being of a very enjoyable character. Captain Clarke, with his cus- tomary kindnees, again placed a steamer at the disposal of the committee, and Mr. and Mrs. Sanderson, of Weaverham, generously catered for the party. A fruit banquet took place on August 30th, the gathering being very interesting. The reading-room had been made additionally attractive by the introduction of a large number of new periodicals, and the Committee had been gratified by the extensive use which has been made of its advantages. The young men's prayer meeting, which was held weekly, had been fairly atten- ded, and much spiritual blessing had attended the efforts of the promoters. On the 20th August, the resignation of Mr. C. Nickson, the secretary, was recieved with great regret, and the Committee took this opportunity of thanking Mr. Hick- son for his valuable services which he had rendered, and was still rendering to the Association. Mr. K. Evans was appointed in place of Mr. C. Nickson. That gentleman aeld the appointment until December 22, when he placed ais resignation in the hands of the committee prior to his de- parture to Australia. To show the appreciation in which his services were held the committee presented the retiring secretary with four volumes of Cannon Farrar's "Life of Christ." They appointed Mr. W. Pownall, jun., as hon. sec. protest. At the end of 1882 the number of members on the roll (honorary, active' and associate) stood at 135, but owing to removals and deaths the number has been reduced to 113; but the committee hopefully looked forward with the active and earnest co-operation of the present members, to a large augmentation during the present year. By the assistance which the committee rendered Professor Andre during his stay in Runcorn, they received a donation from that gentleman of £5, which they gratefully acknowledged. Dr. Steele had expressed a desire to withdraw from the posi- tion of president, which he has worthily occupied for two years; believing that in the interests of the Association pe- riodical changes should take place. The members joined in this regret, and heartily thanked him for his services. Mr. S. C. Baawarr said he had great pleasure in ap- pearing before the meeting in the capacity of a successful treasurer. For some years the association had been labour- ing under financial difficulties, but this year he was glad to say they had a balance in band which was not a fictitious one but real. He adverted to the satisfactory condition of the subscription list, and stated that the receipts for the past year—including subscriptions from honorary members £34 Os 01, subscriptions from active members £24 12s 131, and a balance of £3 4s 7d from the aged people s treat— were 193 Os Id. The expenditure—including £32 for rent, £29 143 2d for newspapers and periodicals, and £9 7s 101 sustained by children's treat—amounted to £B3 13s 51, leaving a balance in hand of £9 7s 81. (Applause.) The CIIMRBIAN, after congratulating the members upon the bright financial prospects of the society, referred to the works el the past year. He thought the committee had 'done wonders, and the present secretary, during his short Iterm of office had performed a great amount of work (Applause.) de had collected all outstanding subecriptions• and for the first time there were no members in arrear. The aged persons' treat had, been the Cause of much pleasure, and the assemblage of the old people was one of the finest sights he had ever soen. (Hear, hear.) He regretted that the membership of the year was not so large as that of the previous year. He hoped, however, that next year would see a large addition of. members to the associa- tion. He thought they should not limit the membership of the association to the better class, but should induce re- spectable workingmen to join. Frequently he saw large numbers standing about the corners of the street, who if they became members, and thoy could well afford the subscrip- tion, could profitably employ their leisure hours. (Hear, hear.) In retiring from the chair, be thanked them for the uniform courtesy displayed towards him, and his heartiest wish was that God's blessing might rest upon the associa- tion. (Applause.) Mr. F. A. LAKE moved the adoption of the report, which, he said, spoke wonders for the labours of the committee. He spoke in favour of the proposed gymnasium, and observed that when. he first came to Runcorn he used to hear of balances of £4O on the wrong side, and the association seemed to be dependent upon the generosity of one or two members to clear off the deficit. He did not believe in societies like that having very large balances, because it might seem that they were not doing all the god that they might with the money. Tne balance they had showed that the association occupied a healthy position. Mr. J. W. WOODLAND seconded the motion. While he agreed with the work the committee had accomplished, lie noticed that there was not much Christian work performed as there was in former times. He should have been better pleased had the report stated that something had ban done in the by ways and hedges, or the alleys and cauraa of the town, but he nevertheless congratulated the members upon the improved position they occupied compared to that held five or six years ago. (Applause.) Mr. BECKETT pointed out that the association had not suitable rooms for evangelical work, and were they to set their members to religious work they might sometimes trench upon the ground occupied by the churches. (Hear, hoar.) His view, was to go as far as opportunity and finances allowed. An effort was made to hold services in the Theatre on Sunday evenings, but the building could not be opened through what he might call the interference of the superintendent of police. The report was then adopted. Mr. W. SHAM proposed that the best thanks of the meet- ing be given to Dr. Steele for his services during the past year in a eulogistic speech. • Mr. S. C. BECKETT seconded the motion, remarking that it was owing to Dr. Steele's shrewdness that the association occupied its present prosperous position. (Applause.) The motion was carried with acclamation. Dr. STEELE briefly responded. On the motion of Mr. S. COVENTRY, seconded by Mr. C. NICKSON, Mr. S. C. Beckett was thanked for his labours as treasurer, and was unanimously elected president for the en- suing year. The newly-elected PRESIDENT then took the chair. In the course of a short address Mr. Beckett commented upon the-past work of the Association, and said he had desired to be released from the acceptance of the post of president, but they continued to press the honour upon Vim so very warmly that he could not do otherwise than consent. (Hear, hear.) He should do his best to carry on the objects of the Association, and strive still further to increase its usef at- flees, spiritually, mentally, and socially. (Applause.) On the motion of MT. WOODLAND, seconded by MT. HOWARD, Mr. J. E. Meredith was appointed treasurer. Mr. W. Pownall, jun., was elected secretary, on the pro- position of Mr. C. NICKSON, seconded by Dr. STEELE, both gentlemen speaking in complimentary terms of his abilities. , The following gentlemen were elected members of the committee :—Messrs. C. Pownall, J. A. Smith, F. J. Nor- man, J. Craig. J. Beveridge, J. Le Contier, and H. A. Han- kinson. Mr. S. H. Dawson was appointed assistant-secre- tary. The following is a list of the vice-presidents :—Revs. Canon Barclay, M.A., W. Prestor, M.A., J. D. Thomas, E. Williams, E. H. Arrason, G. Hack, J. Pickwell, W. Vance; Dr. Steele, Captain Hazlehurst, J.P., Messrs. J. Handley, J.P., G. L. Davies, J.P., R. Shaw, J. Simpson, G. S. Heinlehurst, C. Wigg. T. Norman, J. Meadowcroft, J. 0. Jack3on, W. B. Gibson, T. Handley, W. Whittaker, J. Johnson, and J. Humphreys. A vote of thanks was accorded to the vice-presidents, and Mr. E. M. ARNISON responded. The proceedings concluded with a vote of thanks to the chairman.

GORSYWILIPPING A GIRL.—At the St. Helens Police Court, on Friday, a young man, named James Watervrorth, was fined ss. and costs for striking a girl, named Ellen Rill, with a horsewhip at Parr Flatt, on the previous Sunday.— The girl, it seemed, had been playing at shuttle-cock along with some companions near defendant's house, and he irritated by the noise they were makinrg ran out and struck her with a horsewhip.—At the saran court a man, named Win. Blackburne, waq fined ss. and costs for having assAulted an elderly man, named. George Greee.

div.head: LECTURE AT WIDNES NATIONAL SCHOOLS.
div.p: LECTURE AT WIDNES NATIONAL SCHOOLS.

Mr. J. Croston, F.S.A , of Manchester, on Tuesday even- ing delivered a lecture on the "Antiquity, independence, and continuity ef the Church of England," in the Widnes National Schools. The Rev. J. Wright Williams presided, and there was a good attendance. The lecturer claimed for the Church of England an antiquity as great, or greater than the Church of Rome. When the claims of Christian light flashed upon the darkness of primeval Britain, and when the sacred truths were brought to our shores, the church was established in our land, and from that time to the present had continued. Long before the Roman mis- sionaries came the truth had been brought to England. There was an organiaed church in England before the land- ing of Augustine. England received its Christianity not from Rome but from the Church of Jerusalem. Their chnrch was an independent church, and not a branch of the Church of Rome; it was not founded on St. Peter but on the Apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner-stone. (Ap- plause.) The act of uniformity passed in the time of Charles the Second simply restored that which had been pre- viously in existence. It was said that the State established the Church. But it was a fact that the bishops of the Church being the most learned and cultured men in the kingdom that could be appealed to for counsel and advice, became the advisers of the King and his nobles, and they were instrumental in forming that body which eventually developed itself into a parliament. Thus the Church established the State, and not the State the Church. The State did not pay a farthing towards the maintenance of the church. Every Church of England clergyman was as in- dependent of the State as a Nonconformist minister was. (Applause.) The endowments of the Church belonged to them as long as the incumbent discharged his parochial duties as much as the endowments of a Nonconformist chapel belonged to the minister. The history of the Church was entwined with that of the State, and the Church could not be overthrown without a revolution in the land. (Ap- plause ) The customary votes of thanks concluded the pro- ceedings.

THE FATALITY ON THE RAILWAY AT WIDNES. Mr. Brighouse, the county coroner, held an inquest at the Mersey Hotel, on Saturday, on the body of Frederick William Gougle, a wheelwright, 24 years of age, whose parents reside at 44, Warrington-road, Widnes.—Mr. Fer- rand appeared on behalf of the London and North-Western Railway Company, and Inspector Carter was present. Mr. C. A. Kennion was foreman of the jury.—Evidence was given by Wm. Gough (the father of the deceased), Ernest Moss (signalman at Ann-street crossing), Miss Downie (the matron at the hospital), Alfred Gibson (engine driver, Acton Bridge), and William Kerr (labcurer, Penn-street, Widnes).—lt appeared that en the 26th December, the de- ceased, who lodged at Unsworth's dining rooms, was walking about Ann-street crossing during the greater part of the day, and several times visited Moss, who was his friend, and they left together at 5-20, when Moss went off duty. They parted' at the crossing, Moss stating positively that the deceased was sober. Moss did net see in which direction his friend walked, but a few minutes subsequently Gsugh was found on the down line by Kerr with his leg nearly severed from his body. Aid was obtained, and be was conveyed to the Accident Hospital, where the injured limb was amputated by Drs. Cooper and McLennan. On the 30th December he became insensible, and died without recovering consciousness on the 23rd January.—Miss Dow- nie stated the immediate cause of death was blood poisoning. During a period of consciousness he informed that lady how the accident had occurred. He said whilst walking on the line towards Widnes he heard a train passing on the Ches- kire Lines Railway Bridge overhead, and when in the act of turning round to see if all was right below he was knocked down and he remembered nothing else. The evidence showed that an engine driven by Gibson Hall run over the deceased, as a hat presumably his was found between the cylinder cover and the buffer plank. It was stated by several jury- men that the line upon which deceased was had been used as a public footpath.—Mr. Ferrand pointed out that any person using the line without a special pass could be prose- cuted, and it was Moss's duty to order the deceased away. The Company were now empowered by Act of Parliament to prosecute perscns travelling on the line without giving them previous notice, and the Company intended to make use of these powers.—The Coroner having summed up, the jury returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased was accidentally killed whilst trespassing on the railway. They did not consider the Company or any of their servants to blame in the matter. The coroner ex- pressed his concurrence with the verdict. At the conclusion of the enquiry Mr. Kennion, the foreman, on behalf of himself and the jury, congratulated Mr. Brig- house upon his elevation to the averent office of coroner. They hoped he would enjoy long life and robust health to carry out the duties of the office efficiently, and that he would use his authority in sustaining the averent privileges and customs of the office which they as Englishmen con- sidered one of the bulwarks of English liberty. Mr. W. Tracey, sen., supported these observations, and the Coroner suitably responded, remarking that he would endeavour to perform his duties to the entire satisfaction of the commun- ity. Mr. Atherton, who is a member of the Church of Eng- land Temperance Society, saggested the desirability of hold- ing future enquiries on persons who had died in the hospi- tal in that building, Ile thought such a course would be satisfactory to the ratepayers, and was of opinion there would be no difficulty in obtaining the sanction of the Local Board. The Coronet said he should be very happy to hold the inquest in that buildin2, or anywhere where the ratepayers thought proper. At the eeme time, he must re- mind the jury that the police bad entire charge of the Sr. rangements,

div.head: LIBERALISM IN WIDNES.
div.p: LIBERALISM IN WIDNES.

LECTURE ON TAXATION dr REPRESENTATION. Under the auspices of the Widnes Liberal Association, Mr. Hampden Jackson, of Liverpool, on Wednesday even- ing, lectured on "Taxation and representation; one man, one vote, one tax," in Oakland-street schoolroom. There was a good attendance, the room being nearly filled. Mr. Eustace Carey presided, and he, was supported on the plat- form by the Lecturer, Mr. S. Owen, and Mr. H. B. Shares, whilst amongst the audience were Messrs. I). Wright, Cosier, 1 I:Luellen, Melville, S. Sadler,.J. Betner, J. Taylor, Clarimee, Ireland, Marsh, C. Jones, Briggs, W. Whitby, Coxon, Jack- son, Oakden, and Kteat. Before the lecture-Mr. John Bet- nay, accompanied on the harmonium by Mr. Ogdenrsang the popular Liberal refrain, "The pilot of the state" with , much taste and power, the audience joining heartily in the I chorus. 1

The Cnernmax said he was sure they were all much obliged to Mr. Bailey for his kindness in starting the meet- ing in that harmonious manner. Be hoped they would be as harmonious throughout the coming campaign as they had been that evening so far. (Hear, hear.) He thought, and he had no doubt they all thought, that during the next few months they would probably see some very exciting times. They would have the Franchise Bill brought for- ward, and no doubt Mr. GL.datone's Government would do its best to push the measure through. (Hear, hear.) Whether or not there would be a Redistribution Bill re- mained to be seen. It was most probable that the Fran- ohise Bill would be introduced first, and perhaps some sketch of the Redistribution Bill would be made by Mr. Gladstone at the commencement of the Session. It was quite pos- sible the Franchise Bill would be thrown out by the House of Lords. In that ease there might be a dissolution, and then they would be put to the test as to what the Liberals had been doing in that neighbourhood and all over the country since the last election, when, as they knew, they were ignominously. beaten in South-West Lancashire. He

thought, however:that the work they had been doing threugh- out the district since then would ti its tale when the time came. (Applause.) In the meantime they must do their utmost to make themselves acquainted with the subjects that would be brought before Parliament during next session. Their opponents would attack them, and attack the Government very strenuously upon one or two subjects, especially upon their behaviour and their policy in Egypt. It was impossible for them to judge of what should be done in Egypt, because they were not acquainted with the facts. This was a kind of question which he thought they ought loyally to leave in the hands of the Government. They were all determined, he supposed, if asked any questions on the subject, that they would give their votes, not in favour of the usurious bondholders and class interests in Egypt, but in favour of the cause of civilisation and the good of the people of the country. (Applause.) They all agreed that hatever they did should be done not for the bondholders

or any monied interest,but for the good of the down-trodden people of England, and also for the good of the commerce of, the world. And it was only necessary to ask one question, who did.they think would be the persons more likely to carry out the policy which he had indicated? Did they think the poor poverty-stricken fellaheen safer in the hands of Lord Salisbury or Wihiam E wart Gladstone? (Applause.)

Therefore they had only loyally to leave the' matter in the hands of the present Government. Hear, hear.) Then with regard to the franchise, they had all made up their minds that the absurd anomaly which now existed in the representation of the country sheuld be swept away at the earliest possible moment. They had the borough franchise, with which they were all acquainted, and they also had county franchise. Why one man living on .one side of the street should possess a vote, while his neighbour on the opposite side of the street, who was perhaps equally well qualified, should not possess a vote because he lived in the county was one of those things "no fellow could understand." The sooner that anomaly was done away with and the better, and this was what they had set their faces to accomplish, and they must do their utmost during the next few months to support the Government every way they could. One of the most important ways in w•hich they could assist the Liberal party was to make themselves acquainted with Liberal questions, and it had seemed to the Widnes Liberal Association very important to do this by means of public lectures, and they intended to have a series. (Applause.) Mr. Carey then introduced, Tle Lam-Imm, who said it was. a. principle of the English constitution that representation should go with taxation. Few of them were aware how false that had been in times gone by, and how false it was at the present moment. The labouring interest paid one-third•of.the taxa- tion of the country, and had only one-threchundredth of the representation in the persons of one stone- mason and one miner—Mr. Broadhurst and Burt. He wished they were a hundred times multiplied. (Applause.) The landed aristocracy had had a great deal
r to do with the Government of the country for centuries, and it was quite time that classes should be put on one side, and . .

that Nve'should have a little more of that wholesome ele- ment which Mr. John Morley spoke about at Newcastle. Let them put upon their flag, "One man, one vote." At the beginning of the present century, 1801, we ha it a parliament that represented entirely the landed interest,.and they knew
ho' tenaciously the aristocracy held by the monopoly. Many of those present must remember, and others must . . . . .

have heard their fathers telk the tale that the kingdom was brought within 24 hours of revolution before a change was accomplished in 1832. Before that year out of 658 [nem- hers in the British House of Commons, 425 were returned by 252 patrons. (Shame. There were 513 members of Parliament of England and. Wales, and 309 of these owed their election to private nomination, and 45 Scotch morn- _ .

bets were returned by 35 patrons. That was to say, these persons owned little places that .held charters of incorpora- tion, and they could return whom they liked. The lecturer mentioned several plac,s which had no voters, but returned members to Parliament. and Dunwich which was buried beneath the North Sea, did so up to the time of the Reform Bill. (Loud laughter.) He described bow seats were sold to the highest bidder, and how, when an election occarrel, votes were openly bought and sold. Every member of that Parliament was bound amongst other things to swear that he was possessed of land yield- ing him at least au income of £6OO a year. Was it any I wonder that under a system of representation like that the interests of the landlord alone were cared for in the adjast- ment of national taxation, and that although Parliament had been reformed 50 years the thing was not yet properly righted. Even in the year 1834 there were 42 members of .Parliament sent up by 42 boroughs, with an average popula- Con of 5,900, and an average electoral roll of 730, while there were 162 other boroughs that had no vote at all, with an average population of 20,680. (Shame.) Portarlington, which returned a member to Parliament—of course he was an aristocratlaughter)--had 142 electors, and a popula- tion of 2,400 people. counting all the newly-born babies— , (laughter)-while Battersea,a great suburb of London, with a population of 107,000 inhabitants, had no representation at all. (Shame.) There were 42 boroughs had 42 members, and there were 19 other boroughs, which had 43 members. Now, the 42 boroughs had a total population of only 249,600, while the 19 boroughs had a population of six and three-quarter millions. That was what they called equality of representation. (Laughter and cheers.) The Tories stand by the great rule that represeetation should go with taxation. Well, the 42 boroughs sending 42 members were assessed to Income tax at exactly £2,950,000 per annum. The 19 boroughs having similar representation were assessed at 143 millions of pounds per annum. And that was equality! That was the sort of equality they were going to knock about a bit. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He would now take the counties. There were 19 counties in Great Britain that returned about the same number of members to Parliament as 23 other counties. The 19 had a population of 600,000, and the 23 bad a population of 3 millions with just the same representation. The 19 had 39,000 electors, and the 23 had 200,000; while the former was assessed to income tax at 19 millions, and the latter at 33,610,000. And that was equality in the present Parliament. (Applause.) Out of 639 member now sitting in the House of Commons 272 were related to the landed aristocracy, and exactly two related to labour in the sense of being directly returned as workingmen's representatives; 282 members ware great landowners themselves, and only 150 members were in any way connected with trade, commerce, or manufactures, while 168 were fighting men, who were interested in keep- ing up a large military expenditure. He had not counted the volunteers. He was proud of the volunteer movement. He thought it had saved the country from an enormous military expenditure that they would have incurred in addition to what they now had. (Applause.) It had saved the country from the greatest and worst of all possible taxes—a conscription. (Applause.) Military men had no right to be in the House of Commons—(hear, hear)—being interested in the expendi- ture ; and if he (the lecturer) were a member of the Liver- pool Corporation, and accepted a tender for coal from them, he would lose his seat to-morrow--.(applause)—simply be- cause he was personally interested in the spending of money. In 1884 the House of Lords represented 14k millions acres of land, and I.li millions of pounds rent drawn from that land. An what was their fine House of Commons, the "People's House" so-called?, It was nothing but a small edition of the House of Lords, which represented what it realty, was—a trades union of fettld owners. (Applause.) The House of Commons represented 7± millions acres, with *million pounds of rental. Now, what was to be the cure.for all this evil? He thought the cure would be foundin such a bill as ths,present Govern- ment were likely to present them, giving effect to the prin- ciple Mr. Morley se eloquently laid down—for one man one vote, whoever that man might be. (Laud .nppalawyne. was He a landowner upon. his land, i thought, too, they should have one eax. and f a man was rich. , he should be taxed according to his riches. It was high time that the system of asking the people of the country for money was based upon a little greater intelligence than the system upon which the country was launched in 1660. Up, to :hat year the land of this country belonged, to the people, and the king, as representing the people, leased the land out to his barons for a yearly rental. Before that time the land bad to bear the entire cost of every war, whether civil or foreign; it had to bear the cost of the army and navy, and the cost of Royalty. If they took these items out of the estimates of to-day they would have written them down to what the Yankees called "the thin end of nothing." (Laughter and applause.) But after the Commonwealth, when Charles H. came to ttie throne, the Parliament was packed with Tory barons., and they constituted, themselves landowners instead of land- holders—(applause)—and they put the taxes r,pon the working me,A's beer. The burden of the taxes, was taken from the land rad put upon the poor. The l‘ticturer con- demned the taxing of a man through his h,elly by placing (Wile pqi Variogs articles, and pointed. out that the rich

landowner with his hundreds of thousands only paid truce in the same proportion as the working man with 24e per week, while the and, which by every moral law belonged to ithe peoplerhad but a small burden of taxation. Taxation was the price they paid for the blessings of civil govern- ment. It was the price they paid for peace, for domestic comfort, for safety from foreign enemies, and for equal laws; and that being so every per- son in the State benefited more or less by these things, and every responsible person in the state ought to contribute his quota of taxation. Taxation should be levied in proportion to a man's means. (Applause.) The lecturer, by means of statistics, then showed the inequalities of taxation, national and local, advocating the abolition of the customs and excise duties. Were this done, there would be plenty of work for all people, but while they taxed the trade and commerce of the country and left out the land of the rich man, the country could never be really pros- perous. (Loud applause.) lie moved that the Chairman sign the following petition tO the Rouse of Commons on be- half of the meeting:—" That your petitioners humbly sub- mit that at the end of the currant financial year there is reason to anticipate a surplus which with continued economy in the national expenditure will afford sufficient margin for a considerable remission of taxation. Ttiat a large portion of the revenue is raised by customs and excise duties which extract from the people much more than the State receives, check consumption, restricts home and foreign trade, di- minish employment, and impoverish the pomie. That the fiscal and commercial reformation hitherto effected have proved so beneficial as to warrant further progress in the same direction. That, therefore, the duties on tea, coffee, cocoa, currants, raisins, shall be forthwith abolished. Your petitioners, therefore, humbly pray that your honourable Rouse will be pleased to insist upon the Immediate concession of a free breakfast table for the people." The reading of the petition was received with much applause. and Mr. D. WRIGHT having seconded the motion, it was enthusiastically passed. The petition will be forwarded to Sir R. Cress for presentation. A vote of thanks was heartily accorded to the lecturer, on the motion of he CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr. S. Owmas,and a similar compliment having been paid the Chairman, the meeting terminated.

div.head: FAMILY OF THIEVES AT WIDNES.
div.p: A FAMILY OF THIEVES AT WIDNES.

At 'Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Edith and Lucy Holt, aged twelve and ten respectively, living in Peel House-lane, were charged with stealing a pair -of trousers, the property of Thomas Robinson, publican, and Elizabeth Holt, their mother, was charged with receiving the trousers knowing them to have been stolen.—Mr. Knowles defended. —lnspector Wood stated that on the 23rd January Mrs. Robinson handed the trousers, which were worth 155., to Mrs. Stocks, of Widnes-road, for the purpose of being washed. About noon on the following day the trousers were hang upon a line in a yard near Widnes road, and about twenty minutes past one they were missed. rhe two younger prisoners were in the vicinity about the same time, and Mrs. Stocks therefore went to Mrs. Hoit's house to in- quire if she had seen anything of the trousers. The mother replied that She did not allow her daughters to steal, and if they brought home anything that dui not belong to them she would soon send them back. The next, morning the younger prisoners pledged the trousers with Mrs. Jameson, pawnbroker, Ann-et, for ss. On Friday P.S. etrickland went to the house te make further inquiries, and the elder prisoner denied all knowledge of the stolen trousers, and invited the officer to search the premises. At this time PC. Snowden entered for the purpose of apprehending the young girls, having discovered that they had pawned the trousers, and the mother then said, " Oh, dear me ; Lucy did bring them, and told me she had found them, and I sent them to pledge them to screen us." She afterwards got the pawn ticket from beneath the boarding of the floor, and the three pri- soners were then taken into custody.—These facts were attested to by Mrs. Robinson, Mrs. Stocks, Mrs. Jameaon, P.S. Strickland, and P.C. Snowden.—Mr. Knowles, for the defence, contended that the girls had found the trousers in a ditch, where they had been blown from the lioe.—The Bench considered that the girls had stolen the trousers under the influence of their mother. The, girls were discharged, and the mother was sentenced to a month's harddabour.

div.head: ANNIVERSARY7-OF • RUNCORN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY:
div.p: ANNIVERSARY7-OF • RUNCORN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY:

' The twenty-first anniversary of the Runcorn Co-operative Industrial and Provident Society, was celeb,ated in the Public Hall on Wednesday evening, by a tea party and ball. The proceedings passed off successfully. About 600 people sat down to tea, the tables being presided over by the following ladies:—Mesdames W Rhodes, R Evans, Abrams, Booth, J Stubbs, Hazlehurst, T Withhagton, Rod- , gars' Cropper, Royle, Deacon, Wylde, Bennett, J , ton, Richardson, Bancroft, W Nckson, Gleave, Leathwood, Bowyer, Wilson, Atherton, &waders, Curzm, and Price; Misses Powell, White, Davies Joynson, and Cartwright. Subsequently a meeting was held in the Hall, under the presidency df Mr W Nickson, who was supported by Messrs. W Clucas, W Cropper, T Riley, W Rhodee, T Watson, J Witbington, W Sankey, W Rule W Dwyer W Bates (Patricroft), and Upton ( Sec. pro, tens.) The Chairman observed that he saw several of the originators of the saciety present. None of them had thought it would mach its present enormous proportions. ,In the early days they had often been puzzled to know where the dividerA was to come from, but mow the society's I income could be reckoned by thousands of pounds; and the benefits to the working classes had been manifold.—Mr W Ro3 le delivered,an address in which he traced the progress of the society from the commencement. When they erected theirllrst building they were only taking £&a week, and now for groceries alone in one half-year they received £30,000. CI their nine shops seven belonged to the mem- bers of the society, and this was something to be proud of. He believed that in 10 years instead of taking £30,000 per half year they would be taking £60,000, (Applause.) The total slam the society hat paid in dividends during the 21 years was Z57,505.—Mr. Bate then delivered an address on the Co-operative movement, observing that it was said by some people that the members of the committee were making a grand thing out of the society. If they had any of those people in Runcorn his advice was to put them on the i committee, where they would soon find that there was plenty of anxiety and very little pay. The working ex- penses of the Runcorn society were very small indeed. They were not more than lop on their total sales. The only blot he could find was that they did not devote a single penny to educational purposes. In a village near to Manchester a society there devoted between £7O and £6O every quarter to edacatiotial work, and the members of the society were having. their children properly educated. He reflected with pride upon the fact that the members of co-operative societies began to pay for the education of their children prior to the passing of the Education Act. The speaker then referred to the advantages derived from trading with the wholesale Co-operative Society, and concluded by saying that one of the profoundest tt 'rakers of the day had stated that in the adoption of the co-operative principle the working classes had found out their own redemption. He believed that the movement was the greatest lever for , the elevation of the moral and. social character of the people, 1 and he earnestly hoped they *ight go on to even greater , things than the past had seen. k A.pplause.) In moving a vote of thanks to Mr. Bate for his address, Mr. W. Rhodes pointed out that there was e. Free Library in Runcorn, and the society being large ratepayers, contributed to education ' in maintaining the Library. (Applause.)—Mr. Dwyer seconded the motion, which was carried.—Othe: votes of thanks having been accorded, dancing commencee., and was ' continued until an early hour next morning.

Xetters to the editor. ACCIDENT AT GAS HEATING APPARATUS WORKS. Sir,—ln your issue of the 26th, you state that W. War- burton was admitted ts the Infirmary with serious injuries, "the result of an accident whilst engaged in his work." This is not correct. He was interfering and playing with a polishing machine, from which he had been warned away repeatedly; he had been threatened with instant dismissal if he meddled with it again, and at the time of the accident he was playing with the machine in the absence of the fore- man. A minute before he caught his breakfast can in the machine, and had it torn out of his hands and thrown across the shop. The other men called out to him to come away, and in spite of this he picked up his can and again put it on the machine, with the result that it was again torn out of his bands and thrown violently in his face. If no accident had happened be would have been dismissed at once on the return of the foreman, and it is to be hoped this will prove a useful warning to him in future.—Yours, tkc., Warrington, January, 1884. THOS. FLETCHER.

div.head: PULPIT-FROM. THE PEW.
div.p: THE PULPIT-FROM. THE PEW.

Sir,—The theatre-goer is never tired of hearing of and talking about actors. Irving and Booth, Toole and Terry are names to conjure with, and ef Handel, Reeves, and Titiens the musician is always glad to hear. So to the regular attendant at a place of worship there is an absorb- ing interest taken in preachers and preaching. Reminis- cences of Stanley, Farrar, Parker or Spurgeon are among the most pleasing. The Non-conforming churches have most things in common. They share in a common hatred— if so harsh a term may be employed to describe the super- cilious scorn with which a minister of the Anglican or Roman regards what he is pleased to call a Dissenter. They also share in a common heritage of religious freedom, which having been so valiantly achieved, they will do well to jealously guard. They share likewise in the confidence of the great middle class of the country—the back-bone of the framework of society—the hard-headed merchants and tradesmen in whose hands those commercial interests of the land were entrusted, without which we should lose our prestige and power, and England would be wiped out of the map of Europe. Nevertheless there are a few things that need carefully looking to by these churches, lest their posi- tion be weakened, and the "fine gold become dim." Among many things that might be named is the question of the interchange of pulpits. If a layman may be allowed to step into the sacred precincts of ministerial arrangements, I would humbly suggest that the various churches might have an opportunity occasionally of hearing ministers from their sister churches; not for the purpose of criticising their preaching, but in order to cement the connection which already exists between churches which have so much in common. If one church has an excep- tionally talented preacher, the others ought to share in the benefit. Such a boon could not be enjoyed, however, unless there was a system of pulpit interchange in vogue; for persons who have a stated place of worship do not care to rash about from one church to another, nor is it seemly. Surely there cannot be such a thing as jealousy among brethren of " the cloth." There appears to be the greatest cordiality among them; but they are never seen in each other's pulpits. How many years have elapsed since any preacher, net a Wesleyan, has occupied the pulpit of St. Paul's? At Bethesda, over the way, the case is slightly different. The pulpit has been offered to more than one minister from other churches in the town, but the response to those friendly overtures on the part of Mr. Thomas has been anything hut encouraging, and has led him to remark that there is a sad lack of brotherliness among Runcorn ministers. There seem to be barriers of ice separating the churches from each other, which an occasional interchange of pulpits wonla speedily melt down. Once in three months a change of the kind proposed might be made, and at each recurring visit it would seem like the extending of a cordial greeting frem one church to another.—Yours, A VERY Ley LAYMAN Runcorn, Jan. 28, 1884.

div.head: GAME LAWS.
div.p: THE GAME LAWS.

Sir,—Allow me a small space in the columns of your impartial paper to say a few words in favour of the abroga- tion of this remaining relict of "feudal power" which has been handed down to us from our Norman Conquerors. A more unjust law to my mind does not exist. Although the Ground Game Act was a step in the right direction, yet it is but a short one; and I fear that we have too much of the old Whig element in the present Government to cherish the belief that they will repeal this law. Yet eventually to my mind it will have to be accomplished. But as all tyranny dies hard, so undoubtedly this will. But to come more to the point let me take the case of a tenant farmer, for instance, who has the misfortune to live in a district where game is abundant. He has his crops trampled down and devoured all the summer, and vet he can claim no recompense for the damaga done. Now, sir, Ido not agree with poach- ing in the true sense of the word, but what I say is that the tenant farmer shoald have tke right of killing game on his own ground. So long as they are fed at the expense of the farmer I fail to see bow they can be justly considered the sole property of the lord of the manor. I dispute his right to keep game, providing it is kept at the expense of those who profit by it. But, as the law stands now, a man is in many cases punished as muc.-i for killing a pheasant or partridge as in the case of a violent assault upon a human being, although la the first offence he has not broken any Law of God. But so long as it is'a law we are compelled to abide by it, until the time arrives when it—like many other laws that have been framed for the agrandisement of the few—will have to be repealed. I mast now draw to a close as I feel that I have trespassed already too much on your columns.-1 be to remain, yours, dtc., January, 1884. A CHESHIRE FARMER.
SALE OF GREYHOUNDS. MR. STONE'S "SEA. PILOT" UNDER THE HAMMER.

The great success achieved for our respected townsman, Mr. T. Stone, of Newton-le-Willows, by the magnificent running of his dog Sea Pilot at Kempton Park last week, has given great satisfaction all over the district, and Mr. Stone has been warmly complimented by many of his friends. Sea Pilot ran in the Great Champion Stakes, the first prize in which was £l,OOO, second £6OO, third and fourth £lOO each, while others of smaller amount followed. There were 64 nominations, and the best dogs in the country competed, as the stake is one of the most valuable offered at coursing meetings. On each of the three days required to bring the event to a decision Sea Pilot displayed excellent form' and ran all the courses in brilliant style. Mr. Stone's dog de- feated Markham, the favourite, in an easy manner, and also in the following course bowled over Hotspur, the next fa- vourite. The two last dogs left in were Sea Pilot, and Mr. G. Bell Irving's Manager, and the owners of these animals decided to divide the first and second prizes. On Saturday last a sale of greyhounds took place at Messrs. Rymill's repository, London, and Mr. T. Stone offered Sea Pilot among other dogs for sale. Alluding to the sale, a sporting contemporary says :—" Mr. T. Stone having such a lot of saplings coming on, W 55 compelled to sell off some of his running dogs to make room for them, and the popular Larfeashire courser sent up sixteen, amongst whom was Sea Pilot. The Kempton Park divider was not in the catalogue, as we believe his owner did not make up his mind to part , with him until almost the last moment. Sea Pilot was the ' first of Mr. Stone's lot offered, and after some rather ex- citing bidding he was eventually secured by Mr. E. T. Unwin for 290 guineas, at which price he may be considered well sold, seeing that be is already a fourth season dog. Sanscrit and Sikh, both of whom are pretty certain to win stakes in an open country, cannot be considered dear at 32 and 41 guineas, and if we are not greatly mistaken Mr. Devereux bought Sally Brass well within her value for 60 guineas. Sewing Maid, a daughter of Misterton and Stitch in Time, was purchased by Mr. Moulsworth for 85 guineas, but although she has a touch of her mother's style of run- ning, she cannot be considered other than well sold. Seam- stress, her sister, was sold to Mr. Dean for 35 guineas, and Stitchery, another of the same litter, fell to Mr. Esdaile's bid of 23 gailmis- Mr. Gardner gave 50 guineas for Sleight-of-Hand, and Sea- port, a half-brother to Sea Pilot, who has won several courses this season and has never been led to his hare, found a new owner in Mr. Jenner for 140 guineas. Sabena, a second season bitch, who, like several others sent up by Mr. Stone, has shown good form over the Lytham and Altcar countries, was secured by Mr. Smith for 72 guineas; and School Girl, also a second season bitch, was bought by Mr. A. J. Hum- phrey for 25 guineas. Mr. Dean purchased Squirrel, a third season dog, for 11 guineas; and Salesman, which was the last lot sent up from the Newton-le-Willows kennel, was bought well within his value by Mr. Purvis for 22 guineas." •

THE DEATH OF A SCHOOL-BOY AT BURTON- WOOD. Sir,—As false reports have been circulated about the above case, will you kindly allow use space in your columns for the following particulars :—The boy's parents say they saw bruises on his buttocks on the evening of Monday, De- cember 17th. I most emphatically deny that he was punished at all, by me, on that day, therefore those marks could not have been caused by me. On the next morning, Tuesday, the 19th, I had occasion to give him a slight Punishment for misconduct. He received, standing, four strokes with a willow twig, 17 inches long, and of the thick- ness of an ordinary cane. He was not placed on or across a desk. He had on thick cord trousers at the time, and could scarcely have felt the caning- at any rate he was as lively as ever all the rest of the day. The coroner re- marked that "he instrument." could not have been punished with a sim- pler or lighter Dr. Garton's evidence, founded on the post mortem examination, proved so clearly that the death was from "natural causes," and that the slight punishment he received bad nothing to do with it, that the inquest came at once to gone on, end; but, had it one on, I had plenty of witnesses at hand to swear to the truth of what I have here stated. The evidence on my side would then have received the same. publicity as the one-sided and untruthful statements which have appeared in one or two papers. It is certainly very strange that if, as the parents allege, he had been beaten so severely on the Monday they should have sent him again to school the next day, and his sister all the rest of the week. No complaint was made until Saturday, when I heard of it for the first time. The boy was robust and apparently in the best of health. He was not regular in his attendance. No doctor was called in till the Friday, and he did not see him again till three hours before he qied on the following Sunday. I have hitherto delayed writing, as further proceedings were threatened, but I believe the C3SB is now at an end.—Yours respectfully, T. W. JONES. Burtenwood, Jan. 28, 1884.

On looking over your paper of the 26th ult. I was surprised to see that two of our sanitary officials are about to have a substantial increase in wages. This is properly called the spending committee, about which continued complaints are made of aromatic emissions, costly and inefficient machinery and threatenings of indictments. We may well exclaim "What next." We must, I fear, look in vain for retrenchment so long as the rival political clubs have the selection of our representatives, as they appear to select men whose chief aim is to anticipate the officials' wants and make the poor ratepayers pay the piper. Not only so, but inde- pendent men are prevented from rendering good service. There are also grievances in connection with any extension in the building trades, such as thicker walls, paying sewer rates, and doing work that fairly belongs to the Corpora- tion, and increase in price of land owing to the pernicious system of so-called improved ground rents, whereby land is doubled and trebled in price. As the best experience is that for which persons have paid, I will call attention to the street forming question. In 1872 II paid is 61 per lineal foot for half width Milner.street ; in 1877, paid 13s 6d per lineal foot for Marson-street, and in 1883, for gable ends abetting on Greenall- street £5l 16s Id, being 14s Hid per lineal foot. in the 11 years intervening has the specification been made I more rigid, and are all streets that have sett pavement to be formed alike regardless of the traffic that may be likely to pass over them ? I must leave the transition of our manufactured goods, the reduction in gas, and improved water supply for use in cases of fire in other and better hands, and look forward for a general improvement.—Yours respectfully, JAS. CRAIK. Marson-street, 31st January, 1884.

Ile felt that if those gentle- men who were really respected and beloved in Warrington I were only to go more among the workiog men, there could be no doubt whatever that at the next general election Warrington would return to its old path, and send their chairman to Parliament. Waiting and working for this result, they were more determined never to relax their efforts until they had wrested the borough from the Radi- cals. (Applause.) Captain NicaoLsoN seconded the vote of thanks, and in doing so remarked that if he had been a workingman sitting in that Hall, who bad read the nonsense taught as to Free Trade and Reciprocity in the Radical Press, he should, after the speech of Mr. Ecroyd, be possessed with such a fund of argument against what was written on the subject that would enable him never to ma.ke any mistake in future. (Hear, hear.) After all the whole question amounted to what Mr. Ecroyd had pointed out. After showing the clearest grounds and reasons he had stated that they should ask for a Commission of Inquiry to discover whether the reasons which ,he had given were true, and if true that they should be acted upon. He thought there could be nothing more reasonable than that. They would agree with him that it was the duty of the Government of this country, no matter whether Liberal or Conservative, to cause such an inquiry to be in- stituted. (Hear, hear.) If these causes of loss of trade and loss of prosperity did exist, there should be a remedy, and if the remedy be found in the manner which Mr. Ecroyd put it, why should they not adopt it? Under any circumstances it must be for the benefit of their own nation and their own colonies, and it was to their colonial possessions they must look to, because they were part of themselves. It was said that gratitude was a lively sense of favours to come, and he hoped their gratitude to Mr. Ecroyd would be in that light that he might come among them again when an inquiry had been instituted, and acme , steps had been taken to effect the changes which he pro- posed, that he would explain them still more fully, and be . able to point to their fulfilment as a turning point in the , prosperity of this country. (Applause.) , Mr. ECROYD having replied, Alderman KEAN proposed a similar 'compliment to the chairman for presiding, and ex- pressed the hope that they would be able shortly to con- gratulate Sir Gilbert on being member for the borough of Warrington. The proposition having been seconded by Councillor BURGESS and carried with acclamation, the meeting Separated.

CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT WARRING-TON. A public meeting in connection with* the local Conserva- tive Association was held at the Public Hall, Warrington, on Wednesday evening. The Hall was fairly well filled, but there was nothing like a crush, Sir Gilbert Greenell, , Bart., presided, supported by Mr. W. Ferrer Ecroyd, M.P., Captain Reynolds, Alderman Webster, Alderman Kean, Councillor Burgess, Mr. Robert Pierpoint, Capt. Nicholson, Mr. Peter Stubs, the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, Dr. Mackie, and other gentlemen. Whilst the audience were assembling a popular selection of music was played on the organ by Mr. W. Johnson. The CHAIRMAN, in the course of his remarks, said he be- lieved that the more frequently those meetings were held the more useful they would be. From them they would derive most valuable assistance to their cause. When he came amongst them he had only one feeling, and that was to foster the political feeling which they had amongst them, that political feeling bearing in one direction, and the char- ter of their political creed being this—"Do good tp all ; act justly and 'fairly to each other." (Ap- plause.) They had nothing to regret in the past ; they had done their best, and they were looking to the future in which they were determined to do more. They had much before them that was hopeful. The had now erecting near to them a very handsome, useful, and large building. They were now erecting a large Conservative Club. (Applause ) He would remind them of this good fact, that the club would be theirs and his. (Hear, hear.) They would have the club as a possession • and it was a good thing to have property. (Laughter) But it was only a really good thing to have pro- perty when it was used righeously. They intended the club to be a centre for themselves. He had hoped that he would have been able to announce to them that evening that the foundation stone was immediately to be laid. He hoped that before long the foundation stone would be laid. When he was in London on the previous day he took the greatest possible pains to secure the present and immediate presence of Lord Salisbury. (Applause.) Lord Salisbury in the most candid and friendly terms regretted the utter impos- sibility with his present engagements to come down and lay the foundation stone. Therefore they would have to look out for someone else to lay it. They were disappointed that night in not having the presence of Mr. Robert Davies. (Applause.) Mr. Davies would have been with them had his health permitted. Several other gentlemen were also kept from them by the same reason. Mr. PETER Srmes rose to move the first resolution, which he said was one of considerable importance. When they saw the state of the country marked by a reduction in wages, and in many instances' unfortunately, by strikes and failures, WARRINGTON CHAMBER OF it became the duty of them to inquire and look back on the policy of the Government and into the COMMERCE. . causes which had led to all those failures, at least some of them, both agricultural and commercial. PICKETT i alluded to the good that had resulted from temperance tract distribbition and personal solicitation, and spoke of the suc- cess which attended open air meetings at Haydock some years ago. He thought much good might be done in Earles- town by similar efforts.—Mr. JOHN flomorocH thought the paper read by Mr. Tayler contained valuable information and suggestions, and that the idea of instructing teetotallers in the principles of total abstinence, so that they would be able to readily show it was beneficial to them ought to be carried out.—Mr. JOHN PRESCOTT pointed out that many of , the friendly society lodges of the district held their meet- ings in public-houses, and said it behoved all parents to be careful what societies their sons joined. Pub- licans, for the sake of custom, would find the required room free, but it was like setting a sprat to catch a mackerel. (Laughter and applause.) He knew of young men who had been led astray in consequence of public- honse meetings, and he thought it would be useless for tem- perance workers to continue their labours if they were to be always robbed in that fashion. (Hear, hear.) When young men entered the public-houses they were exposed to great temptation, and the evil of it was seen 14 years ago, when a purely temperance benefit' society was started, which had been most successful, and at present it stood better than any other society. He looked upon it with great pleasure, and he believed it was doing a great and noble work. Temperance work was only in its infancy in Earlestown, and he thought their labours would have great result in the future. (Applause.)—Mr. RICHARD HIGGINS recommended the holding of out-door meetings and the dis- tribution of tracts as means by which much good could be accomplished.—Mr. JOHN HOLLYOCK again spoke, drawing attention to the great temptation to Sunday School scholars through shops being opened on the Sunday. It was a great Inducement to children to commence bad habits such as Sab- bath-breaking, and tended to counteract the work which Sunday school teachers had to do.—Mr. G. F. KERLIN : Would it be possible to get a return of the number of Sun- day school scholars and Church members who are teetotal- lers? Mr. PRES4I,TT : Yes, I should think so.—The CHAIRMAN : We should have to bring the matter before Sunday school teachers and superintendents in each case and have their sanction.—Mr. KERLIN stated that he was most anxious as to the position of their young men and young women upon the question and he thought much good would result if they could have a return of the kind he had indicated. If he was in order he would move that the committee be requested to take into consideration the advis- ability of obtaining a return from each Sunday school as to the numbers of those who were abstainers and non- abstainers.—Mr. Paßscorr seconded the motion, which was unanimously carried, the CHAIRMAN observing that the resolution would much strengthen the committee in the application they would have to make to the officials of the various schools. The CHAIR- ' MAN briefly pointed out the various subjects ' that had been touched upon by the speakers; ' after which the Rev. W. C. TAYLER rose to criticise the remarks upon his paper. He expressed his pleasure that they had held the conference, and he thought such gather- ' ings proved very useful and beneficial to temperance , workers. He was glad that they had passed a resolution • about a canvass of the Sunday schools, because they felt the , temperance question was one for the various religious I societies to take up. (Hear, hear.)—After a slight discus- cuesion as to raising of funds by public meetings and sei- mons, Mr. GEORGE CLARKE, in moving a hearty vote of thanks to the Rev. W. C. Tayler for his excellent paper, ' said bethought the committee ought to be supported by a I resolution of that meeting, and suggested one which should be moved.—Mr. Jimmies seconded the vote of thanks to Mr. Tayler, which was passed with acclamation.—Mr. U. E. HAYNES afterwards moved that in the opinion of that ' conference it was advisable for the committee to as far as possible arrange and carry out the various points ' suggested and brought before them. Mr. W. WALTON seconded the resolution, and it was passed.— , Mr. J. G. MuLuess then formally moved That • this conference of representatives of temperance organisa- tions in Earlestown records its conviction that Her Majesty's Government ought, without further delay, to deal with the liquor traffic in the spirit of the local option resolution, ' which has been thrice affirmed by increasing majorities in r the House of Commons; and that the people should have the power to stay the course of that evil, which Mr. Glad- stone admitted, exceeded the results of war, pestilence, and famine combined."—After the motion had been seconded , by Mr. JOHN PRESCOTT, it was unanimously passed, and the conference was then brought to a close with the Bene- diction.

THE TEMPERANCE CAUSE IN EARLES TOWN. IMPORTANT CONFERENCE. An important conference of temperance workers, under the auspices of the Earlestown and Newton United Band of Hope and Temperance Societies was held in the Baptist School, Earlestown, on Tuesday, when the Rev. W. C. Tayler, of Earlestown, read a paper on " The best means of promoting temperance work in Earlestown." The chair was occupied by Mr. J. H. Graham, and there was a pretty fair attendance of members of the various temperance societies in the town. The proceedings were commenced with sing- ing and prayer, after which the CHAIRMAN explained the objects of the conference, stating that it was to consider the bast means of continuing the temperance work in aides- town. The United Committee of the Earlestown and New- ton Bands of Hope and Temperance Societies were anxious to hear the thoughts and suggestions of the individual tem- perance workers, and with the view of having the subject properly introduced they had secured the kind services of the Rev. W. C. Tayler, who had consented to road a paper on the best way to promote temperance work in Earlestown. They were desirous of seeing less drunkenness, less vice, less gambling, and less swearing than there was at present, and they wanted to see the matter taken up more earnestly in their various churches. In some place the subject of temperance was treated with very great indifference, bat that was not as it should be. The committee wanted to rouse some of the teetotallers who were standing aloof from every society and did nothing to help the cause, and he hoped their end would be attained by that conference. (Applause.)—The Rev. W. C. TAYLER was warmly received. In commencing he said he was somewhat ignorant of the working of the committee, and he hoped he might be excused if he said anything which they might consider uncalled for. They had given him a chance to say something upon the temperance question by asking him to speak upon the best means of promoting temperance work in Earlestown. He found in Earlestown they had adult and junior temperance societies, and he also found that they had recently formed themselves into a union—each society sending two or more representatives, so that the proper work of the union might be carried out. With thank- fulness to Almighty God first, and thankfulness to the Committee of the Union second he would say that the Union for the short time it had existed had done admir- able work. There was a needs be for its existence and it had shown that it had a right to exist. It was in the direc- tion of union that his remarks were to tend. He would take it for granted that each separate society was doing its own work in the best way possible for its own success and pros- perity, and he would endeavour to throw out a few sugges- tions which might help them in their united work. fie understood that their present union was the Earlestown and Newton Temperance Union—a union of adults and juveniles without distinction—but he submitted that they should be regarded as distinct, for they needed different treatment for their full development. That idea was recognised in their religious life, for they had not only the church and congre- gation, but the Sunday school, which was managed by its own officers and worked along its own lines. He thought they should more distinctly recognise the difference between the two classes of societies, as it would be for their advantage. He suggested how the Union should be governed, by a general committee or sub-committees for the adult and juvenile societies, and went on to say that of course they all knew no Union should come into existence for mere existence sake. When that was the case with any Union the best thing they could do with it was to bury it decently and express the fervent hope that to it there should be no resurrection. (Laughter.) A Union existed for action and work—(hear, hear)—to do which it might not be in the power or ability of any separate society. All members of temperance societies should have an intelligent grip of the reasons why they were such, and a powerful public opinion in favour of temperance should be created. Those two things should be the purpose of their Union, for they would then have the means of promoting temperance work. The first could be brought about in various ways—by arrang- ing with the separate societies for lectures or addresses upon distinct temperance subjects, which cored be given at very little expense. Gentlemen, whether ministers, doctors, or others belonging to the neighbourhood might be got to do that work willingly and gladly. There was too much of the amusing and too little of the instructive and teaching in their members' meetings. (Hear, hear.) Recitations, dialogues, and songs were all very well in their place, and some of them contained much that was instructive, but they wanted more direct teaching. (Hear, hear.) It could also be brought about by obtaining diagrams, pictures, or even magic lanterns illustrating temperance subjects, and by arranging for examinations of the members in tem- perance subjects. As to the second, that a powerful public THE ALLEGED POISONING WITH opinionia favour of temperance should be created; it was to all intents and purposes the work of a union. After an absence of twenty minutes, the jury returned with the following verdict:—" That the boy Samuel Yates died from the effects of the overdose of a mixture called Indian tincture, which was administered to him as medicine by his mother by misadventure." They also de- sired to say that although William Ashall was not crimi- nally responsible for the death of deceased, they thought - he deserved some censure for not informing the mother of deceased when she bought the mixture that the dose WaS as it appeared upon the label of the tor ttle produced, which he kept in the shop; and that Mrs. Yates was also to blame for not inquiring what should be given to the child. They further desired to make a presentment that they thought all shopkeepers ought to be absolutely prohibited by law from selling Indian tincture and mixture of a similar kind ; and if in this case the law rel ding to the Inland Revenue had been broken by the manufacturer of this Indian tincture they hoped steps would be at once taken by the proper authority to enforce the penalty fixed by law. Mr. Yates and Llr. Ashall were then called into the room, • and censured by the coroner.

Under the auspices of the above, a representation of" The trial of John Barleycorn" took piece in the Hayton Park Schools, on Tuesday evening, in aid of the Temperance and Band of Hope Societies Funds. The rooms were crowded, and the celebrated " trial " was thoroughly enjoyed. The several parts were taken principally by members of the Tem- perance Society of St. Helens in characteristic costume°, and the characters were well enacted, and afforded an in- structive as well as amusing exposition of the temperance principles. The following ladies and gentlemen took the different characters : BENCH.

div.head: IMPROVEMENTS AT ST. HELENS STATION.
div.p: IMPROVEMENTS AT ST. HELENS STATION.

It will be pleasing to the townspeople of St. Helens, and particularly to those members of the Council who have exerted themselves in so laudable a fashion to bring it about, to know that the long-promised improvements at the railway station have now been commenced. From the facts made known it would seem that the London and North.. Western Company intend to make alterations of a very ex' tensive and satisfactory character. With regard to the approaches it is intended, we understand, to place the pre- sent boundary wall, from a point near the end of George- street, back a considerable distance. A double set of entrance gates will then be erectad one for carriages and pedestrians to the passenger station, and the other for rolleys and other vehicles, which are continually passing W and from the goods yard. This, it is needless to say, will remedy a good deal of the inconvenience attendant upon the present arrangement of the approaches. The internal alterations will be extensive. It is intended to leave the booking-office much as it is at present, but the waiting - rooms and offices are to be re-modelled, a separate exit pro. Yided, and a more extensive covering constructed for the protection from the weather of persons alighting from vehicles, or using them to leave the station. The up-line (to the North) platform will be considerably widened from Mews. Smith and Son's bookstall down to the level crossing near Raven Bridge. This will be done by taking up one line in the siding and placing it near to Shaw-street. On the down-line (to Live-pool) side of the station the present block of waiting rooms will be swept away, and a more commodious and convenient suite of rooms will be erected to extend parallel with those on the up-line. There will be another set of metals running through the station on the off side, and trains for Widnes, Manchester, Warrington, Crewe, and London, will as a rule be despatched from the double platform, and opposite to the main entrance. The mineral traffic from Pocket Nook tO Sutton will also be conducted through the station over additional lines on the Parr side. The platforms are all to be covered by a light iron and glass roof, supported on pillars. The inclines for the subway will commence on the up,platform near the stop-blocks in the aiding, and on the down-line at a point nearly opposite. The present bridge for passengers will remain, but new approaches will be ' formed.
DEPUTATIONS TO MR. GLA.DSTONE.
OUR INDIAN POLICY, THE FRANCHISE QUES- TION AND LONDON GOVERNMENE

Mr. Gladstone received several deputations on ThurAaY• First came one representing the Indian community resident in England, who wished to congratulate the right hon. gen- tleman on his having entered upon his 75th year and ex- press their admiration for him, and also to declare their ap- preciation of the beneficent policy of the Government in India and of the Viceroy's administration. Mr. Gladstcine assured the elemstation that this country endeavoured ill every way to promote the substantial interests of the people of India, and the Government firmly believed that in carrying out this object their views were the same is those which animated the hearts of the people of India. The next deputation was from the Leeds Liberal Conference, and Mr. John Morley, M.P. stated the resolu• tion at which the Conference had arrived as to the urgencY of electoral reform. Mr. Gladstone said the members of the Government had not forgotten their engagements On this subject, and but a few days would elapee before the country' would be made aware of their intention to devote thelfl. selves to the redemption of their pledges. What was wan' ted was that there should be union in the Government it• self, clear apprehension of the purpose it bad in view, and resolute determination to strive fer the attainment of that purpose. But it was also necessary that the country should be upon its guard against indirect methods of oppositiors for diverse methods would probably be adopted for the purpose of baffling and frustrating a movement which it was felt difficult to confront with an open and frank resistance. Subsequently a deputation represent- ing the Trades Congress presented a memorial in favour of the extension of the household franchise to the counties. After hearing Mr. Broadhurst, MT., Mr. Burt, M.P., Mr. Arch, and other members of the deputation, Mr. Gladstone replied. He said that if his mind had been in any doubt an to the universality of the desire for the extension of the oc- cupation franchise to the counties of the three kingdoraS, and for its extension upon principles reco&nising the equality of the three nations bound together under one con' stitution, the deputation would have done much to remove that doubt. He believed that there were no surer supporter,' of the rights, claims, and privileges of all classes of the country than those who constituted what was called the working classes. The Government were conscious Of the work they were undertaking, and were determined te make use of every resource lying legitimately at theit command for the prosecution of that work; yet after all it was national opinion, manifested by constitutional means, which alone eoald give them the power requisite to enable them to overcome the patent and hidden obstacles which lay in their way. By patent obstacles he meant direct or position, and by hidden obstacles he meant indirect oppos" tion. Replying to a deputation from the Metro" politan Liberal Associations, the Premier said he must frankly admit that the condition of London with regard tO municipal and local government was nothing less than a scandal, the responsibility for which belonged not to alai party or personage particularly, but to the Legislature of the country. What the Government wanted was assistance in their endeavours to enable Parliament to overtake ifo,. work, and he urged the deputation to watch with the utraoSt jealousy all the means that might be adopted in some quer' term for preventing Parliament from overtaking its work. The Government would do their part. They had certahl powers which they would not fail to use, with whateve! privileges the House of Commons allowed them, in respeCE to the progress and arrangement of business.
