div.head: FOOTB ALL.
div.p: FOOTB ALL.

Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street, Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

WARRINGTON V. WIGAN. The second team of the Wigan contingent journeyed to Warrington on Saturday lest to play the return match with the above club in anything but plea- sant weather, and like its predecessor the game was ash nrt one, but short as it was the Wigan youngsters succeeded in gaining their fifteenth consecutiva victory. Score—Wigan, one goal, three touchdowns, and two dead balls Warrington, one touchdown, two 'ead balls, and one touch-in-gcal WARRINGTON V. WIGAN —On Saturclas, the Warrington first team journeyed to Wigan to play their return match with Wigan first. The weather was of the most stormy nature, and only a moderate number of spectators assembled in the field. The game was commenced in torrents of rain, and the ground was in such a state as to prevent anything like good football being played. Wigan started with the hill against them, and for a time Warrington kept uncomfortably near the horns goal line, but at length the ball was got away and worked up the field. Wigan scoring a dead ball. When about fifteen Minutes had been playel, and the players were drenched to the skin, hostilities were abandoned, the home team having the best of the game by a dead ball to love LOWTON V. PAGEFIELD (lAT). On Saturday last Lowton visited Wigan to play the concluding match of the season with gagefield. and although the rain came down in torrents it was Weed to play 15 minutes each way. At tine call of half-thne Use score stood—Pagefield one try (gained by W. Whittaker) and three minor points, to Lowton nil. In the second half Pagefield scored One minor point, and Lowton one minor point. Pageffeld could only muster a poor team, owing no doubt to the weather and also to the fact that some of their best players are on the sick list. There can be no doubt that when nine • good players ape missing from a team it makes a vast deal of difference in the scores. Pagefield let have only played eight matches this season, but have won five, drawn two (both in their favour) and lost one. The second team have played 15 Matches, and have won 10, drawn one, and lost four.
DARESBURY HIGHWAY BOARD.

A special meeting of the Daresbnry Highway Board was held in the Sessions House on Thursday afternoon. There were present: Messrs. Edward Greenall (chairman), Joseph Cliff (vice-chairman) James Knowles, Wm. Wilkinson, P. Percival, J. Yarwood, W. Bradford, J. Baguley, J. Parr, T. Bennett, P. Derbyshire, H. Houghton, D. T. Baguiey, C. T. Whitley, T. S. Burgess, W. Turner, J. Handley, W. Long, H. Lina.ker (clerk), and J. Datbyshire (surveyor.) THE SHIP CANAL SCHEME AND THE BOARD'S DISTRICT.

A report which had been prepared by the Surveyor in Order to see how far the proposed ship canal will affect the various roads in the Board's district was read. In the re- Port the SuavEvon stated that in the township of Acton Grange the roads affected would be Bellhouse-lataa and the toad leading from Grange Green farm to Baxter's turn- bridge. The former road was proposed to be crossed by arches, 25f I. span and 15ft. high. The latter road would seem to pass under the high-level viaduct. In the township Of Walton Inferior, the road under Walton Arches, it seeme4, would ,be unaltered, and also that crossing Morley Common; both roads being crossed by bridges of 25 feet span and 15 feet high, carrying the new railway. A new road was shown on the plans as com- mencing near the Stag Inn, and running into Warrington tht ough Arpley meadows. This road would effect a saving or distance of about 440 yards. The length of the Warrington and Chester main road was to be stopped, and the proposed ar- ---ran.g tnPrlt would.give a small decrease in the length of -road-to be maintained by the Board. Ample facilities, he thought, Should be here afforded in order that the traftle might not be delayed in crossing the canal and the intended lock work. With respect to the highways in this township, he thought there was insufficient road accommodation, as for instance, there ought to be better accommodation between Baronet Farm or any houses which might be left on the north-west side of Mill Pool and VVilderapool, also between the latter place and Higher Walton. Tom Payne's Bridge was to be sheduled, and he concluded would be abolished. It was not shown how the Warrington and lklerthwich road at Twenty-steps Bridge would be carried over the canal, but stringent provision should be made to avoid the delaying of the traffic, as there might be a swing bridge. In the township of Latchford Acker's-lane and Common-lane Would be partly done away with next the railway, and connected by a new road, from which will run a cross road passing under the deviation railway which is proposed to be carried over this read by an arch 2511. span and 151 t. high. He thought that the span of this arch ought to be 30ft. This alteration would slightly increase the length of road to be maintained by the Board. It was not shown by what means the road „ would cross the canal, but presumably by a swing bridge. Knutsford-road erould be stopped, and a new road sub- stituted which would run parallel with the canal, and lead into the real now passing Latchford Station. This would involve an increase in the leneth of the road of about 200 yards. The road by Latchford Station would be unaltered in level, and the railway would be carried over it by means Of an arch 351 t. span and 1611. high. Cross-lane was shown with the level unaltered, and was to be crossed by means of an arch 601 t. span and 4911. high, it being a portion of the intended high level railway viaduct crossing the canal. It was not indicated how Cross-lane would pass over the Canal. In the township of Grappenhall the Thelvrall-road would be stopped as the new locks were shown to absorb a portion of it, together with a portion of Bradshaw's-lane. The new road was shown to take place at the Thelwall-road and to join Cross- lane. The railway would pass over this road near to its junction with Cross-lane Isy Askew Bridge, 60 feet span and 48 feet high, it being a portion of the high level rail- way viaduct. The alteration would increase the length of road between Thelwall and Latchford. Bradshaw's-lane was intended to be blocked. The road froln the Dog and Dart Inn to Lymn, now going over the railway at an in- cline of one in twenty-two, was intended to pass under the railway at a decline of one in thirty, the road being lowered 21i feet and crossed by an arch 85 feet span and 16 feet high. In conclusion he stated that about 71- miles of the intended canal would run through the Board's district, and that he thought if the tanal were made the Board would Obtain over at least a portion of their district advantages Which would in some degree compensate for the disturb- ances and hindrances to traffic which would of necessity follow if that valuable addition were made to the district. —After considering the report and the various plans placed before them, the Board came to the conclusion that many of their roads would be seriouslysaffected, and in order to obtain a number of modifications and to secure certain altera- tions and rights, it was resolved to enter notice of opposi- tion to the scheme, the notice to be withdrawn if the re- quirements of the Board are acceded to. There was no other business of public importance, and the Board rose.

A collection was made at the NEWTON CRICKET AND BOWLINO CLUB. general meeting of the members of this club has beennntia •cently held at the Pied Mill Hotel, Newton. Mr. B. B. Glover presided. The report for the past year was read and Passed. Messrs. Thomas Stone, W. H. Hindley, and W Dudgeon were elected captains for the ensuing year; Dagnall was appointed bowling captain in the room of Mr. George Hilton, retired; Mr. Thomas Stone was elected pre- sident, and Mr. James Fairdough (Warrington) vice-presi- dent. Mr. W. H. Hindley was appointed corresponding secretary, and Mr. J. A. Gowenlock financial secretary. PLAYING AT PITCH AND Toss AT EARLESTOWN: CAUTION TO ABSENT DEFENDANTS.—At the Newton Patty Sessions on Saturday last, Robert Taylor, and Patrick Duggan, were charged with playing at pitch and tees at EarleStoWn, on the 20th instant. The defendant Taylor pleaded guilty, and Duggan did not appear.—P.C. Hunt deposed that about 20 minutes past three on the afternoon of the previous Sunday, he saw the defendants and another man gambling at pitch and toss in Legh-street, Barlestown. Before they found out who he was he got close to them and picked up a Penny.—Taylor was fined 5s and costs and Duggan 7s 6d and costs, the fine being increased in the latter case because the defendant did not appear. EAHLEsTOWN CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE So- crwry.—A very pleasant gathering in connection with the Barlestown branch of the Church of England Temperance Society, was held in the Infants' Schoolroom, Market-street, on Wednesday evening, when there was a crowded attend- ance. The chair was occupied by the Rev. H. E. Smith (curate), who expressed the pleasure it gave him to see so many present, and went on to say that strong drink was the source of all evil—or nearly so—that existed in this coun- try. He advised all to work hand in hand and to do their utmost to remedy the present sad state of things. A capital Programme of songs, recitations, &c., wasthen gone through, in excellent style, the meeting concluding with a hearty vote of thanks to the Chairman.

Queen's Chambers, Market-street, Manchester, write (Jan. 31st) : As is usual for the week in which the settlement occurs, busi- ness has been somewhat restricted, and nothing has occurred to enliven the market generally to counteract this customary in- fluence. On the contrary, the prevailing movements have been downward, and this, as is natural, does not conduce to the transaction of brisk business, and some trouble in settlement has further depressed prices in the several stocks affected. Foreign funds, however, have been fairly strong, and several substantial advances are to be recorded, whilst the cases in which lower prices are marked are few. Higher I Spanish 2/ to 2, Egypt unified , ditto pref. \ ]fr. ditto Dalva Sanleh 1, Russian t, Turkish stamped to t, Italian . and Peruvian Lower Argentine Public Work I, and Mexican 3 per cent. Mexican Railways, without showing any violent fluctuations, are lower (it to ttr. The trams return was again a decrease, and though not worse than expectation, the mice receded. Mis- cellaneous shares have undergone considerable revision in quotations, a number being consequent on quotations being now ex dividend; but apart from these, the changes are numerous. The balance of alterations is on the whole pretty fairly maintafned, only Telegraphs showing a decidedly weaker tendency and lower prices without corresponding favourable changes to counteract them. The aggregate of mis- cellaneous business reported is but small and of a general character.

SUDDEN DEATH AT ST. HELENS.-0a Monday last a man named Richard Boardman, Who lived at 18, High-street, St. Helens, died from the effects of a fall. On the 21st ult. it ' seems he was crossing the railway when he stumbled and I fell. The leg was fractured, and although he received medical attention he became worse and died on Monday. A Suspicious InnunEn.—On Thursday, at the St. Helens Police Court, an old man, named Michael Mac- donald, was charged with having been in an outhouse, in the occupation of James Johnson, of Eccleston Park, on the previous night for unlawful purposes —P.C. Millington stated that at 20 minutes to 12 o'clock the previous night, he found the prisoner in a closet at the back of Mr. John- son's house. He brought him to the police office, and on searching him found in his possession a piece of iron which could be used as a lever, and also a key. The officer also added that for a few nights previously Mr. Johnson had net been sleeping in the house.—The prisoner stated that he had not gone into the closet for any criminal purpose, but in answer to the Bench the officer dated that prisoner attempted to prevent him from entering the cleset.—A remand for a week was granted to allow of inquiries being made.

THE COTTON STRIKE AT GOLBORNE. The workpeopla formerly employed by Messrs. John Brewis and Company, manufacturers, Parkside Mills, Gol- borne still remain out on strike against the proposed reduc- tion Of 10 per cent. in their wages. We understand that the firm have offered to reduce the reduction from 10 to a per cent., but this offer meets with very little, if any, favour from the hands. Another formal meeting of the latter was held on Monday afternoon, When there were about 50 per- sons present, representing the whole of the workpeople. The meeting pledged themselves to still further act unitedly and not to give way only on the old terms, viz., the with- drawal of the notice of the reduction. This appears to be the general feeling of the strike-bands, and sso far as ap- pearances go, it seems to be the only grounds upon which work will be resumed.

WARRINGTON LIBERAL ASSOCIA- TION. ADDRESS ON "THE COUNTY FRANCHISE.: WHY IT SHOULD BE EXTENDED." The fourth of the series of lectures in connection with the Warrington Liberal Association, was delivered by Mr. James Jackson, of the National Reform Union, in Wycliffe Hall, Bewsey-street, on Wednesday evening, on the subject of "The County Franchise Why it should be extended." Councillor Charles Broadbent presided, and there were also On the platform Mr. F. A. Roberts, Mr. Henry Roberts, and Mr. Bounell. A letter was read from Ziba Armitage, Esq., J.P., regretting his inability to attend the meeting teeing to Multitudinous engagements. The Ceteanatex (who was cordially greeted) said he had great pleasure in introducing to their notice Mr. James Jackson, who would give them a lecture on a subject which was exciting a great deal of interest at the present time. Much had been said lately of the effect which the new rule regarding elections would have, and . that new modes and influences would have to be brought into action at their elections in some respects different frem their old-fashioned methods. He believed that no influence that they were able to bring to bear would be of greater advantage then that of having lectures on important political subjects from time to time, in order that electors might have the beet means of thoroughly under- standing the great political questions which were brought before Parliament ; and that there was a need for that political education he thought was shown by the large meeting that was held at the Public Hall on the previous night in favour of what was called fair trade, but what might more properly be termed in favour of protection. (Hear, hear.) If he understood the argument of Mr. Ecroy,d, the central part of that argument was that they should have free trade with their colonies, bet that they should not be at liberty to buy the produce of other coun- tries unless the latter were willing in return to take their manufactures. Now, they as free-traders believed that they ought to hold themselves free to buy the produce of other countries, and that they should be able to go into the cheapest market for whatever they wanted, and that they should not be shut out from the markets of the world whether other countries were wise or foolish enough to adopt a policy of protection on their part or not. (Hear, hear.) Coming to the subject immediately before them, that of the county franchise, he thought they had made up their minds longeago thet it was simply a matter of justice, and that it must be conceded. (Applause.) He should think that the only difficulty which Mr. Jeckson would feel that night would be that the arguments is fevour of that reform were so obvious that he would find the ground almost too easy and too plain sgiling for him. , (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Even their political opponents did not go so far as to contest the justice of the claim for householders in the counties to have a vote, and yet they heard on all hands that this measure was to be hotly con- tested and opposed in Parliament. It seemed to him that there could be no question whatever that the householder outside the boundaries of the borough was, as usual, en- titled to the vote as the householder within the borough. , (Applause.) At one time it might be sold that education had not sufficiently gime into the country, that the people ought not to have votes because they were not sufficiently educated, but they as Liberals could see, and they believed that the best education a man could have was to be possessed of a vote. (Hear, hear.) The best preparation he could have in political education was himself to have the right of exercising the franchise—(hear. hear,)—but there was a special reason why the dwellers in country districts should have a vote at the present time, because in consequence of the new educational law in operation there were great changes made as regarded the schooling of their children. (Hear, Lear.) He was not goitag to say whether too much or too little education was given—he would not enter on that point—but he would say that householders of the countieti ought to have a vote in what affected them so much, viz., the education of their children. (Applauee.) He then ' called upon Mr. Jackson to deliver his lecture. The LEcertingn, in commencing, remarked that that was the first time he had addressed a meeting on this question in a Parliamentary borough, and he was so accustomed to speak at meetings composed for the most part of persons not in the possession of the franchise that it might be with some difficulty that he would remember throughout his ob- servations that night that most of his hearers were in pos- sion of a vote. With reference to a remark which fell from the chairman that the arguments in favour of the extension of the county franchise were so clear and forcible, and that he should find it too plain sailing, he wished to say that if he used in his subject that night any facts and arguments which were very familiar to them he must ask them to bear with him because in the audience which he frequently ad- dressed, in the county of Northamptoashire, where he lived, he bad found it necessary to use very plain language, and very simple facts, as he felt that in every audience there were some minds like his own which liked to have things very plainly stated so that they could take them in and understand them. (Hear, hear.) Although the majority of those present were in possession of the franchise, he thought he could appeal to them for symp tthy, coming as he did from a district where they had not the seine broad franchise. Those present were in possession of a right, a privilege, or gift, call it what they liked, which they in county districts did not possess. That question of the extension of the franchise to counties was very prominently. before the country, and it would engage the attention of the House of Commons withia the next few weeks; he hope.' it would engage the attention of the House of Lords within the next few months. (Hear, hear.) Therefore he thought it was most desirable that they should get a clear view of the question in all its bear- ings and a complete understanding of it, because it was just possible that they might have a dissolution of Parliament, and they, the electors of Warrington. would be asked to give their opinion on the policy of the Government, and more especially in reference to this question. He should speak from the point of view of one who had not a vote. They might take an interest in politics, but they bad no power of giving an adequate expression of their opinions. In many of their shoe manufactories in Northamptonshire there was. as great an interest tine in political questions as there was in the towns in Lancashire. Well, the shoemakers of many places, although taking a great interest in politics, yet when elections came they had to stand up and see their better-to- neighbours vote, and to decide who was to represent them in the House of- Commons. The reason why those living in country districts had not the same political or voting power as they had in the towns—he meant Parliamentary boroughs —was owing to the difference in the electoral law. The law which existed in Parliamentary ' boroughs and cities regulating the election of members of Parliament was widely different from the law regulating the electoral power at counties, and the dif- ference was this. In Warrington, roughly speaking, every male householder every twelve months, from the 15th July in one year to the 15th of July in the succeeding year. who was not a criminal, nor a pauper, or foreigner, every male householder, however humble his dwelling might be and however lowly his occupation, was entitled to ba placed on the list of voters to vote in the election of a member of Par- liament. It was widely different in the counties. There householders might vote it was true, but the house in which the man lived must be of a particular value, and the actual wording of the Act of Parliament regulating county voting enacted that every house or premises of the land which a roan occupied should be of the rateable value of £l2 per annum. He knew what that meant in Northamptonshire and the Midland counties. it ,neant that a man's house should be rested at £l5 to £1.5 per year, and they knew perfectly well that the vast majority of their fellow-country- men, not only in his own dirtrict but in theirs, lived in houses the rents of which were not so high as that. (Hear, hear.) The main difference then was that in the towns every householder, however poor his cottage might be and however low Me rent might be, was entitled to a vote, but in the counties he must live in houses of a certain value. That WAS the difference which existed at the present time, and _

WARRINGTON CORPORATION AND THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.

From the proceedings of the Corporation Committees we fin 4 that the River's Committee met on the 11th, 13th, and 21st January, and conferred with the General Purposes Committee upon the Ship Canal Scheme. On the 13th January the General Purposes Committee passed a recom- mendation that the promoters of the Ship Canal Bill be asked to adopt a schema suggested by the borough surveyor for doing away with the Wilderspool level crossing. A further recommendation was adopted that the bill of expenses in connection with the opposition to the Bill be taxed as required by the Statute. On the the 21st January the same committee passed the following recommendation : " That, Mr. Wolfe Barry be requested to advise as to the feasibility et an eight-foot draught of water being obtained and maintained in the river between Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Company's works and the" eastern boundary of the Borough, and as to the effect upon the river of taking away the water from it required for the purpose of the canal, and what provision is necessary and practicable for pre- venting any injary to the river, and to avoid any inter- ference with the sewers, or other prejudical effect to the town."

was mentioned by Mr. Cory in the opening of his address— partly sad and partly pleasing. He had not the slightest I doubt that they all of them felt the greatest regret in part- ing with the gentlemen whom they had been so accustomed to see in their Parish Church. (Applause.) That the regret was universal was evidenced he thought by two sr three things; firstly, by the great number of persons who had subscribed to the testimonial, and secondly, by the value of the testimonials themselves. It showed that the feeling of regret was great amongst a great number of the persons in connection with the Parish Church. But mixed with this feeling of regret there was a sense of gratification that the services of Mr. Cory aad Mr. Mitchell had been appreciated to the extent of which the testimonials were an evidence. Of course, in common with themselves, he dare say those two gentlemen also felt regret at leaving them. They were starting, as it were, into the world afresh; they were leaving a sort of home that they had made to themselves, where they were beginning to make themselves appreciated; and they were leaving them, as he had said, to enter into the world afresh. A cloud was over them, and over those who they were going to leave, but every cloud had a silver lining. (Applause.) Let them hope that the silver lining would soon make itself evident, and that when the cloud had passed away those two gentlemen might find themselves in spheres of increased usefulness in the work which they had so much at heart. With Mr. Pierpoinr, they all wished them God speed, and hoped that their future might be happy. (Applause.) This, he thought, was their united feeling on this occasion. He had no doubt that it would be deeply gratifying to Mr. Cory and Mr. Mitchell when, in the future, their minds reverted to that large assembly and the enthusiasm which characterised the proceedings. (Applause.) Mr. R. PIERPOINT said that at the risk of wearying them he must again rise to address them, and it made an old bachelor like him nervous to have to address so many ladies. (Laughter.) He was more used to addressing large numbers of men than women, so that they must excuse him if his nervousness made him a little remiss. He had now to present a testimonial to their friend Mr. Mitchell. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Mitchell, they knew, had had charge of the Bank-street Mission, and he had done his duty there, work- ing most assiduously for its advancement. He had in- creased his schools largely, and, he believed, the school under Mr. Mitchell's care was flourishing. Mr. Mitchell would not consider that he (the speaker) was entering upon theological subjects when he said that he (Mr. Mitchell) was an example that evening of " justification by works." (Applause.) He was sorry to say that in church he (the speaker) had sometimes behaved badly, because he sometimes thought he would not be wasting his time alto- gether if when the sermon was going on he read Job. (Laughter.) Job was a great favourite of his, and he was never tired of reading him but when Mr. Mitchell was in the pulpit Job could not hold him. (Laughter.) He had tried it again and again, but it was no use. He was sure they all wished Mr. Mitchell success, and although they regretted the necessityeof that meeting, yet granted the necessity they were glad to show that they appreciated the endeavours of Mr. Cory and Mr. Mitchell for the well-being of those with whom they had come in contact. (Applause.) Mr. Pierpoint then formally made the presentation. The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL, in accepting the testimonial, said that for the second time during his ministerial career he rose to receive from those among whom he had minis- tered a token of their esteem and goodwill. It recalled to his mind what took place three years ago. He remembered two never-to-be-forgotten meetings on two successive nights, , when he parted from those friends he had met in the dis- charge of his duty, who were friends then, and he thanked God, were friends now. (Applause.) The pain ha expe- rienced at parting from those whom he had learned to love caused him to desire that he should never experience the same pain again, and he had had almost a desire that he might never be called upon to go through the ordeal of such a testimonial, but he acknowledged that he was not wise in so desiring, and that he had not succeeded in that respect he thought that that enthusiastic gathering VIAS a sufficient indication. But at the same time he would say that he thought such meetings as that, although they were painful in the extreme, and although they were a trying ordeal and one's feelings might be harrowed, they were a very grave necessity. And that for two reasons. In the first place they showed them unmistakably that those among whom they ministered appreciated their weak, imperfect efforts and labours—and he might say that the parishioners of a parish and the congregation of a church were fit and proper judges in this respect—(applause)— and secondly, such a meeting as that was a necessity as an encouragement, for they mast know how many and how serious were the discouragements in their own lives. The discouragements that arose to the priest in the discharge of his duties were neither few nor far between. Therefore they needed encouragement, and something to stimulate them and send them forward with renewed energy and zeal to overcome the obstacles and difficulties which came in their path. He thanked them all most heartily, not merely for that very beautiful testimonial and the purse of gold and the other gifts which they had been pleased to present to him, but for the sympathy, the affection, and the love which those presents expressed and indicated. (Applause.) Ile would tell them something in confidence, and he hoped they would keep it a secret. That was that he intended to keep those presents as heirlooms, and to hand them down to his children. (Laughter.) But with this proviso,if he ever had any. Perhaps they would think that that was a pretty speech for art unmarried clergyman, but the Church of England allowed her clergy to marry, and it was a good thing for the Church and also for the nation, and it was a good thing for the priests themselves, especially those who were not well up in the art of housekeeping. (Laughter.) Ile remembered leaving the beautiful scenery of the south of Devonshire and journey- ing to Warrington, how as tne smoke grew denser and denser and the chimneys more numerous his heart sank within him, and as the rain came down in torrents he said to him- self, "If it knows nothing else in Warrington it knows how to rain." (Laughter.) He felt something like the Queen of Sheba felt when she oisited Solomon—that he had no more spirit left in him. But it was not because of the beauty and the glory of Warrington, nor the ease and the luxury of a palace ;he would leave them to judge. (Applause.) There was a piece of poetry whieh said that "he who fights and runs away may live to fight another day." He desired to run away, and leave the fighting to some more pugnacious individuals. (Laughter.) But he said to himself, "Some one must try to do the work in this parish, and why should not I? " and instead of running away he tarried. He was thankful that he remained in Warrington, that he had been numbered among their pa,stors in connection with the Parish Church, and that he was now enrolled amongst the number of their friends. (Applause.) He Was also thankful that he had gained useful and beneficial experience among an honest, a sympathetic, and a plain-speaking people. (Ap- plause.) That experience, he felt, would serve him all the days of his life. He might say that there was another kind of experience he had gained which might be very useful to him sometime, and that was a very varied experience of housekeeping. (Laughter.) He had often heard people say " dirty, smoky Warrington," and be had no doubt it was dirty and smoky. But it would be a mistake to judge the people of Warrington by external appearances. Warrington was really better than it looked. He could not pass on to make any further remarks without making an allusion to his brother worker, Mr. Cory. He was glad to say he had much to thank Mr. Cory for; in fact, if Mr. Cory had been a disagreeable, cantankerous curate he would have been more inclined to run away than he was. Mr. Cory had made bachelor life so pleasant and attractive—the fair ladies must be merciful to him—that he might now be forced into the unhappy position of marrying in haste and repenting at leisure. (Langhter.) They would begin to think that he was long-winded, but his tongue had been silent so long— (laughter and applause)—he was going to say that his tongue had grown very lone, and it had had plenty of time to grow long lately. (Laughter.) But what he wanted to express was that he had two feelings in his mind, that was to say there was a feeling of 'regret and a feeling of thank- fulness, of regret that so little had been accomplished, and of thankfulness that that which had been done had been duly appreciated. They had been bearing and considerate wt h him, and be would say this, that any priest in the Church of England who did his duty faithfully and man- fully would net fail to gain the respect and esteem of those in the Church of England, and even those outside the pale of the Church. (Hear, hear.) But if a priest was elevated, and thought himself hotter than others, if he forgot the baptismal covenant that "all men are alike in the sight of God," his influence in the parish or in the district would be nil. If the people saw that a priest was guilty of dandyistn and truckling to the rich he would never be respected, nor would he ever succeed in doing Christ's.blessed work among Christ's blessed people. (Applause.) If there was one thing that gave him greater joy than another in connection with the testimonial, it was because he was conscious that a large number of those who had contributed was composed of the poor of the district of the Parish Church. He could not express the thanks he felt, and the best way to show them would be to give his friends the infliction of coming down occasionally to see them. (Applause.) As London was only 4 hours' or 4i hours' journey from Warrington, it would give him no trouble, but the greatest possible pleasure, to come and see them when- ever the opportunity presented itself. And as London was now the great city to which all the tribes of the earth go up, he hoped to occasionally see some of the Warrington people at St. Luke's, Kentishtown. (Applause.) Mr. CAWLEY, in a few remarks, said they were all very sorry to part with Mr. Cory and Mr. Mitchell, whom they respected and esteemed. On behalf of the committee, he thanked all those who had contributed towards the testi- monial.

PRESENTATIONS TO THE WARRING- TON PARISH CHURCH CURATES. A large meeting was held its the Co-operative Hall, Sankey- street, on Wednesday evening, for the purpose of making presentations to the Rev. F. W. Cory and the Rev. A. M. Mitchell, mates of the Parish Church, Warrington. Each lof the reverend gentlemen was made the recipient of a handsome illunahrated address and a purse containing 40 guineas. The number of persons who subscribed to these was 305. In addition to the presents just mentioned, hoe/- ever, there were also testimonials from Bank-street Mission, Crossley-street Mission, boys' Sunday school, girl? Sunday school, and bible classes, the subscribers to these numbering 350, thus making a total of 715. To the Rev. A. M. Mitchell, Bank-street Mission presented a handsome case containing bronze candlesticks, knife, tray, and inkstand, a statuette of parian marble entitled "Fount of mercy ;" the boys' Sunday school presented a stationery cabinet; and the young men's bible class an albem. To the Rev. F. W. Cory, Crossley-street Mission presented a silver ink- stand; the girls' Sunday school presented a stationery case with inkstand, letter scales, and other writing requisites; and there were also a number of private presents The addresses, which were similar with the exception ot the names of the gentlemen to whom they were presented, ieed as follows:—" Reverend and dear sir,—We, the par- ishioners, in our several callings, either as Sunday school teachers, scholars, or worshippers of this church, learn with sincere regret that your labours amongst us must very soon terminate, and we desire to express our high appreciation of your unwearied ministrations during your sojourn amongst us. We have found in you a genial, faithful friend, as well as a kind and sympathising pastor, and shall always have a grateful memory of your earnestness and zeal in all things that have tended to deepen our spiritual life. In bidding you farewell, we pray God to bless your future labours, and beg your acceptance of the accoinpenying purse of-gold, with the good wishes of the parishioners and friends whose names are annexed.—Warrington, 30th January, 1884." The names then followed. Mr. R. T. Fairclough presided, and there were also on the platform Alderman Webster, Mr. R. Pierpoint, Mr. Ellison, Mr. W. Gill, Mr. Pearse, Mr. Cawley, Mr. Coates, and Mr. Tauranac. The CRA.IRMAN, in opening the proceedings, said he had just had a note placed in his hands which explained in a few words the steps which led to their meeting together that evening, and he would read it to them. It said: "At a meeting of a number of the parishioners held on the Bth January in ,Mr. Naylor's room, Howley, it was decided to raise a testimonial to the Rev. F. W. Cory, and the Rev. A. M. Mitchell, as a tribute of esteem and in recognition of the services done by them during teeir curac,es in Warrington. No sooner was it made known that a testimonial was to be raised to the curates than a number of ladies and gentlemen volunteered to raise subscriptions, and they met with such hearty response that in no less than a week £7O was sub- scribed from both young and old, rich and poor, in sums varying from a penny upwards. (Applause ) The number of subscribers to the general testimonial is 365 ',equal to the number of days in a year), besides the subscribers to separate testimonials from Crossley-street Mission, Bank- street Mission, boys' Sunday school, girls' Sunday school, and bible classes, which would make about 350 more, mak- ing a total of 715. The total amount subscribed is £9l lie., which, after deducting expenses, will enable us to present to each of the reverend gentlemen a purse containing 40 guineas." (Applause.) He need not say, after reading the foregoing, that Mr. Cory and Mr. Mitchell were two of the best curates they had ever had at the Parish Church. (Applause.) And he thought it would have been a very great mistake if the pariebieners had not shown their gratitude to them for the manner in which they had done their work. (Applause.) They had visited the sick and the poor in the parish; in fact, they had never had curates who had worked so hard in that respect. (Applause.) They might be seen constantly going about in the poor districts doing all in their power to alleviate distress, and the work they had done in the schools was incalculable. (Applause.) He would not take up their time by making any further observations, but would call upon Mr. Pierpeint to make the presentation. Mr. R. PIERPOINT said that he felt highly honeured that they had seen fit to commission him to do the work of making the presentation. It came now and then upon him to address large meetings on controversial matters, when many who were present that night might differ from him, but it was a pleasure to him to know that he had not now to address to them one single controversial werd. About anything he would say respecting Mr. Cory and Mr. Mit- chell he was sure that there was not one lady or gentle- man in that room who would disagree with him. He was old enough to remember many curates. (Laughter.) He was old enough to remember Mr. Hamilton, and he was old enough to remember the time when Mr. Powys was removed to the Isle of Man; but from what he knew of the two gentlemen to whom they had come to do honour that evening, he had not seen two curates in the Parish Church who had conducted the services in that church and the various duties appertaining to their curacies in so able and thorough a manner as those gentlemen had done. (Applause.) Mr. Cory had been with them three years, and they regretted very much that he should leave them, but they sincerely hoped that whenever he went or wherever he went success might go with him. (Applause.) He supposed he must address himself at present to Mr. Cory, because he had two strings to his bow, and he must play one string at once. eLaugh ter.) Mr. dory had charge of thrtGrossley-street Mission, and he had greatly increased the congregation there. He had also increased the attend- ance at the schools. A curate's life was not always a bed of roses, and he apprehended that a curate's life was not more a bed of roses when it was in a large manufacturing town like Warrington. In some places it might be an easy life; in a place like Warrington it was not an easy life. He would meet with the appreciation of his parishioners who would be glad to see him, but he would also meet with people who would not waat to see him. He believed that Mr. Cory had duly carried out his duty with respect to visiting both these classes of people, and the large gather- ing that evening was a witness. He might say that he had given te no subscription with greater willingness than when he gave to the subscription which was the cause of that evening's meeting. He might tell them before he made the presentation that the 40 guineas which constituted the , money part of the testimonial were contained in purses worked by certain ladies, who, he was sorry to say, did not wish him to divulge their names. He rather apprehended that there must be some feeling akin to the anonymous gifts that curates sometimes got from the ladies of their congregations—(laughter)—such as, he had been told, slip- Pers—(laughter)—andaes had even heard braces. (Renewed laughter.) But ..he never yet heard that a donor of either slippers or braces wished her name to be publicly mentioned. (Laughter.) He thought there mast be some feeling working upon the modesty of these ladies in wishing their names to be kept a secret. The beautiful address which he held, in his hands had been worked" gratis, free, and for nothing," from the personal esteem that was felt for Mr. Cory and Mr. Mitchell by Messrs. Wm. Brooks and Son, of Bewsey Chambers. (Applause.) Turning to Mr. Cory he con- tinued : I have now, Mr. Cory, to present to you not only on my own small behalf, but on the behalf of all that are here now, this puree and this testimonial as a mark of the appreciation and high esteem, and I may say, I think, of 1 affection felt by all of us for you. (Applause.) Wherever you go and- whenever you go, I am sure I am not exceeding my commission when I say, we all wish you success, pros- perity, and God speed. (Applause.) The Rev. F. W. CORY said thet if he broke down that evening he was sure they would make allowance for him, be- cause he was placed in a most novel and trying position. lie had read that when a man had plenty of thoughts in his mind he would be easily able to find words to express those thoughts, but he took it that there was no rule without an exception, and he thought that an occasion like that, when pastor and people were about to be separatai, wholly against their will—(applause)—in accordance with the wishes of the powers that be—he took it that such an occasion might certainly rank among the exceptions to the general rule. As he looked upon the many well-known faces assembled there he felt that he had many thoughts in his mind, and some were sad and some pleasant, but he was sure that that evening he would not be able to say one-tenth of what he wished to say or what he ought to say to them. Egotism was a very bad thing, but on this occasion circumstances compelled him to speak somewhat of himself. Three years ago he came to the good old town of Warring. ton, and he remembered quite well the Monday morning after he had preached his first sermon at the Parish Church —he was told that it was a bad sermon—(laughter)—some- one came to him and said, "I hope you are going to stay with us." That was the first word of welcome he received, but from that time to the present he had received nothing but consideration and kindness from those with whom he had come in contact. He had had the privilege of enjoying the happiness of home life amongst many of them; and he was so often in the family circle that he had come to look upon Warrington as his own home. (Applause.) A little time ago he came across a magazine in which he found an article written by a gentleman who had spent three months in Russia. Restated thet he found in Russia the laity bad great veneration for their clergy, but simply in religious matters. When it came te being associated with them they shunned and spurned them like vipers. How was it in Eng- land ? He was always welcomed with open arms, and he would venture to say that if anything ever did happen to the Church of England in the way of disestablishment or dis- endowment— and be trusted that it might never arrive—if the clergy as a body received the same kindness all the way round as Mr. Mitchell and himself had received at their hands, they would do very well, whether disestablishment or disendowment came. (A pplause.) And now the outsiders would naturally ask "If your circum- stances have been so favourable, why are you on the point of leaving the good old town of Warrington ?" (Applause.) That was the burning question of the day,but he was not go- ing to endanger the tips of his fingers by touching it in any way. (Applause.) This, however, he wished to say, that it should be well understood be felt that while a man might have perfect loyalty to the Rector, Mr. Quekett, he might also show sympathy to the curates. (Loud applause.) He thought if there was anyone who disagreed with him in that opinion, he was wanting in that true independence of which every true ;triton boasted. (Applause.) He thanked the Chairman most heartily for taking the posi ion he had done that night, and he felt indebted to him for coming there and showing that he was not afraid to show sympathy to the curates. (Applause.) He also thanked all those who had been connected with the beautiful testimonial wed the touching address which had been read. (Applause.) Alderman WEBSTER said he thought the feeling prevlent with most of them on that occasion was akin to that which

A vote of thanks was accorded the chairman on the motion of Mr. Ellison, and a similar compliment was paid Mr. Pierpoint on the motion of Mr. Tauranac. At intervals during the evening songs were contributed by Mr. Wallington, Mr. Price Mr. Caulfield, Mr. Fair- clough, and Mr. Pearse, Mr. George Riley ably officiating as accompanist.

THE PAVING OF WARRINGTON STREETS. REPORT BY THE BOROUGH SURVEYOR. The Borough Surveyor, Mr. Thomas Longdiu, submitted the following report to a recent meeting of the Paving and Sewerage Committee:—" Gentlemen,—At your request I beg to.. hand you the following cost of different classes of carriageway paving. It is requisite and essential in all private streets a foundation should be laid to receive the paving, and I know of none cheaper, and for its cost more effective, than the one now in use, viz., hand-pitehed Bur- stone. The following prices are for the setts and paving only, as the foundation will cost the same for either class of paying. The costs are based upon current prices of material. 6-inch best Lonkey Rawtenstall setts, 5s Id per square yard ; 4-inch Newry granite cubes, 5s lid per square yard; 4-inch Scotch granite cubes, 6s 61 per square yard; 4-inch Welsh granite cubes, 5s 104 per square yard. The cost to the owner of property for setts and paving in a street hav4ic, a 22 feet carriage way for a house having a frontage of 4 yards, which is about an average cottage house frontage, would be as follows, viz. :-6-inch Rawten- stall setts, £4 3s 10d; 4-inch Newry cubes, £4 17s 7d ; 4-inch Scotch cubes, £5 78 3d; 4-inch Welsh cubes, £4 1643 d. It may, be taken that with ordinary traffic and repair the life of the setts will be as follows :—Rawtenstall 13 to 16 years, Newry or Scotch granite 15 to 18 years, Welsh granite 30 to 40 vears.—Yours obediently, THOMA S LONGDIN," The Committee have recommended to the Council that the following apportionments of the cost of forming and pav- ing of the following streets be approved :—Furness-street John Bolton, John-street, £3O 16s 8d ; Josiah Furness, Lythgoes-lane £37 8s 4d; Joseph Southern, Foundry. street, £35 Os 9d; John Appleton, £lO4 lb 2d—£2o7 16a 11d. Clare-street : J. E. Wright, Wilson Patten-street, £127 8s U.; Cheshire Lines Committee, £23 12s 9d—£lsl Is 51 'r en-street: T. E. Wright, Wilson Patten-street, £64 19s 81; John Bolton, John-street, £3B ss; John Appleton, builder, £53 28 6c1—£156 78 2d. Upper Ellesmere-street: Robert Dayies and Co., solicitors, £5l 16s 3d; John Appleton, £6O Ils 2d; Peter Knowles, £69 6s 21; Patrick Farrell, Heywood-street, Moss Side, Manchester, £l2O 14s 61; James Strange, Latchford, £4O 3s; The Newton, Haydock, and Golborne Building Society, per Mr. James Adams, Newton-le-Willows, £3O- 158 10d— £381 17s. The following apportionment of the cost of forming and paving Lower Ellesmere-street was also approved by the committee :—Mr. W. S. Pierpoint, Winwick-street, £9B Ils 8d; Mr. Alfred Wright Brundritt, Church-street, £22 5s 7d; Mr. Peers Marsh, Winwick-road £ll is id; the Executors of the late Thomas Porter, £67 14s 101 ; Messrs. Gibson and Son, Church-street, £BO 16s 11d—£260 108 Id. Plans and specifications for the forming and paving of THE SAVAGE ASSAULT AT ST. HELENS.—OG Friday, at Brook-street have been approved by the committee, and the the St. Helens Police Court, Michael Kelly was again Town Clerk has been instructed to eerve the necessary charged with having dune grievous bodily harm to a man notices upon the owners or occupiers requiring them to form and pave such street in accordance with such plans named O'Connor Don, under the circumstances narrated in and specifications pursuant to the Public Health Act. our last issue. It was stated that Don was still in the cottage hospital and unable to attend court. A remand for another week was in consequence granted. A CANTANKEROUS RATEPAYER. —Thomas Haig, who did ' UNJUST VVErortTs AT ST. HELENS —At the St. Helena not appear, was on Friday fined lOs and costs, at the St. Police Court, on Monday, two persons who keep stalls in Helens Police Court, for having caused an obstruction to the St. Helena market-place, named Elizabeth Norbury and the footpath at Sutton by leaving flour bags upon it? The Wm. Boardman, were charged with having had unjust officer who proved the charge said the defendant when told weights in their possession on the 19th ult.—Supt. Johnston to remove his bags said he paid his rates and had as much proved the charges, and the first-named defendant was right to the footpath as anybody. Therefore he would put fined is. and coats and the latter-named Sc, and costs, his bags upon it whenever he chose.

div.head: WARRINGTON LIBRARV AND . MUSEUM.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON LIBRARV AND . MUSEUM.

The Curator of the Library and Museum reports that dur- ing December the visitors to the Museum numbered 2,326,an increase of 44 per cent. compared with December, 1682; that the number of volumes issued to subscribers was 2,230, a decrease of 4 per cent., and that the number issued to readers was 1,210, an increase of 53 per cent. At a recent meeting, the thinks of the Library, Museant, and Arts Cernmittee were ordered to be sent to the donors for the following gifts :—Mr. J. Paterson, Historic Society, vols. 23-4; Anonymous (per Mr. Belmont), a collection of Soutk American Mosses; Mr. Nathan Heywood (Manches- ter), Five Lancashire Tokens of the 17th Century; Mr. James Taylor, spec,inens of seaweed; Itay. J. B. Johnstone (Dumfries), minute book of the Warrington Bible Society, from 1811 to 1819 ; specimen of granite from Criffel ; Mr. William Diggle, specimens of indigo and yellow prussi- ate, bust of Socrates, and maps of Lancashire and Cheshire, 1818; Miss Kendrick, five maps of Lancashire &c., speci- mens of pottery and other remains train Wilderspool, &c. (12 boxes). 53 local pamphlets, 83 local broadside prints, Ste., and 300 miscellaneous pamphlets ; Mrs. Pickmere (weiehpool), specimen of Kanri gun greenstone ornament, two stone implemmts and obsidian, all from New Zealand. The Manchester Free Libraries Committee, Wroe's Sermon on the Countess of Warrington, 1691 ; Mr. John Peers, Molineux's Byrom's Shorthand and local pamphlets; and Mr. Beansont, his Memoir of Hamlet Winstanley, and Chatham Society, vol. 3. A VIOLENT PEW/MR.—John Brown, a young man, wag- on Friday, charged at the St. Helens Police Court with hay, ing refused to quit the licensed premises of James Glarritv, and also with having assaulted P.C. Hurst. The o ificer stated that he had been called into Garrity's house to eject the prisoner, who, however, had to be forcibly put into the street. Whilst being ejected and whilst on the way to the police office Brown, it was stator], kicked the officer.—For refusing to quit he was fined 5s and costs, tend for the as- sault 7s Cid and costs.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

Mr. Parnell arrived in London yesterday afternoon. The hon. gentleman appears to be in very good health. A bulletin issued esterday states Lord Pembroke to be progressing favourably. He may now be considered out of immediate danger. Colonel North, M.P. for Oxfordshire has issued an address to his constituents stating that it is not his intention to offer himself for re-election.

• Mr. Montague Nelson, partner in the firm of Nelson and Co., galatine manufacturers, is mentioned as second Conser- vative candidate for Warwick at the general election. PROPOSED ENLARGEMENT OF THE SUEZ CANAL.—A Central News Port Said telegram says that French engineers are making extensive surveys with a view to the enlarge- ment of the Suez Canal. STRANGE SUICIDE OF A SCHOOL•BOY.—A boy named James Welsh committed suicide at West Bromwich yester- day by hanging himself from the ceiling. The boy's mother said her son had seemed much depressed in consequence of being unable to pass the sixth standard at school. A ver- dict of temporary insanity was returned. The Central News learns that the new North Staffordshire Coal and Iron Company have suspended payment owing to depression in the coal trade. The colliery is one of the largest in the kingdom, employing about 1,200 men, and turning out about 1,000 tons a day with concurrence of creditors for about £lOO,OOO.

SUPPOSED SUICIDE THROUGH MELANCHOLIA.—The body of a woman who lived with her widowed mother at Bacup was found in a lodge by a postman on his round. The de- ceased left home the previous day, and was not seen alive again. She was of a melancholy temperament, and a con- stant reader of novels, and it it is supposed that her mind was unhinged. She had been very moody and silent for a long time. FALL OF A RAILWAY BRIDGE : TRAIN PRECIPITATED INTO THE RIVER: TEN LIVES LOST.—A train from In- dianopolis for New York was on Thursday crossing a bridge over the White River, seven miles from Indianopolis, when

the structure gave way, and the train was precipitated into the river. Four of the railway officials were drowned and six passengers are missing. The river has been very high of late, and the abutment of the bridge had become under- mined by the action of the current. COLLISION ON THE LANCASHIRE AND YORKS HIRE RAILWAY —Yesterday, whilst a goods train was being shunted at Chorlev station, on the Lancashire and York- shire Railway, another goods train from Liverpool for Blackburn having overrun the signal placed against it, came op with slackened speed and dasked into the standing wagons, two of which were smashed to atoms. The Liver- pool engine was greatly damaged, and the line was blocked for about five hours. MYSTERIOUS DISAPPEARANCE OF A CLERGYMAN.—The Salisbury Journal states that much anxiety is felt by rela- tives and friends of the Rev. W. Fenwick, vicar of- Fisherton Delamere, Wiltshire, who hns been missing for more than a month. Mr. Fenwick left Avranche, France, for Cher- bourg, en route for Clevedon, where he was to be joined by his family. He was seen at Cherbourg on the following day, but has not since been heard of, although every effort has been made to discover his whereabouts. GREAT FIRE IN PARIS: ONE HUNDRED FAMILIES ROME- LEss.—A Paris telegram, dated yesterday, says :—A great fire broke out last night in the Cite Joly, near the Cemetery of Pere la Chaise, by which a lace and trimming manufactory, several coal depots, and some shops containing scenic deco- rations for several Paris theatres were destroyed. Five work- men's houses were also burnt down. Two women leapt from the window of a house to save themselves and were se- riously injured. Several children are:missing. About one hundred families have seers rendered homeless. EXTRAORDINARY ROBBERY AND RECOVERY OF A SAFE.

—Early yesterday morning the premises of the Express Dairy Company, Bloomsbury, London, were entered and a large safe containing over £BOO in gold and silver was Mien. Information being given to the police a constable on the beat stated he had seen a pony and cart in the neighbourhood in the morning, and having his suspicions he took the address painted en the latter. As a consequence, a marine store dealer's premises at Stepney were entered, and the missing safe recovered unopened, and the dealer was apprehended. MR. GOSCHEN ON GENERAL GORDON'S MISSION.- -

Speaking at a luncheon given by the Mayor of Ripon yes- terday, Mr. Goschen said the good wishes of every English- man would follow General Gordon in the difficult mission he bad undertaken. All parties would see in him a courageous Englishman, who did not flinch from any danger in the discharge of his duty. They would hope to see him finish his task to the honour of his country. There were more than European interests to be considered in Egypt, and it would be a deplorable sight to see England turn her back upon continued efforts made for the suppres- sion of the slave trade in that very home of slavery—the Soudan. SHOCKING GAMBLING TRAGEDY: WIFE MURDER AND SUICIDE.—A few days ago, at the hour when all fashionable Nice was abroad, a great crowd assembled at the entrance . . .

of the Rue Adelaide, drawn thither by a —crime then just committed, and now already forgotten. A woman, fifty- seven years of age, who had made money by keeping a orivate gambling saloon, had married a young husband. This man made continual demands upon her savings in order to meet his own losses at the roulette table at Monte Carlo, and she at length refused to comply with his requests, which became daily more exorbitant and imperious. In a moment of fury he first cot her throat, and then shot him- self through the heart.

A CLERGY/SAN SUSPENDED FOR DRUNKENNESS: A SAD CASE.—A fortnight since a commission of inquiry was ap- pointed by the Bishop of Chester to inquire into eleven specific charges of drunkenness during the past two years against the Rev. John Wesley Aldom, rector of Thornton Rough, Cheshire. The Commissioners reported that a prima fame case had been made out against the rector. Among the witnesses called in support of the serious charge was Mr. Stephen Williams, M.P., one of the reverend gentleman's parishioners. After the report to the Bishop, the rector of I Thornton Rough submitted himself unconditionally to his diocesan, and his punishment has just been published, namely, suspension from his clerical office for a period of two years. The Rev. John Wesley Aldom is a noted scholar and linguist, and had a brilliant university career. LOST IN A SNOWSTORM: A SAD STORY. The Central News Dundee correspondent telegraphs :—News has only Just reached Dundee that last Saturday six men left the villages of Shodder and Arno- tin, Lewis Island, to look after sheep. Shortly afterwards a blinding snowstorm set in ' and the men were unable to find their way home. Search parties were sent out when the storm abated, and one of the missing men was soma discovered eight miles from home. Ile was much exhausted, and had only kept himself alive by walk ag about. The search was continued, and ultim- ately the other five men were found at Shepherds' Cottage, 20 miles distant. They had managed to keep themselves alive by constant walking, and for food had killed two sheep, part of which they ate raw, using the skins to keep them- selves warm. Other men were out in the same storm, and it is feared must have perished. Search for the bodies is now proceeding.
